studies.applyIt: Take one thing you keep entirely private, not a secret exactly, just something you would rather nobody watched. Ask yourself plainly whether you would still do it if it were visible. If the answer is no, you have learned something useful today without having to do anything about it yet. Sit with the answer before you decide what follows.
studies.explainEasier: God says what he has really banned. Shameful acts, whether people see them or not. Wrongdoing, and pushing past what is yours. He also bans setting up partners with him, and saying things about him that you do not know.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: Not By A Single Hour
studies.meaning: The subject is a community, not a person, which is unusual. Nations are given set terms the way individuals are. The ayah closes both directions at once. When the term arrives it cannot be pushed back, and it cannot be pulled forward either. Early scholars note that the second half is not spare. Fear wants delay and impatience wants arrival, and the passage refuses both. What is described is a fixed point. No amount of alarm or eagerness can move it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Quraysh had watched other Arabian powers rise and disappear. Their own position rested on arrangements a century old at most. This ayah sits between the destroyed towns at the surah's opening and the long run of communities that follows. So it states as a principle what the stories will show as a pattern. No specific occasion of revelation is reported for it.

keyTerms.note: Shares a root with the word for mother, and can mean a group, a generation, a way of living, or even a stretch of time. It names a collective with a shared character, not a population count.
The ordinary commercial word for the due date of a debt. A term in this sense is agreed in advance and known to the one who set it, which is what makes the closing clause follow.
Used here for the smallest unit worth mentioning rather than a measured sixty minutes. With the definite article elsewhere in the Quran the same word names the final Hour itself.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian trade ran on credit with fixed due dates, since goods moved on a caravan and payment waited for its return. A debt with a term was recorded in memory and witnessed, and the date could not be moved by either party once set. Everyone in a Meccan market understood a term as something binding on the person who owed and the person who was owed. The ayah borrows that whole apparatus.
studies.didYouKnow: This sentence comes back almost word for word in at least four other places in the Quran. They are in surahs 10, 15, 16 and 23. It always has the same shape. It is always attached to a warning that people wanted brought forward. It is one of the Book's fixed forms of words, repeated rather than reworded. The classical scholars treat that as deliberate.
studies.theologicalSignificance: History is given a structure without being given a schedule. Communities end on a timetable that is real and set. Every detail of it is withheld. That leaves prediction out of reach and leaves complacency with nothing to rest on. The passage also moves moral attention from persons to groups. A society can build up a condition and reach its term as a whole, whatever its members are doing one by one.

crossReferences.why: The same formulation, given as the reply when they demand to know when the promise will arrive.
Places the identical principle beside the statement that no town was destroyed without a known decree.
Applies the same rule to the individual soul rather than the community, with the same finality.

studies.applyIt: Pick something you have been treating as permanent because it has lasted a long time: a job, a neighbourhood, an arrangement in your family. Say to yourself, plainly, that it has an end date you do not know. Then do one small thing you would do if you knew it was closer than you think. One thing, today, not a plan.
studies.explainEasier: Every people has a set time in front of them. When that time comes, they cannot put it off by even an hour. They cannot bring it forward either.

studies.title: Messengers From Among You
studies.meaning: The condition attached to the messengers is easy to read past. They come from among you, which rules out the arrival of a being of another order and makes recognition possible and refusal harder. Their work is described with a verb meaning to follow a track. Then the response that secures the outcome is given as two things, not one: guarding oneself, and putting right. The second is active and outward. What follows is the Quran's recurring formula about fear and grief, in its conditional rather than its declarative form.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, addressed to the whole human line rather than to one audience, which is why it is phrased as a standing condition rather than an event. The Quraysh had objected that a messenger should be an angel or at least a man of greater means, and the wording answers that objection without arguing with it. No occasion of revelation is reported. The surah is about to give six such messengers in sequence, all of them local men.

keyTerms.note: From the root for following footprints. The messengers are described as tracking the signs rather than composing a message, which puts them in the position of guides reading ground already marked.
The root means to place a shield between yourself and harm. It describes protective care rather than dread, so the usual translation as fear catches only the reason for the action, not the action.
A verb for mending what is broken, used of reconciling parties and of restoring land to use. Paired with self-protection, it turns an inward posture into work done on something outside oneself.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A messenger in Arabia was a known figure with a set role. Tribes sent men to carry terms. His standing came from being one of the people he spoke for. A stranger could not be trusted to deliver a message faithfully. Nor could a stranger be held to account for it afterwards. To say the messengers would be from among you was to describe the only arrangement the audience already found believable.
studies.didYouKnow: The Arabic here uses a strong conditional build. It joins two particles and adds a heavy verb ending. The Quran keeps that form for things presented as certain to happen, not merely possible. The English if or when cannot carry it. In the grammar of the sentence it says: when they do come, and they will.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Prophecy is defined by ordinariness, not by spectacle. A messenger is one of the people he addresses. That makes his life part of the message. It also removes the excuse that the standard was set by a different kind of creature. The safety promised is tied to a pair: guarding and mending. An inward turn is not accepted on its own. What settles the matter is whether anything was repaired.

crossReferences.why: Puts the same condition to jinn and humans together, messengers from among you relating My signs.
Records the objection this wording answers, that people refused to accept a human being as messenger.
Gives the same promise about fear and grief at the moment of the descent to earth.

studies.applyIt: Find one thing in your immediate reach that is broken and could be mended by you this week: a rift with a cousin, a promise you let lapse, a mess in a shared space that everyone steps around. Fix that one. The passage pairs inward care with outward repair, and only one of the two leaves evidence.
studies.explainEasier: God says messengers will come to people from among the people themselves, telling them his signs. Anyone who takes care and puts things right will have nothing to fear. They will not be sad either.

studies.title: Too Proud To Accept
studies.meaning: Two things are named, and they are not the same. The first is calling the signs false, which is a judgement about content. The second is being too great for them, which has nothing to do with evidence. The Arabic build of the second verb implies turning away from a thing as beneath you. Putting them together supports the classical reading. The verdict often follows the posture rather than producing it. A person decides they are above being taught, and the arguments arrive afterwards.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The leading families of Quraysh objected again and again that the message had come to a man of no particular standing. They also objected that its early followers were poor men and slaves. That is an objection about rank, not about content. This ayah sits directly after the promise made to those who guard themselves and put right. It gives the alternative in the same breath. No specific occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form, so it means to pronounce something a lie rather than merely to doubt it. The Quran uses it far more often than the word for disbelief, because it names an act of judgement made aloud.
The same root as the refusal earlier in this surah, in a form meaning to seek greatness for oneself. Followed by the preposition used here, it means turning away from a thing as unworthy.
The ordinary word for the people you keep company with and belong among. Applying it to the Fire describes belonging rather than sentence, which is a quieter and stranger idea than imprisonment.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meccan society was arranged by precedence, and precedence was performed daily. Who spoke first in the assembly. Who was seated where at a feast. Whose guarantee a stranger needed. A man of the leading clans could not be seen taking instruction from someone below him. The whole city would notice. So the cost of accepting the message was social before it was anything else, and it was paid in public.
studies.didYouKnow: The two verbs used here, for denial and for self-magnifying, come back as a pair throughout the Quran. They appear together in this exact combination in several surahs. The classical scholars observe a pattern. The Book almost never treats rejection as a failure of the mind alone. Wherever the refusal is described at length, something about standing or pride is named beside the argument.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Belief is located partly in the will, not wholly in the mind. The passage does not say the deniers lacked evidence. It says they were too great for what they were given. That makes openness a moral condition. The claim is uncomfortable. A person can be perfectly able to follow an argument and still unable to accept it. It explains why the Quran so often appeals to humility before it appeals to proof.

crossReferences.why: The first refusal in the surah, made on exactly these grounds and answered with expulsion.
Says God seals the heart of every arrogant tyrant who disputes the signs without warrant given.
Describes one who hears the signs recited, persists in arrogance as if unhearing, and mocks them.

studies.applyIt: Notice today whether there is anyone whose correction you would find it hard to accept, not because they are wrong but because of who they are. A younger colleague, a sibling, someone whose life you privately consider less successful than yours. Let one such correction land this week without adjusting for the source. That is the whole exercise.
studies.explainEasier: Some people call God's signs lies and are too proud to take them. They are the ones who belong to the Fire. They will stay in it and will not leave.

studies.title: Where Are They Now
studies.meaning: A question is asked that expects no answer, pairing invention against God with denying His signs as the extreme of wrongdoing. Then a phrase early scholars read in two ways: their share of the Book reaches them, meaning either what was decreed for them of lifespan and provision, or their portion as recorded. Both readings agree the point is that nothing is cut short. The scene that follows is the moment of death, and the envoys ask one question. The answer, when it comes, is a confession nobody demanded.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, addressed to people who kept go-betweens at the sanctuary and expected them to speak up for them before God. Their objection to the message was not that God did not exist but that these figures had standing with Him. This ayah does not argue the point. It moves the question to the one moment when the arrangement will be tested. The answer is given by the people who made it.

keyTerms.note: From a root for cutting leather to a pattern before stitching it. A fabrication in Arabic is something cut and assembled to fit, which describes invented religion more precisely than the word lie does.
From the root for paying a debt completely. Death is described as a collection of what is owed in its entirety, with nothing left outstanding, rather than as a seizure or an ending.
The verb for losing one's way, here with the objects doing the straying. What was relied on is described as having wandered off, which is a deliberately undignified word for a failed patron.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Patronage was the security system of Arabia. A man without a strong protector had no recourse if he was robbed or killed. The arrangement was renewed in public, so everyone knew who stood behind whom. Failing to appear when your client called was the worst thing a patron could do to his own name. The scene here uses that vocabulary exactly. The protectors are summoned at the one moment they are needed. They are simply absent.
studies.didYouKnow: The testimony at the end is given by the people themselves, against themselves. No accusation comes before it. The pattern recurs across the Quran's death and judgement scenes. Witnesses are called, records are opened, limbs speak. But the deciding statement is often the person's own. The classical scholars note that the Book almost never needs to convict anyone who has not first agreed.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The falseness of an arrangement is not located in an argument against it. It is located in the moment the arrangement has to work. Whatever a person leans on will either bear weight then, or it will not. The Quran is content to let that be the test. It also insists that nothing owed is held back in the meantime. The lifespan runs its course, the provision arrives, and the reckoning waits. That describes patience on God's part, not indifference.

crossReferences.why: The same scene of arriving alone, with the intercessors relied on described as cut away and lost.
Repeats the question directly, where are your partners now, and receives the same admission of absence.
Shows what was invented straying from them at the reckoning, using the identical verb for going astray.

studies.applyIt: Name, honestly, the thing you assume will hold you up if everything else fails. Savings, a qualification, a particular person, your own competence. Do not disparage it; most of these are real supports. Just ask whether you have quietly promoted it from a help to a guarantee. That distinction is the whole subject of this passage, and it is worth ten minutes.
studies.explainEasier: Nobody does worse than the person who makes up lies about God or calls his signs false. When death comes, they will be asked where the things they prayed to are now. They will admit those things have left them.

studies.title: Each Curses Its Sister
studies.meaning: The instruction is to enter among communities that went before, jinn and human together. That places the newcomers in a line, not in a category. Then comes the behaviour. Each group entering curses the one before it. When all have arrived, the last address the first. They ask for their punishment to be doubled and name them as the cause. The reply grants the doubling and extends it to everyone. It closes with a clause that refuses to explain: but you do not know.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, spoken to a society organised entirely around following. A man's religion, trade, alliances and enemies came with his clan, and the defence that one had simply done what one's people did was the most natural thing a person could say. The surah has already recorded that defence in the mouths of those who appealed to their fathers. Here it is heard again, at the point where it is tested.

keyTerms.note: Communities are given a kinship word, since the noun for a community is grammatically feminine. Calling the earlier group a sister makes the cursing a family quarrel, which sharpens rather than softens the scene.

A verb for successive groups overtaking one another until all are gathered. It carries the sense of a crowd arriving in waves, each catching the one ahead, rather than of a single assembly convened at once.
The word means a fold or a doubling and can indicate more than twice over. The same root gives the Quran's word for multiplied reward, so the vocabulary of increase runs in both directions.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian society had no individuals in the modern sense. You were of a clan, and the clan answered for you: it paid your blood money, avenged your death, and bore your disgrace. Turning on your own people was close to unthinkable, and the poets treat it as the last collapse. A scene in which each generation curses the one that raised it would have struck the first listeners as a description of the end of the world.
studies.didYouKnow: The reply to the request for a double punishment does not deny it. It does not adjust it, and it does not defend the leaders. It grants the doubling and extends it to those who asked. Then it closes with a clause telling them they do not know. The classical scholars note that the Quran often answers a question in judgement scenes by widening it, not by explaining it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Following is not accepted as a transfer of responsibility. Both parties carry a double weight. One weight is for leading. The other is for choosing to be led. The passage refuses to let the second be reduced to bad luck. The cursing back and forth makes a further point. What bound these groups together was never loyalty in the first place. It dissolves the moment there is nothing left to gain from it.

crossReferences.why: Records the same complaint, we obeyed our chiefs and they misled us, with the same request for doubling.
Shows the leaders answering that they had no power over the followers, who chose to respond.
States that close friends will be enemies to each other on that Day, except those who guarded themselves.

studies.applyIt: Think of one thing you do mainly because the people around you do it, and that you would not choose on your own. It does not have to be wrong. Just identify it accurately and say why you do it, without the usual softening. Owning a borrowed decision as yours is not the same as changing it, and it is the part that is actually available today.
studies.explainEasier: God tells them to join the crowds who went into the Fire before them. Each crowd curses the one that came first. The last ones blame the first for leading them there, and ask for their punishment to be doubled.

studies.title: No Advantage Over Us
studies.meaning: The reply completes an exchange begun in the ayah before. The followers had asked for their leaders to receive double. The leaders now answer that the followers hold no advantage over them. Early scholars read the word for advantage in its ordinary sense of surplus or superiority. So the argument is that nobody's position was better and nobody was forced. Then the closing clause gives the standard being applied. Not who led whom, but what each one earned.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a passage built as a courtroom scene with the parties speaking in turn. The audience lived under a system where a clan chief answered for his people. Their conduct was credited or debited to him. This exchange takes that arrangement apart in two sentences. It does so from the chief's side. The leaders are the ones who deny that anybody was carried.

keyTerms.note: The root means what is left over, and the same word elsewhere in the Quran means God's bounty. Here it is used for social advantage, so the two senses sit one root apart.

A verb from eating and hospitality, used across the Quran for punishment arriving. Tasting is direct and personal knowledge, which is why the word replaces any expression meaning to suffer or undergo.
The everyday word for acquiring by work or trade, used of wages and profit. It makes each person's record an account they built themselves rather than a verdict handed to them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Responsibility in Arabia was collective by design. If a man killed, his kin paid. If a clan gave protection, every member was bound by it. That is what made a chief's word worth following. It is also why the followers in this scene expect the arrangement to hold. The reply describes a place where the accounts are separated out. For that audience, this was the strangest part of the picture.
studies.didYouKnow: The exchange is arranged with unusual symmetry. The later group speaks first, blaming the earlier. The earlier group answers. The divine reply has already come between the two, granting the doubling to everybody. The classical scholars note that the Quran lets both parties make their case in full before the verdict. Neither argument is refuted. Each is only widened.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Answering for what you do is individual here, and influence is still real. The leaders are not let off. The divine reply has already given them a double portion. What is refused is the follower's claim to be a bystander in his own life. Both facts are left standing at once. That is harder than saying people are simply products of their circumstances. It is also harder than saying circumstances do not count.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same dispute at greater length, with the weak and the arrogant each answering the other.
States the principle behind this scene: no bearer carries another's load, and each has what he strove for.
Applies the same rule across generations: that community has passed, theirs is what they earned.

studies.applyIt: Think of a habit you picked up from someone you looked up to and still half attribute to them. Try describing it once today in the first person, with no mention of where it came from. It is your habit now, whoever handed it over. The sentence is uncomfortable to say and it is accurate, which is the point.
studies.explainEasier: The first group answers the last one. They say the later ones were no better off than they were. Then they tell them to taste the punishment for what they earned themselves.

studies.title: Until The Camel Passes
studies.meaning: Two things are refused, and the pair matters. The gates of the sky will not open. They will not enter the Garden. Early scholars connect the first to the rising of deeds and souls, so the closure works both ways. Then comes the impossible condition. It reads as flatly in Arabic as it does in English. Some classical authorities record a second reading of the word for camel. It would make it a thick twisted rope, better suited to a needle. The tradition keeps both and settles neither.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, addressed to men whose refusal of the message was bound up with their standing in the city. The image draws on things the audience handled daily, since Mecca ran on camels and every household had a needle. No occasion of revelation is reported. The passage sits between two judgement scenes and states the outcome plainly before the surah returns to the dialogue between the two groups.

keyTerms.note: The first word means a small aperture, the same one behind the word for poison, which enters through the smallest opening. It names the hole precisely rather than the needle in general.
From the root for spreading something flat and soft, used elsewhere in the Quran of the earth prepared as a cradle. Applying the word of comfort to this place is the whole force of the line.
A plural for things that cover something over, from a verb for enveloping. Paired with the bedding beneath, the two words assemble a made bed, which is a colder image than flames would be.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The camel was the largest thing in Arabian life. It was the measure of everything valuable: bride price, blood money, a family's whole estate. The needle was among the smallest things anyone owned. Every woman who mended a tent or a garment carried one. Putting the two together was not an exotic figure of speech. It set the biggest and the smallest objects in their world side by side.
studies.didYouKnow: The word rendered as bedding here is used elsewhere in the Quran for the earth itself. There it is spread out as a cradle for human beings. The same noun serves for the ground under a sleeping child and for what this ayah describes. The reversal is carried entirely by the vocabulary. Nothing in the text states it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage names arrogance twice. Once in the description of the offence, and once in the closing formula about wrongdoers. That puts the whole scene under a heading with nothing to do with error of the mind. It also handles impossibility carefully. It does not announce that entry is barred. It states a condition and lets the condition be absurd. The door is not so much locked. It is a door nothing of that shape fits through.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word for a spread bed of the earth itself, made ready for people to live on.
Describes good words and righteous deeds ascending, which is what the closed gates of the sky imply.
Repeats the charge of arrogance towards the signs and asks whether Hell is not the abode of the proud.

studies.applyIt: Pick the smallest opening in your day, the one place where something good could get through if you let it: two minutes before you sleep, the walk from the car to the door. Put one thing in it. Not a programme, one thing, the same one for a week. The passage is about apertures, and small ones are the only kind most of us actually have.
studies.explainEasier: People who call God's signs lies and are too proud for them will not have the gates of the sky opened. They will not enter the Garden. That waits until a camel goes through the eye of a needle.

studies.title: Never Beyond Its Capacity
studies.meaning: A clause interrupts the sentence. The ayah is describing those who believe and do sound works. Before it reaches its end it stops. It says that no soul is charged beyond what it can hold. Early scholars read the break as deliberate. It falls exactly where a listener would start measuring themselves against the standard just named, and finding themselves short. Only then does the sentence finish. The break is not an exemption from what is asked. It is a statement about how the demand was set.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a run of ayat that alternate between the two outcomes. The early community in Mecca included slaves, the poor, and people with very little freedom to act. For them a demand for sound works could have read as a demand for means they did not have. No occasion of revelation is reported. The clause in the middle meets that difficulty directly. It does not alter the description around it.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to burden with something costly or troublesome. The verb assumes the task is difficult, so the clause does not deny hardship; it sets a ceiling on it.
From the root for breadth and room. The word names how much space a thing has rather than how strong it is, so the measure is individual and can differ from one person to the next.
From a root meaning to be fit or in good order, and used of mending what is damaged. Righteous deeds in this vocabulary are things that work rather than things that impress.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Loads were weighed up constantly in a caravan economy. A camel was packed to a known limit. A driver who overloaded an animal lost it on the road. So the whole trade rested on honest guesses about what each beast could carry over a given distance. The words for laying on a burden and for capacity were technical and familiar. Everyone knew the limit varied from one animal to the next.
studies.didYouKnow: This clause appears three times in the Quran with almost identical wording. One of those is the closing prayer of the longest surah. There the community asks not to be charged with what it cannot bear. Here the same sentence is not a request. It is a statement, placed inside a description rather than at the end of a prayer.
studies.theologicalSignificance: One clause settles the relation between what is asked and who is asked. Capacity is not a concession granted afterwards. It is the measure the demand was framed by in the first place. So what is asked is already fitted to the person before they meet it. That removes the excuse that too much is being asked. It also removes the fear that a person is simply built unable to answer.

crossReferences.why: Opens with this exact clause and turns it into a prayer not to be burdened beyond endurance.
Attaches the same principle to giving full measure, where perfect accuracy would be impossible.
Applies capacity to spending, and adds that God will bring ease after hardship.

studies.applyIt: Take the religious thing you feel worst about not doing, and ask honestly whether the version in your head was ever sized for your actual life. Then set a version that is. Smaller, and real, and repeatable this month. If it feels disappointingly modest, that is usually the sign that you have finally described something you will still be doing in June.
studies.explainEasier: People who believe and do good work belong in the Garden and will stay there. In the middle of that promise, God says he never puts more on anyone than they can carry.

studies.title: We Would Never Have Found It
studies.meaning: The first thing described is a removal, not an addition. Whatever grudge was in their chests is drawn out. Early scholars take that as the condition of the place, not a separate reward. Then comes the speech, and its structure is careful. First, praise for being guided here. Then at once the correction: they would never have found the way themselves. Then the admission that the messengers had told the truth. The answer that comes back ties the Garden to what they did. It uses the language of inheritance, not of payment.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The early community was small and drawn from very different clans. Some of those clans had long-standing quarrels with each other. For this audience, an inherited grievance was a serious matter. No occasion of revelation is reported. The passage is one of the Quran's fullest accounts of the Garden's inner condition rather than its furnishings. It comes in a section otherwise given to judgement.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to enter something stealthily, and the same root gives the word for an iron collar. Rancour is pictured as a thing that got inside and then held its owner fast.

keyTerms.gloss: you are made to inherit it
keyTerms.note: The passive of the verb for inheriting. An inheritance is not earned and not bought, which sits deliberately alongside the clause that follows about what they used to do.
Praise given for what someone is as well as for what they have done, unlike thanks, which answers a specific favour. It is the word the Quran opens with, in the same construction as here.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Feuds in Arabia outlived the men who started them. A killing between two clans could be avenged forty years later. The avengers were grandsons who had never met the original parties. Poets kept the accounts alive by reciting them at every gathering. Carrying a grievance there was not a private failing. It was a duty of honour. A place with that taken away would have sounded to them like a wholly different kind of society.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran repeatedly describes the Garden as inherited rather than bought or won. It uses the same verb in several surahs. The classical scholars square that with the clause about deeds. They say entry rests on God's mercy, while rank inside answers to what a person did. The two halves of this ayah are the usual evidence cited.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The speech given to the people of the Garden corrects a sentence they have just spoken. They praise God for guiding them here. Then they add that they would never have been guided otherwise. That withdraws any hint that they found the road. The correction is placed in their own mouths, in the one setting where praising themselves could do no harm. It says something firm about where the tradition puts the origin of guidance.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the removal of rancour from the chest, adding that they face one another as brothers.
Names the inheritors, who will inherit the highest garden and remain in it.
Treats the same problem in this life, calling believers brothers and asking for reconciliation between them.

studies.applyIt: Name one grudge you are still carrying and estimate, honestly, how many hours of your life it has taken. Not whether it is justified; it probably is. Just the hours. Then decide whether you want to keep paying that rate. You do not have to resolve anything today, and you may find the arithmetic does more than a decision would.
studies.explainEasier: God takes away whatever bad feeling was in their hearts. Rivers run below them. They say they would never have found the way if God had not guided them, and that the messengers told the truth.

studies.title: We Found It True
studies.meaning: The question put across the divide is not a taunt about position. It is about verification. We found what we were promised to be true; did you find yours true. Both groups were told something in advance, and both have now checked it. The answer is a single word, and its bareness is the point. Then an announcer speaks between them, and what he proclaims is not a sentence of punishment but a distancing, since the word for curse in Arabic means being put at a remove from good.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The dispute in Mecca was largely about whether the promise and the warning were real. The Quraysh treated rising again as the least believable part of the message, and said so openly. This scene answers by moving to the moment after the question is settled. The confirmation is supplied by the people who had denied it, not by an argument.

keyTerms.note: From the root for making something heard, the same one behind the call to prayer. The Quran uses this exact noun only twice, here and in the Joseph account, both times for a public proclamation.
The root means driving something away and keeping it at a distance. A curse in this vocabulary is exclusion from good rather than a wish for harm, which changes how the proclamation reads.
The neutral verb for a promise, used in the Quran of both the reward and the threat. Its neutrality is what allows the same question to be put to both groups in identical words.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian society had no written contracts to fall back on. A promise was tested only when it came due. Reputations were built entirely on that record. Merchants gave credit on a man's word and found out a season later whether it held. To ask someone whether they found the promise true was the standard question of that economy. Everyone listening knew what the answer settled.
studies.didYouKnow: The reply from the other side is one word in Arabic. The Quran does not expand it. The classical scholars note how tight it is. After a lifetime of arguments, objections and demands for proof, the whole position is given up in a syllable. The narrative moves on at once and lets nobody comment on it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Truth is shown as something that can be found, not only argued. The verb both groups use is the verb for coming upon a thing. That puts the promise and the warning with facts about the world that declare themselves in the end. This is why the Quran so often treats disbelief as a matter of patience rather than proof. Its position is that the evidence arrives on its own schedule.

crossReferences.why: Asks the same verifying question at the Fire and receives the same admission, by our Lord, yes.
Gives the answering praise from the other side, that God made His promise to them true.
Records the demand for verification in this life and the instruction to answer that it is certainly true.

studies.applyIt: Think of a promise someone made you that they kept, quietly, at cost to themselves. Tell them you remember it. Most kept promises are never mentioned again by anyone, which is why keeping them is such a good measure of a person. One message today is enough, and it will land harder than you expect.
studies.explainEasier: The people of the Garden call across to the people of the Fire. They say they found what God promised them was true, and ask if the others found the same. The others answer yes.

studies.title: Men Upon The Heights
studies.meaning: The wrongdoers are described first by what they do to others: blocking the road and trying to bend it crooked. Then the scene widens. A partition stands between the two groups, and on the elevated ground above it are men who recognise everyone by their marks. They greet the people of the Garden and have not entered. The last clause is the one early scholars dwell on: they are hoping. Who these men are is one of the genuinely open questions of the classical tradition, and the range of answers is wide.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. This passage gives the surah its name. It is among the Quran's most discussed scenes, because the text holds back any naming. The early scholars record several positions. Some say people whose good and bad deeds balanced exactly. Some say people of high standing placed there to watch. Others say something else again. Al-Tabari collects the reports without backing one. No occasion of revelation is attached to it.

keyTerms.note: From the root meaning to know or recognise, and used of any raised ridge or crest. The same root supplies the verb in the next clause, so those on the heights are literally on the place of recognising.
A mark placed on something to identify it, used of a brand on livestock and a badge worn in battle. Recognition here is by a visible sign rather than by memory of a face.
A verb for wanting something you have reason to expect but do not yet hold. It sits between confidence and mere wishing, which is why the ayah can end on it without resolving anything.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Branding was how ownership worked in a herding society. Every tribe had its mark, burned onto camels so that a beast strayed onto other grazing could be identified at a glance from a distance. Battle too was fought with signs worn to tell one side from another in the dust. Recognition by a mark rather than by acquaintance was the ordinary way of knowing who someone belonged to.
studies.didYouKnow: The word that names this surah occurs in only two places in the whole Quran. Both are within three ayat of each other, here. So surah 7 is named after a scene of about four ayat, in a chapter of over two hundred. It is also named after a group whose identity the Book deliberately never specifies.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage shows that the two-sided picture of judgement is not the whole of it. Something stands between. The people there are not described as suffering. They greet, they watch, and they hope. That introduces a state that is neither settled nor lost. The tradition's refusal to close the question teaches something too. The Quran gives a place on the map without labelling who is on it. The early scholars left it that way.

crossReferences.why: Describes a wall raised between two groups, with mercy inside it and punishment on the outer side.
Uses the same idea of recognition by marks, where the guilty are known by their appearance.
Names those genuinely unable to act, whom God may pardon, a category the tradition often reads alongside this.

studies.applyIt: Notice how quickly you sort people into two groups: sound and unsound, ours and theirs, serious and not. This passage introduces a third position and then refuses to define it. Pick one person you have filed under a heading and try holding them unfiled for a week. You do not have to conclude anything. Just leave the folder open.
studies.explainEasier: Between the two groups there is a wall. On the high ground above it stand men who know everyone by their marks. They call peace to the people of the Garden. They have not gone in yet, and they are still hoping.

studies.title: Do Not Place Us There
studies.meaning: The verb is passive. Their eyes are turned towards the other side; nobody says they looked. What follows is a prayer, and its content is worth noticing. They do not ask to be admitted to the Garden and they do not ask for the sight to stop. They ask not to be placed among the wrongdoing people. Early scholars read the request as being about company rather than location, since the Arabic names a people rather than a place, and the whole appeal turns on who one ends up standing with.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, within the scene on the heights that gives the surah its name. Its speakers are the men described in the preceding ayah, whose identity the classical tradition never settled. No occasion of revelation is reported. The surah is at this point building its longest continuous piece of dialogue, moving the reader's viewpoint between the two sides and then, here, placing it with people who can see both.

keyTerms.note: A passive verb for diverting something from its direction, used of turning a rider or a stream. The grammar takes the initiative out of their hands, so the sight is something they are shown rather than something they seek.
From the root for meeting or encountering. The word describes direct facing rather than a glance, which is why the ayah reads as a confrontation with a view rather than a passing look.

The ordinary word for a body of people bound together. The plea names a company rather than a punishment, which shifts what is being asked from a place to the question of whose side one is counted on.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Belonging was survival in Arabia. A man's protection, his marriage prospects and his standing in any dispute all followed from the group he was counted with. Being thrown out of a tribe was a sentence in itself, whatever the physical conditions. To ask not to be placed among a certain people was the most serious request available in that world. It addressed something that mattered more than comfort.
studies.didYouKnow: This is one of very few prayers the Quran records after the reckoning has begun. It asks for something modest. Most prayers reported from that setting are laments, or requests to go back. The classical scholars note that this one is phrased as a petition still in progress. That is part of why the passage leaves the speakers' outcome open.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The prayer treats company as the consequence. What is dreaded is not mainly pain. It is being counted among a particular people. That suggests the tradition's picture of the two outcomes is as much about who you are with as about what you feel. The passage also shows a request being made where requests are usually described as closed. So hope keeps working inside the scene, not only before it.

crossReferences.why: Asks in this life for the same thing, to be gathered with the righteous rather than among others.
Uses the same construction when facing an overwhelming force, asking for help against a disbelieving people.
Abraham's prayer to be joined to the righteous, which is the positive form of this request.

studies.applyIt: Look at where you spend your unstructured hours and who is in the room, physically or on a screen. Not their character, just the direction they are travelling. You are being shaped by that company whether or not you approve of it. Add one hour this week with someone travelling where you would like to end up, and keep it in the calendar.
studies.explainEasier: When their eyes are turned towards the people of the Fire, they pray. They ask God not to put them with the people who did wrong. They do not ask for anything else.

studies.title: Your Hoard Did Not Help
studies.meaning: The same men who recognise everyone now address particular figures. What they name is exactly what those figures had been known for. The word translated as hoardings can mean the wealth a person amassed. It can also mean the numbers he could muster. The classical scholars take it both ways, since in Arabia the two were nearly the same asset. Alongside it stands the arrogance, named separately. The verb for availing comes from the root for wealth. So the line says, almost literally, that their riches did not make them rich.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The men who led the opposition were heads of the wealthiest trading houses. Their argument against the message was often an argument from position. The leading families had not accepted it, so it could not be sound. No occasion of revelation is reported for this ayah. The challenge is put in the mouths of onlookers, not of those proved right. That keeps the scene from reading as revenge.

keyTerms.note: The noun covers both a hoard of wealth and a gathered body of men. Early scholars read it either way, and in a society where retainers were bought with wealth the ambiguity is not much of a gap.
The verb comes from the root for wealth and independence, so it means to make someone self-sufficient. The sentence therefore uses the vocabulary of riches to say that riches produced nothing.
The same verb the surah applied to the first refusal, in a form meaning to seek greatness for oneself. Its continuous tense makes it a practice rather than an incident.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wealth in Mecca was not stored in a vault; it was visible and mobile. It looked like camels, like the number of men who would ride out with you, like the guests at your table during the pilgrimage season. A rich man was rich in the sight of others by definition. This is why the loss described here is total rather than partial: the asset and its display were the same thing.
studies.didYouKnow: The Arabic here contains a quiet play on words that the English cannot carry. The verb for availing or benefiting is built from the root that gives the words for wealth, riches and self-sufficiency. One of God's names in the Quran is formed from it. So the ayah states that their wealth did not enrich them, using one root twice.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Property is not condemned in itself here. What is denied is its reach. The passage names the specific claim wealth makes, which is that it will be enough. It then reports the point at which that claim is tested. Naming arrogance alongside it suggests the tradition sees the two as linked, not as a coincidence. What piling things up most reliably produces is not comfort. It is the sense of standing above the need for anything else.

crossReferences.why: States the same thing of one man: his wealth and what he earned did not avail him.
Names the day when neither wealth nor sons benefit, except one who comes with a sound heart.
The owner of two gardens argues from being greater in wealth and men, and loses both.

studies.applyIt: Work out what you would still have if the number in your account were halved. List it: skills, relationships, the ability to sleep, whatever is actually on the list. Do it on paper. Most people find the list is longer than they assumed and that almost nothing on it was bought, which is worth knowing before the question is put to you rather than after.
studies.explainEasier: The men on the high ground call out to people they know by their marks. They tell them that all they piled up did them no good. Acting big did not help them either.

studies.title: Are These The Ones
studies.meaning: A question is put that quotes an old oath back at the people who swore it. They had sworn that God's mercy would never reach a certain group. That group is now indicated with a gesture. Then, with no transition, the words of admission are spoken. Early scholars differ over who is addressed by them. It may be the people just pointed at, or the men on the heights themselves. The Arabic supports both, which is part of why the passage has been discussed for so long.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The leading families dismissed the early believers precisely by class, objecting that the message had been taken up by slaves, freedmen and the poor, and asking whether God would favour such people over them. That objection is what the oath in this ayah refers to. The Quran answers it not with an argument but by staging the moment when the swearers are shown the outcome.

keyTerms.note: The formal verb for taking an oath, the strongest form of assertion available in Arabic. Quoting it back makes the point that this was not a passing opinion but something they staked their word on.
A verb for obtaining something by reaching out for it, used of picking fruit within arm's length. It makes mercy something that extends towards a person rather than something they climb to.
Grief for something already lost, as distinct from fear, which looks forward. The Quran regularly pairs the two so that both directions of time are covered by a single assurance.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca was a city of ranked families, and the ranking was kept up by public speech. Who could be addressed familiarly. Whose son could marry whose daughter. Which men's opinions counted in the assembly. Early converts from the weakest layers of that society were an offence to the order itself. Several leading men said openly that they would not sit where such people sat. The oath recalled here belongs to that vocabulary.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran's recurring assurance about fear and grief appears many times. Almost always it is in the third person, as a statement about others. Here it is spoken directly to its recipients, in the second person. It is an address rather than a description. That is a rare form for a phrase that otherwise works as a formula.
studies.theologicalSignificance: This is the sharpest limit the Book places on judging other people in religion. To swear that mercy will not reach someone is to claim a decision that was never anyone's to make. The scene answers it by simply showing the outcome. It also implies the error is not merely social snobbery. It is a mistake about God. The oath assumes access to information that belongs to Him alone.

crossReferences.why: Forbids driving away those who call on their Lord, and names the testing of some people by others.
Tells those who exceeded all bounds not to despair of God's mercy, which covers everything.
Asks whether they are the ones who distribute their Lord's mercy, when God apportions livelihood.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone you have privately written off as beyond changing. Say their name and then say, out loud, that you do not know what will happen to them. That is all. You are not obliged to like them or to expect anything. You are giving back a piece of information you were never holding in the first place.
studies.explainEasier: God points to the people the proud ones had sworn he would never show mercy to. Then the word comes: go into the Garden. There is nothing for you to fear, and you will not be sad.

studies.title: Pour Some Water Over Us
studies.meaning: The request is precisely worded. They do not ask for a share; they ask for what overflows, using a verb that means to pour out in abundance, and they name an alternative in case water is not available. The reply is brief and it does not gloat. It states a condition rather than a refusal by the speakers, which early scholars note keeps the people of the Garden from being made into the ones withholding. What is described as closed off is not water in general but water for this.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, addressed to people for whom water was the substance around which the whole society was organised. Mecca itself existed because of a well. The scene follows several ayat of dialogue between the two sides and reverses the direction of the last exchange, since the earlier call went the other way. No occasion of revelation is reported for it.

keyTerms.note: From a root for overflowing, used of a basin brimming over. The same imperative describes the pilgrims surging away from the standing place, so the word carries volume and movement together.
The verb for provision arriving from outside a person's own effort. Its use here concedes the whole argument, since the request acknowledges that what the other side holds came as a gift.
From a root meaning to set apart and make inviolable, the same one behind the words for the sanctuary and for a person under protection. It names a boundary rather than an act of denial.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Water rights were the hardest currency in Arabia. Wells were owned, guarded and inherited. A tribe's whole position could rest on one. Refusing water to a traveller was among the deepest disgraces a host could incur. Giving it freely was the standard boast of a generous man. An exchange in which water is asked for and cannot be given would have struck the first listeners as a world with its rules turned upside down.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used in this request appears in the pilgrimage passages of surah 2. There it describes the crowds moving away from the standing place, in the same imperative form. The root describes a liquid overflowing its container. By extension it describes a crowd pouring forward. So the same word covers a brimming basin and a moving multitude.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage says something exact about what is lost. It is not that the people of the Fire have nothing. It is that the ordinary channels by which one person's abundance reaches another are no longer open. The Quran's picture of this life is full of such channels. Hospitality, charity, the well shared with a stranger. Their closure, rather than any described torment, is what this scene chooses to depict.

crossReferences.why: Warns of a day with no trading, no friendship and no intercession, which is the arrangement this scene shows.
Shows a request for light being made across the same divide, and a wall raised between the two groups.
Urges spending before a day comes in which there is no bargaining and no friendship left.

studies.applyIt: Give something away today that costs you almost nothing and that you would normally keep: the last of something, a seat, twenty minutes. Do it without deciding it is significant. The passage is about a moment when the pipes between people are shut. The only useful response is to keep yours open while they still are.
studies.explainEasier: The people in the Fire call to the people in the Garden. They ask for water, or for some of what God has given them. The answer is that God has put those things out of reach for them.

studies.title: Taken As A Diversion
studies.meaning: Two words are used for what they made of religion, and the Quran elsewhere applies that same pair to worldly life. Here the terms are reversed onto religion itself, so what should have been the serious thing became the entertainment. Then a statement early scholars take care over: We forget them as they forgot. Since forgetfulness cannot be attributed to God, they explain it as treating them as one forgotten. The following ayah answers the charge of ignorance in advance. A Book was given, set out in detail, on knowledge.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Quraysh often answered the recitation with mockery rather than argument. Several ayat record them talking over it, calling it old tales, and making sport of the warnings. No occasion of revelation is reported. The description of the Book comes immediately after the charge of frivolity. That closes the excuse that nothing clear had been provided to be serious about.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to be turned aside from what matters. It names amusement by its effect rather than its content, so anything that occupies attention harmlessly can qualify.

keyTerms.gloss: We set it out in detail
keyTerms.note: From the root for a joint between two bones, and for separating things at their natural divisions. A detailed book in this vocabulary is one articulated at its joints rather than one that is merely long.
The classical scholars agree that forgetfulness is not attributed to God, and read this as treating them as one forgotten. The wording deliberately mirrors what they did, phrase for phrase.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca's entertainment was recitation. Poets held audiences at the seasonal fairs. Verses were learned by heart and repeated. A striking poem could make a man's name across Arabia. This is exactly the box the opposition tried to put the Quran into. A poem could be admired, quoted, and then set down. Treating a thing as a performance was a known way to defuse it. Nobody had to answer it.
studies.didYouKnow: The pair of words used here for diversion and play appears several times in the Quran. Everywhere else in the Book it describes the life of this world. This is the place where the terms are turned around and applied to religion instead. So the ayah accuses its subjects of exactly reversing which of the two was the serious business.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage names a failure that is not disbelief and not hypocrisy. Religion is kept, and it is held lightly. It becomes one of the pleasant furnishings of a life organised around something else. The reply is measured in kind rather than in severity. What was treated as marginal is answered by being treated as absent. And the Book is described as detailed on knowledge. That closes the defence that the matter was never made clear enough to take seriously.

crossReferences.why: Instructs leaving those who took their religion as play and diversion, deceived by worldly life.
Applies the same two words to this life itself, which is their usual object in the Quran.
Gives the same reciprocal wording, you forgot Our signs and so today you are forgotten.

studies.applyIt: Look at where religion actually sits in your week: the slot it occupies, the attention it gets compared with the thing you would not miss. Do not judge the answer, just describe it accurately. Then move one thing up a single place in the order, this week only. Not a reform, a reordering, and a small one you will actually complete.
studies.explainEasier: Some people treated their religion as a game and a bit of fun, and this life fooled them. So God will leave them as they left the meeting of that day. He had already given them a clear book.

studies.title: Could We Be Sent Back
studies.meaning: The question opens with a word whose root means what a thing comes back to. It is not asking whether they understand the Book but whether they are waiting for its outcome to arrive, which is the only interpretation that will still be available then. Two requests follow, and they are made in the right order and far too late: intercessors first, and failing that, a return to act differently. Nothing answers them. The ayah closes in the third person, reporting the loss as already complete.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The listeners kept figures at the sanctuary precisely on the expectation that those figures would speak up for them before God. They also treated the promised reckoning as a story rather than a date. Both assumptions appear in the two requests here. No occasion of revelation is reported. The passage closes the surah's long judgement sequence. After it the surah turns to the account of creation, and then to the messengers.

keyTerms.gloss: its outcome, what it comes to
keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to return to an origin. The Quran uses the same noun for the interpretation of dreams, so it covers both what a thing means and the event in which the meaning arrives.

From a root meaning to make a thing even by adding a second, as an even number is a pair. An intercessor joins himself to a petitioner so that one becomes two, which is precisely what is missing here.

The passive of the verb for returning something to where it came from, used of goods returned to a seller. The request asks to be handed back, not to go, which concedes that the movement is not theirs.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Speaking up for someone was the ordinary machinery of Arabian life. A man in trouble did not approach a chief directly. He found someone with standing to speak alongside him. The whole system of clients and patrons existed to make that possible. Nobody in Mecca thought of it as a religious novelty. It was how you got anything done. That is why its absence in this scene is described as the thing that fails.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for the arrival of the outcome is the same one that governs the whole Joseph account. There it means the reading of a dream that later comes true. In both places the root does double duty. It names the meaning of a thing and the moment that meaning walks into the room.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates recognising the truth from being able to use the recognition. What they say when the outcome arrives is exactly what the messengers had said, word for word. So the content of belief is no longer in dispute at all. What has run out is the time. In that time, believing was an action rather than a thing observed. That is the Quran's usual account of why the warning comes early and is repeated.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same request to be sent back to do righteous work, and the flat refusal that follows.
Shows them wishing to be returned, and states they would return to exactly what they were forbidden.
States the condition intercession operates under: none intercedes with Him except by His permission.

studies.applyIt: Name one thing you would do differently if you could go back five years. Now ask what the equivalent thing is today, the one you will name five years from now. It is usually not mysterious. Write it in one sentence and put it where you will see it tomorrow. The passage is about a request that arrives too late; yours has not.
studies.explainEasier: On that day the people who ignored the warning will say the messengers were telling the truth. They will ask for someone to speak up for them. They will ask to be sent back to live differently. Nothing answers them.

studies.title: His Is The Creation
studies.meaning: After a long stretch of judgement scenes the surah turns and gives its foundation. Creation in six days, then the establishing on the Throne. The classical scholars accept that as the Quran states it, while declining to say how. Some gloss it in terms of sovereignty. All agree it implies nothing bodily. Then motion: night pursuing day at speed, the heavenly bodies pressed into service. The summary divides everything in two. His is the making, and His is the ordering. Those are not the same claim.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Quraysh did not deny a creator; they held that God had made the world and then delegated its running to lesser powers whose favour was worth cultivating. This ayah answers that arrangement precisely, by separating creation from command and assigning both to the same one. No occasion of revelation is reported. It opens the surah's second half, which will be a sequence of messengers all saying the same sentence.

keyTerms.note: The early scholars accept the word as revealed without describing a manner for it, and several explain it in terms of sovereignty assumed. All agree the language rules out anything bodily or spatial.
From a root for urging an animal forward. It turns the succession of night and day into a chase, with one always closing on the other and never quite catching it.
From a root meaning to subject something to work without payment. The sun and moon are described as labourers under orders, which removes them from the category of powers worth appealing to.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Desert life ran on the sky. Travel happened by night to avoid the heat. Direction came from stars that every guide could name. The month began with a sighting of the moon, and the whole calendar of markets and pilgrimage followed from it. These were not decorative objects to that audience. They were the instruments by which people found their way and knew what day it was. That is why several of them had drawn worship elsewhere in Arabia.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran states that the heavens and earth were made in six days in seven separate places. It always gives the same number, and never a breakdown of what happened on each. The classical scholars note that the word rendered as day is used in the Book for stretches of very different length. They do not assume it means a solar day here.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The closing line does a specific piece of work. Creation and command are separated as two categories. Then both are assigned to one owner. That closes the position that a creator might have withdrawn. It rules out leaving the ordinary running of things to go-betweens. It is a claim about the present tense, not about origins. And sun, moon and stars are described as put to work. That quietly demotes every heavenly power the surrounding cultures honoured.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the six days and the Throne, then adds that no one intercedes except after His permission.
Draws the practical conclusion: do not bow to the sun or the moon, but to the one who made them.
Describes the sun unable to overtake the moon and night unable to outrun day, each in an orbit.

studies.applyIt: Go outside tonight, if you can, and find one thing in the sky you can name. Just one. Stay with it for a minute without reaching for a phone. The people who first heard this ayah navigated by these objects and some of their neighbours worshipped them, and almost nobody now does either. Recovering the first is a decent way to feel the force of the second.
studies.explainEasier: Your Lord is God. He made the sky and the earth in six days, and then he took his place on the Throne. Night chases day. The sun, the moon and the stars all run under his command.

studies.title: Humbly, And In Secret
studies.meaning: Two manners of calling are given, rather than two times. Lowered, and hidden from other people. A warning about transgressors follows. Early scholars attach it to the manner of asking as much as to conduct in general, since the subject here is prayer. The second verse adds a ban on wrecking what has been set right. Then it returns to prayer with two feelings held together, fear and longing. Mercy is described as near, and the nearness is given a direction.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from a surah largely concerned with communities that were given a settled land and then ruined it. The ban on corrupting the earth after its ordering sits inside that argument. That gives it a historical edge a reader can easily miss. Early scholars report no occasion for these two verses. They read them as instruction placed between the accounts of those communities.

keyTerms.note: From a root for lowness and for the udder of an animal, the part that yields when pressed. The word describes a bearing that gives way rather than a feeling, so it can be adopted before it is felt.

Concealment from other people rather than from God. Early scholars read it as protecting the request from performance, since a prayer nobody hears cannot be made for anyone's benefit but the one praying.
A strong word, closer to greed than to hope, used of wanting something almost within reach. Paired with fear, it keeps the asking from collapsing into either despair or presumption.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Public supplication in Arabia was a performance with an audience. Tribes called on their gods aloud at shrines and before battles, and poets composed the appeals. Rainmaking ceremonies were communal and noisy, and the noise was part of what was thought to work. Telling people to lower their voices and hide the asking removed the social function of prayer entirely.
studies.didYouKnow: The pairing of fear and eager hope recurs across the Quran as a description of how the righteous pray. In one passage it describes those who leave their beds at night to call on their Lord. The two words are almost never separated. Classical scholars treat the pair as a single instruction rather than as alternatives.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Prayer is given a form as well as a content, and both parts of the form work against display. Lowering and hiding remove the two things that turn asking into performance. That is a precise diagnosis of how devotion goes wrong. The closing clause then places mercy. It is not described as near in general, but as near to those who do good. That ties the answer to conduct without making it a trade.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same pair of words for those who call on their Lord at night.
Shows Zachariah calling on his Lord in a hidden voice, the practice described here.
Earlier in the surah, calls for devotion offered sincerely to Him alone.

studies.applyIt: Ask for one thing tonight that you have never said out loud to anyone, in a voice only you can hear. Do not tidy the wording. The verse asks for two things, lowness and privacy, and the second is easier than people expect once you notice how much of ordinary asking is shaped by an imagined listener.
studies.explainEasier: God tells people to call on him quietly and without showing off. He also tells them not to spoil the earth after it has been put right. Ask him with both fear and hope, because his mercy is close to those who do good.

studies.title: Ahead Of His Mercy
studies.meaning: The winds arrive first, described as carriers of good news sent out in front of the mercy that follows, and the mercy in question is the rain itself, named without a comparison. Then the clouds are lifted, driven to a land that is dead, and water comes down. Fruits of every kind come out. Only after all this does the ayah state its purpose: this is exactly how the dead are brought out. The argument for resurrection is not made from logic but from something the audience watched every year.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Resurrection was the single claim the Quraysh found most absurd, and they returned to it constantly, asking who would revive bones that had crumbled. This passage does not answer with a proof. It points at an annual event that everyone in Arabia depended on and had watched all their lives, and asks them to notice what shape it has. No occasion of revelation is reported.

keyTerms.note: From a root connected to the skin, since news of this kind shows on a face before it is spoken. The winds are cast as messengers running ahead rather than as weather.
From a root meaning to be small or light. The verb means to find something light enough to pick up, so heavy clouds are described as an easy load for the wind that carries them.
The ordinary verb for driving livestock to pasture or to water. Clouds are herded, which continues the picture of the whole system as animals moving under a driver's hand.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Rain in Arabia was an event, not a season. A wadi that had been bare stone for a year would carry water within hours, and grazing appeared where nothing had grown. Whole tribes moved on the report of it, and scouts were sent to watch for cloud on the horizon. Nobody in that audience needed to be told what a dead land looked like or what happened to it three days after water arrived.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah changes speaker in the middle. It begins with He sends the winds, in the third person. Then it shifts to We drove them, We sent down, We brought out. It returns to the third person at the close. This turning is a recognised feature of the Quran's style. Here it places the divine voice directly inside the sequence, at the moment the water falls.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Resurrection is shown as a familiar process, not an unheard-of one. The passage does not argue that God is able to do it. It argues that He is visibly doing it, on a schedule. It happens in front of people who have stopped noticing what they watch. Calling rain mercy without a comparison makes the same move the other way. An ordinary physical event is treated as a direct instance of a divine attribute. It is not treated as a picture of one.

crossReferences.why: Points at the traces of God's mercy reviving the earth and draws the identical conclusion about the dead.
Gives almost the same sequence, winds stirring clouds driven to a dead land, ending on the resurrection.
Calls the water blessed, lists what grows from it, and names it as the coming out.

studies.applyIt: Find something growing near you that you did not plant: a weed in a pavement crack, a tree on your street, moss on a wall. Stand near it for thirty seconds and work out where its water came from. The passage rests entirely on people noticing a process they were already living inside. This is the smallest available version of that.
studies.explainEasier: God sends the winds before the rain. They carry heavy clouds to land that is dead. Water comes down and all kinds of fruit come out of it. That is how the dead will be brought out too.

studies.title: The Good Land And The Bad
studies.meaning: Two plots of ground receive the same rain and return different things. The good land yields its growth. The poor land gives up almost nothing, and the word for what it produces means grudging and meagre at once. The classical scholars read the two grounds as a likeness for two hearers of the same revelation. The ayah follows directly on the rain that was just described as the pattern of resurrection. The closing clause names who benefits from signs being turned about in different forms. The qualification is thankfulness.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in the run of ayat that use the natural world to answer objections about resurrection. Arabia had both kinds of ground within a day's ride: fertile pockets around springs and oases, and salt flats and stony ground where the same downpour produced a few bitter shoots. The comparison needed no explaining. No occasion of revelation is reported for the passage.

keyTerms.note: A word for what is pleasant, clean and fit for use, applied in the Quran to food, speech, dwellings and land. It names suitability for purpose rather than moral goodness in the abstract.
A rare word describing something given up unwillingly and in small quantity. The Quran uses it nowhere else, and it carries both the poverty of the yield and the reluctance of the giving.
From a root for turning a thing this way and that, used of changing the winds' direction and of exchanging currency. The signs are described as presented from different angles rather than repeated.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A farmer at an oasis knew his ground plot by plot and could tell you which corner would repay the water and which would not. Palm cultivation depended on that knowledge, and land was valued by it. Salt ground looked identical to good ground after a rain, and the difference showed only weeks later at harvest. The comparison here therefore describes something slow and only visible in the yield.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for varying the signs recurs across the Meccan surahs. Each time it is attached to a different audience. Here it is people who are thankful; elsewhere it is people who understand, or people who know. The classical scholars treat the changing endings as significant. The same material is presented again and again, and the Quran keeps naming a different quality that lets it land.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Openness to the message sits in the receiver, not in the message. The rain is the same rain. The difference in outcome is entirely a property of the ground. That puts the weight of hearing where the passage has been putting it all along. Naming thankfulness as the qualifying condition is unexpected. One might expect intelligence or sincerity instead. It suggests that what prepares a person for revelation is the habit of noticing what has been given.

crossReferences.why: Uses a matching likeness of water in valleys and metal in fire, separating what stays from what is carried off.
Sets a good word as a rooted tree against a corrupt word as a shrub torn from the surface.
Describes rain falling on a rock with soil on it, washing it bare, as a likeness for spoiled giving.

studies.applyIt: Think of a piece of good advice you were given twice, once when it bounced off and once when it landed. Nothing about the advice changed. Work out what was different about you on the second occasion. Whatever that was, it is the thing worth protecting, and most people find it had something to do with what they had recently been grateful for.
studies.explainEasier: Good ground gives its crop when the rain comes. Poor ground gives back almost nothing. God says he turns his signs around in different ways for people who are thankful.

studies.title: I Fear For You
studies.meaning: The surah begins its sequence of messengers here, and the first speech sets the pattern all the others will follow. The address is intimate: my people, spoken by a man to his own community. The instruction is one clause, and the reason is one clause. Then a sentence that is easy to misread. The Arabic preposition makes it fear on their behalf rather than fear of them. So what is stated is not a threat delivered but an anxiety carried. That is a very different posture for a warner to occupy.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Every messenger in this stretch of the surah speaks to his own people, and the parallel with the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) addressing the Quraysh is left for the reader to draw rather than stated. The Quran gives the flood tradition without the surrounding detail found in older scriptures. No occasion of revelation is reported. The sequence runs from the earliest of these communities forward, ending with one the audience could still visit.

keyTerms.note: The possessive ending is doing the work. He does not say O people but claims them as his own, which places him inside the community he is warning rather than opposite it.
From a root whose related words include a path worn smooth by walking. Worship in this vocabulary is a settled course of life rather than a set of occasions.

The preposition turns the fear outward onto them. A warner who says he fears for his audience is describing his own distress, not issuing a threat, and the wording is preserved in every parallel telling.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The men who spoke for a tribe were its elders and its poets. Their authority came from being of the blood. An outsider bringing a warning could be ignored. A man of your own clan telling you the arrangement you all lived by was wrong was far more disturbing. He had nothing to gain and everything to lose. That is the position every messenger in this surah occupies, and it was the Prophet's position in Mecca.
studies.didYouKnow: This exact sentence, worship God, you have no god other than Him, is spoken by four different messengers in this surah. The Arabic is almost identical each time: here, and then by the messengers to three later communities. The Quran presents them as delivering one message, not founding four religions. It makes the point through repetition rather than by stating it.
