studies.theologicalSignificance: Prophecy is defined here by content rather than by biography. What makes a messenger is the sentence he says. That sentence is shown to be the same across huge stretches of time and wholly unrelated peoples. The warning that follows is presented as care, not as force. That sets the tone for the whole sequence. Each of these men will be refused, and none of them is described as having wanted the confrontation.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same mission at length in a surah devoted to it, with the call described night and day.
Repeats this sentence word for word, showing how fixed the formula is across the Quran.
The parallel opening, where he calls himself a clear warner to his people in the same terms.

studies.applyIt: Think of a warning you once gave someone that came out as an accusation. Most do. The difference is usually one preposition: I am worried about you rather than you are doing this wrong. If there is someone you need to say something to this week, try building the sentence around your own worry instead of their fault, and notice how differently it is received.
studies.explainEasier: God sent Noah to his own people. He told them to worship God, because there is no other god for them. He said he was afraid for them about the punishment of a great day.

studies.title: I Know What You Do Not
studies.meaning: The objection comes from the notables, and it is a diagnosis rather than an argument: we see you in obvious error. The reply is remarkable for what it does not do. It offers no counter-accusation and no proof. It denies the charge in a single clause. Then it states a position. Then it gives three activities in order: I deliver, I counsel sincerely, and I know from God what you do not know. Early scholars note that the last is the only claim of superiority made in the whole exchange. It is a claim about a source rather than about a person.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The word for the notables describes the men who filled an assembly and whose opinion settled matters, and it recurs throughout this surah as the standing source of opposition. That was the Quraysh arrangement too, where a handful of clan heads spoke for the city. No occasion of revelation is reported. The Quran presents the same social pattern across every community in the sequence without commenting on the repetition.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to fill. They are the men who fill a gathering, whose presence makes it official. The word is social rather than legal, describing weight of standing rather than any formal office.

They charged him with straying using one form of the word; he answers with a different form that names a single occurrence. Early scholars read the switch as denying even the smallest instance rather than only the general charge.
From a root meaning pure and unmixed, used of honey without wax. Counsel of this kind has nothing of the counsellor's own interest folded into it, which is the whole of his defence.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A tribal assembly met in the open and decided by weight rather than by vote. A few men spoke, the rest listened, and a proposal that the leading voices dismissed was finished. Speaking against that consensus meant standing alone in front of everyone you knew, with no procedure to appeal to. The scene here is not a debate between equals. It is one man answering the room that decides what the community believes.
studies.didYouKnow: The reply reverses the sentence structure of the accusation rather than contradicting its content. They said we see you in straying. He says there is no straying in me. The word moves from a place he occupies to a thing that might be inside him, and it is denied there. The Arabic makes the shift visible in a way English translation cannot easily carry.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Claimed knowledge rests on transmission, not on insight. The messenger does not say he is wiser. He does not say he reasoned his way to something. He says he knows from God. That makes his authority wholly dependent, and so checkable against the message rather than against his person. That distinction runs through the Quran's whole account of prophecy. It is why messengers are shown correcting themselves and being corrected.

crossReferences.why: Has him disclaim knowledge of the unseen, treasuries and angelic status, limiting the claim precisely.
Gives the same confrontation, where the objection is that the lowest people follow him.
Puts the identical limitation in the Prophet's mouth: he follows only what is revealed to him.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time you are told you are simply wrong, with no reason attached. The instinct is to argue or to fold. There is a third option here: deny the charge once, plainly, say what you are actually claiming, and stop. It takes about fifteen seconds and it ends more conversations well than either of the alternatives.
studies.explainEasier: The leaders of his people told him they could see he was clearly lost. He answered that he was not lost at all. He said he was a messenger from the Lord of the Worlds, passing on what he was given.

studies.title: A Man From Among You
studies.meaning: The question turns the objection into the evidence. They found it strange that the reminder came through an ordinary man of their own community. The ayah asks why that should be surprising. It might have been expected instead. Three purposes are then given in a rising order. To warn. So that you may guard yourselves. And so that you may be shown mercy. The sequence moves from an unpleasant beginning to a merciful end. That reframes the warning as the first step of a favour rather than as the point.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Quraysh objection to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was in exactly this shape. They knew him, his family and his circumstances, and the familiarity was the problem: a message of that weight ought to have arrived by way of an angel or at least a great man of one of the two cities. Putting the same objection in the mouth of a far older community lets the answer be given without argument.

keyTerms.note: From a root for wonder and astonishment. The question is not rhetorical padding; it asks them to examine their own surprise, on the assumption that the surprise itself is the thing worth explaining.

Indefinite, so a reminder rather than the reminder. Calling revelation a reminder assumes the content is already partly known and that the failure being addressed is inattention rather than ignorance.
Both words matter. He is a man, not another order of being, and he is from you, so his life and lineage are known and his conduct can be checked against what he says.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Familiarity was the difficulty. In a city of a few thousand, everyone knew who had been a boy running errands twenty years earlier. They knew whose uncle had failed in trade, and who had married into which clan. Nothing about a man was hidden. Prophethood gave him no new appearance and no new voice. The people being addressed had watched the messenger grow up, and that was precisely the evidence they used against him.
studies.didYouKnow: This question appears twice in this surah in nearly identical words. It comes once here, and once a few ayat later, addressed to a different people entirely. The Quran does not remark on the repetition. It simply lets the same sentence be spoken to two communities separated by an enormous span of time. The reader is left to notice that the objection had not changed.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ordinariness of the messenger is defended as a feature. It is not excused as a limit. A message brought by a being of another order could be admired without being followed. Nothing about that life could be copied. The passage also arranges its three purposes. Mercy is the destination and warning is only the road. That sets a frame for every threatening passage in the surah around it.

crossReferences.why: Reports the identical astonishment that revelation came to a man from among them, and calls it plain sorcery.
Records the objection in its social form: why was this not sent to a great man of the two towns.
Answers the objection directly, saying an angel messenger would have suited angels, not people.

studies.applyIt: Think of something true you dismissed because of who said it: a relative you find tiresome, a colleague you had already filed away. Go back to the content once, in your head, with the speaker removed. If it still holds, act on it this week without telling them where you got it. The point is not to give credit. It is to stop losing information.
studies.explainEasier: God asks why they find it odd that a reminder came to them from their Lord through a man of their own. He came to warn them and to help them do right. The point of it is that they might be shown mercy.

studies.title: A People Without Sight
studies.meaning: The entire flood is given in a single ayah. There is no ark-building, no mockery from the shore, no waters bursting from the earth, no bird sent out. Three verbs carry it: they denied, We rescued, We drowned. Then the closing judgement, which is not about wrongdoing but about perception. They were a blind people. Early scholars uniformly take this as blindness of the heart rather than of the eyes, since the whole preceding exchange has been about men who looked at a messenger and saw an error.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Surah 11 and surah 71 give this account at length, with the building of the ship, the exchanges with the community, and the loss of a son. Here the compression is deliberate, because the surah is running six of these narratives in sequence and the shape they share is the subject rather than any one of them. No occasion of revelation is reported for the passage.

keyTerms.note: An unusual noun that takes the same form whether one vessel or many is meant. The Quran uses it for a single ark here and for whole fleets elsewhere without changing a letter.
From a root meaning to bring something out to high ground away from danger. Rescue in this word is removal to safety rather than defence in place, which fits a flood exactly.

The plural of the ordinary word for a blind person. The early scholars read it here of the heart, and the Quran elsewhere states directly that it is not the eyes that go blind but the hearts in the chests.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabia had ships. Coastal traders sailed the Red Sea, and Meccan merchants knew vessels from the ports at Jeddah and Shu'ayba. But the interior had nothing of the sort. Water arrived there only as flash flood in a dry valley. A rescue by ship was therefore a foreign and slightly exotic picture to an inland audience. Drowning in a wadi that filled without warning was something whole caravans had died of.
studies.didYouKnow: The flood occupies one ayah here and most of a surah elsewhere. Surah 71 is named after this messenger. It gives his complaint in his own words across twenty-eight ayat, while surah 11 supplies the ark and the son. Reading them together shows the Quran deliberately telling one story at several lengths, depending on what each surah is doing.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Denial is diagnosed as an incapacity rather than a conclusion. The community is not called stubborn or wicked in this summary. It is called blind. That locates the failure in what they could take in, not in what they decided. The Quran uses this diagnosis carefully. It appears at the end of long exchanges, after the arguments have been given and refused. It explains why more argument would not have helped.

crossReferences.why: States the principle behind this verdict: eyes do not go blind, hearts within the chests do.
Gives the account this ayah compresses, including the ship, the waves and the son who refused.
Tells the same events in short rhythmic lines and calls the ark a sign left behind.

studies.applyIt: Ask someone close to you what they can see about your situation that you cannot. Then do not explain, defend, or supply the context they are missing. Just write it down. Blindness of this kind is defined by not being visible from inside, which means the only way to check for it is to borrow someone else's eyes for five minutes.
studies.explainEasier: They called him a liar. God saved him and the people with him in the ark, and drowned the ones who turned his signs down. They were a people who could not see.

studies.title: And To Aad, Their Brother
studies.meaning: The second messenger arrives with almost no preamble. He is introduced as their brother. Early scholars take that as kinship of descent rather than of belief, since he came from among the people he addressed. His opening sentence is word for word the one just spoken by the messenger before him. Only the closing clause differs. It is a question rather than a statement of fear. The build of the ayah itself makes the argument: two different peoples, separated by generations, receiving one message.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Aad were an Arabian people, placed by the Quran in the sand dunes of the south. Their ruins and reputation belonged to the audience's own inherited history, not to a foreign tradition. Along with Thamud they are part of the Arabs' account of themselves. Putting them in a sequence beside the flood generation was a claim. Local history and universal history are the same history.

keyTerms.note: Used across this sequence for each messenger. The early scholars read it as brotherhood of lineage, since each man was of the people he was sent to, which is what made ignoring him difficult.

An ancient Arabian people the Quran associates with the sand tracts of the south. Their name entered proverb: something very old was said to be from the time of Aad long before this surah was recited.

A question built from the verb meaning to place a shield between yourself and harm. Asking rather than commanding leaves the audience to supply the answer, which is why the sequence uses it repeatedly.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Aad were proverbial in Arabia the way ancient empires are proverbial elsewhere. Poets called on them for age. The phrase from the days of Aad meant impossibly long ago. Southern Arabia held visible remains of large settled peoples, and the incense route ran past them. When this surah names them, it is not bringing in an unfamiliar people. It is picking up a name the audience already used in ordinary speech.
studies.didYouKnow: Aad and Thamud are the two peoples in this sequence with no parallel in the older scriptures. Both are Arabian. The Quran sets them among the flood generation and the communities of Lot and Midian, and marks no difference in status. That places the audience's own regional past inside the same account as the traditions they had heard from their Jewish and Christian neighbours.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The repetition of the identical opening sentence is itself a claim. Suppose every messenger says the same thing. Then the differences between religious communities are not differences in what was sent. Each community's tradition is a version of one message, not a rival to the others. The word brother matters for the same reason. Revelation arrives inside a people, in their own language and lineage. It is not imported.

crossReferences.why: Places this messenger and his people among the sand dunes, and repeats the warning he gave them.
The parallel introduction in surah 11, with the same brother formula and the same opening sentence.
Describes what became of them and names the boast that preceded it, who is greater in strength.

studies.applyIt: Learn one thing this week about a religious tradition near you that you know almost nothing about. Use a source inside it rather than a summary written by an outsider. Not to agree with it. The passage insists that messengers came to every people in their own idiom. Finding out what someone actually holds is the smallest form of taking that seriously.
studies.explainEasier: God sent Hud to the people of Aad, and he was one of them. He told them to worship God, because there is no other god for them. Then he asked whether they would not take care.

studies.title: A Trustworthy Adviser
studies.meaning: The charge escalates from the one made to the messenger before him. That one was called mistaken; this one is called light-minded and, in a second clause, suspected of lying. The reply follows the same pattern as before, denying the charge in one clause without returning the insult. What is new is the ending. He does not say he knows what they do not; he offers a description of himself as an adviser who can be relied on, which is a claim about character that the audience was in a position to check.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The word he uses of himself was a title in that city, not an adjective. The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) had been known as the trustworthy one before revelation began. His reputation for it had been settled in disputes the Quraysh themselves brought to him. Putting the same word in an ancient messenger's mouth let the audience hear their own knowledge of a man's record as a form of evidence.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning lightness and flimsiness, used of thin cloth and a slack rope. It accuses him not of being wrong but of being insubstantial, which is a harder charge to answer than an error.

The verb covers supposition, suspicion and confident opinion. They are not claiming proof, and the wording concedes as much, which is why the accusation and the emphatic particle attached sit oddly together.
From the root behind the words for faith, security and safety. Someone described this way is one with whom things can be deposited, and the word was used in Arabia of a man who held goods for others.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Commerce in Mecca ran on deposits. Merchants left goods and money with men they trusted while they travelled, with no paper and no court to enforce anything, so a reputation for holding what was not yours was the most valuable asset a man could own. It took years to build and one incident to destroy. To call yourself reliable in that setting was to invite the whole city to check.
studies.didYouKnow: The word this messenger uses of himself is the same one the people of Mecca had used of the Prophet for years before the first revelation. It had been used so long that it functioned as his name in disputes. The Quran does not point this out. It simply has an ancient messenger use the word, in front of an audience that had used it themselves.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two kinds of credential are set beside each other across these exchanges. One messenger appeals to knowledge from God, which cannot be checked from outside. This one appeals to a record of conduct, which can. The Quran presents both as legitimate and neither as sufficient alone. The pairing suggests that a message is authenticated by the life carrying it as much as by its source. That is why the sequence keeps describing what these men were like.

crossReferences.why: Has the earlier messenger describe himself in exactly these words, a trustworthy messenger to his people.
The king describes Joseph with the same word after testing him, establishing it as a public verdict.
Applies the same word to the angel bringing the revelation, obeyed there and trustworthy.

studies.applyIt: Think of one thing someone has left in your keeping: money, a confidence, a task nobody is checking on. Do the reliable thing with it this week before anyone asks. Trustworthiness is not a feeling and it is not a claim. It is a record that builds up quietly and is only ever noticed when it is missing.
studies.explainEasier: The leaders of his people said he was foolish and thought he was a liar. He said there was nothing foolish in him. He was a messenger from the Lord of the Worlds, and an adviser they could trust.

studies.title: Remember The Favours
studies.meaning: The same question is asked as before. Then the argument changes direction entirely. Instead of pressing the warning, he tells them to remember two things. They were made successors after the earlier community. And they were given an increase in build. Early scholars read that increase as physical stature, as strength, or as scope and abundance generally, and the word is broad enough for all three. Then comes a general instruction to recall God's favours. Prosperity is the stated outcome, rather than escape from punishment.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Aad were remembered in Arabia for size and power, and their own boast, recorded elsewhere in the Quran, was that nobody was stronger than they were. The argument here takes that boast and returns it to them as a gift received rather than a quality possessed. No occasion of revelation is reported. The passage sits between the objection and the refusal, as the last attempt made before the exchange breaks down.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to follow behind and to take another's place. Being a successor implies a predecessor who is gone, so the word contains a warning inside a compliment.
From a verb for spreading a thing out and opening the hand. Early scholars read it of bodily size, of strength, or of abundance and reach, and the word does not force a choice.
An unusual plural for good things given. It is the word repeated as a refrain throughout one whole surah, asking which of the Lord's favours the hearers would deny.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Succession was how Arabs understood the map. A tribe held a territory because another had held it before and had gone. That earlier tribe was driven out, absorbed or destroyed. Every well and grazing ground had that history attached. Nobody thought of their land as originally theirs. To be reminded that you are the successors of a vanished people was to be reminded of something you already recited in your own genealogy.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for favours is rare. It is the one repeated as the refrain of surah 55. There a single question about the Lord's bounties is put thirty-one times. Its appearance in this speech connects a warning to an ancient Arabian people with the Quran's most sustained list of what has been given.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Gratitude is offered as an argument rather than as a duty. And it is put to people who are refusing a warning. The reasoning is that a community which correctly names where its strength came from will not mistake the strength for a guarantee. That is why the passage names the vanished predecessors in the same breath as the gift. The two facts belong together. Holding only one of them is what produces the confidence being addressed.

crossReferences.why: Records their boast, who is greater than us in strength, which this ayah answers in advance.
The refrain built on the same rare word, asking which of the Lord's favours would be denied.
Names humanity as successors on the earth, raised in ranks, and calls the arrangement a test.

studies.applyIt: Write down three things about your circumstances that you did not arrange: where you were born, a body that works, someone who taught you to read. Then note who held that same advantage before you and no longer does. The passage puts the gift and the predecessor in one sentence. It is the pairing rather than either half that does the work.
studies.explainEasier: He asks why they find it odd that a reminder reached them through one of their own. He tells them to remember that God put them in place after the people of Noah. God also made them bigger and stronger.

studies.title: God Alone, And Abandon
studies.meaning: The objection is precise and it is worth reading slowly. They do not refuse to worship God. They refuse the word alone, and they name the cost attached to it, which is leaving what their fathers served. Early scholars point out that this is the actual point of friction in every one of these narratives: not the existence of God but His exclusivity, since exclusivity requires abandoning something. Then the demand, which changes the subject from argument to spectacle. Bring the thing you threaten, if you are telling the truth.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the objection is a transcript of the Quraysh position. Mecca acknowledged a supreme God and kept many lesser figures at the sanctuary. Their upkeep was tied to the city's standing and income. What the message asked for was not belief in a creator, which they already had. It asked for the removal of everything else, which touched livelihood and lineage together. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah.

keyTerms.note: A single word carrying the whole dispute. Their complaint attaches to it rather than to the name of God, which is why the Quran's argument with them is so often about exclusivity rather than existence.
An old verb the language uses in only some of its forms. It means to let something go and walk away from it, which names the actual expense of the demand being refused.
The neutral verb for a promise, used here of a threatened outcome. Its neutrality lets the sentence be read as a dare, since they are demanding delivery of something offered as a warning.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A tribe's gods were inherited property. They were kept in a household or at a shrine, and tied to specific places, seasons and rights. Abandoning them was not a change of opinion. It was walking away from an inheritance. It meant breaking with the men who had held it before you. It meant telling your relatives that they had spent their lives on nothing. The social cost of the word alone was the whole difficulty, and everyone in this exchange understood it.
studies.didYouKnow: The demand at the end of this ayah is bring us what you promise, if you are truthful. It reappears almost word for word later in this same surah, from a different community entirely. The Quran gives the identical challenge to two peoples with nothing else in common. That is one of the ways the sequence makes the pattern visible without stating it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage locates disbelief in cost rather than in doubt. These people accept the argument and refuse the consequence. That is a different condition from being unconvinced, and it is treated as more serious. Demanding the punishment as proof completes the picture. They are willing to have the question settled by an event they cannot survive. They are not willing to settle it by a change they would have to make while alive.

crossReferences.why: Describes their chests shrinking when God alone is mentioned, and lifting at the mention of others.
Records the Quraysh saying the same thing, that making the gods one god is an astonishing demand.
Gives the same dare in Mecca: send down stones from the sky if this is the truth from You.

studies.applyIt: Identify one thing you would have to give up if you took your own convictions completely seriously. Not a vice, necessarily; more likely a habit, a comfort, or an arrangement that suits you. You do not have to give it up today. Just stop pretending the reluctance is an intellectual difficulty. Naming it accurately as a cost is the honest first move.
studies.explainEasier: They asked whether he had come to make them worship God on his own. They did not want to drop what their fathers worshipped. Then they told him to bring the thing he kept warning them about, if he was really telling the truth.

studies.title: Names You Yourselves Gave
studies.meaning: The reply opens by stating that something has already fallen on them. The word used has a classical range running from defilement to punishment to divine anger, and the early scholars record the spread without settling it. Then comes the sharpest sentence in the sequence. Are you disputing with me about names, which you and your fathers named, for which God sent down no warrant. The argument is not that the objects of worship are weak. It is that they are words, given by people, and that nothing beyond the naming was ever added.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the argument transfers exactly to the Quraysh. The figures at the sanctuary had names, genealogies and stories, all of local manufacture. The Quran repeatedly presses the question of who authorised any of it. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah. The closing line, wait and I am waiting with you, ends the exchange without a further appeal. That is how several of these confrontations in the surah close.

keyTerms.note: The early scholars differ over its sense here, reading it as filth, as punishment, or as divine displeasure. All the readings agree that something has already settled on them rather than being merely threatened.
Indefinite and plural, so mere names. The argument reduces the objects of the dispute to labels, and then observes that the labelling was done entirely by the people now defending them.
In the Quran this word usually means the proof that licenses a claim rather than political power. Nothing was sent down to back the names, so the whole structure rests on assertion.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Naming was a serious act in Arabia. A poet could fix a nickname on a man that his descendants carried for centuries, and tribes took their identity from an ancestor's name and defended it. Words were understood to make things real in a way that a written culture finds harder to feel. This is why the reduction of the gods to names is such a pointed argument, and why it would have stung rather than seemed obvious.
studies.didYouKnow: This exact argument appears in three widely separated places in the Quran. It always takes the same form: they are only names which you and your fathers named, with no warrant sent down for them. One instance is spoken by an ancient messenger here. One is spoken by Joseph in a prison. One is about three specific figures venerated in Arabia.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage puts a test to religious language itself. A name can be inherited, defended and fought over while nothing behind it was ever proved. The Quran treats the gap between the word and the warrant as the thing to examine. It is an argument that cuts inward as much as outward. Any tradition can pick up terms that carry weight because they are old, rather than because anything was sent down about them.

crossReferences.why: Joseph makes the identical argument to his cellmates, that they serve only names their fathers gave.
Applies the same sentence to three figures venerated in Arabia, following conjecture and desire.
Notes that they serve what God sent down no warrant for, and of which they have no knowledge.

studies.applyIt: Pick a word you use in religious conversation that you have never actually defined for yourself. Everyone has several. Write down what you mean by it in one sentence, without borrowing a phrase. If you cannot, that is worth knowing, and the fix is a question to someone who can, not an argument with anyone who uses it differently.
studies.explainEasier: He told them that anger from their Lord had already fallen on them. He asked why they argued with him about names that they and their fathers had made up. God had sent nothing down to back those names.

studies.title: Cut Off At The Root
studies.meaning: Two outcomes are given in one sentence, and they are attributed differently. The rescue is said to be by a mercy from Us, with a cause named. The destruction is described by its effect. The reason attached is what they did: they denied the signs and were not believers. Early scholars regularly notice this imbalance across the Quran. Deliverance is credited upward and ruin is credited to the people themselves. The pattern is consistent enough that its absence would be conspicuous.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. This closes the account of the second community in the surah's sequence, and it is the shortest of the endings. The Arabs remembered these people as having been swept away by a wind, a detail the Quran gives elsewhere but withholds here. No occasion of revelation is reported. The compression keeps the reader's attention on the shape of the outcome rather than on the mechanism of it.

keyTerms.note: Indefinite, so a mercy rather than the mercy, and explicitly sourced. The phrase supplies a cause for the rescue where the ayah supplies none for the survival being deserved.
From the root for what is behind. It names the hindmost part of a body of people, so cutting it off means leaving no continuation rather than defeating those in front.
The active verb of pronouncing something a lie, rather than a word for doubt or ignorance. It makes the cause of the outcome an act performed, which is why the ayah can attach it as a reason.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabs thought of a tribe as a line rather than a population. The worst thing that could be said of a house was that its rear had been cut. That meant no descendants carried the name. Genealogies were recited aloud, and a family without continuation simply disappeared from them. To describe destruction this way was to name a loss that outlasted the people it happened to.
studies.didYouKnow: The exact phrase about cutting off the last remnant appears in four places across the Quran. It comes once of a general judgement, and once here. It comes once of a battle fought during the Prophet's own lifetime, and once of another vanished city. It is one of the Book's fixed expressions for an ending that leaves no remainder behind it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The asymmetry in how the two outcomes are explained is the point of the ayah. Nothing is said about what the rescued had earned; a mercy is named as the cause and left there. The ruin, by contrast, is given a reason that lies entirely in what the people did. The Quran's usual grammar of salvation is visible in miniature here: deliverance is a gift with a source, and loss is a consequence with an author.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same phrase as a general statement about the last of a wrongdoing people being cut away.
Names the wind sent against them over ill-fated days, the detail this summary leaves out.
The parallel ending, which adds that they were delivered from a harsh punishment by mercy.

studies.applyIt: Take one good thing in your life that you usually explain by your own effort, and try explaining it once the other way: as something given to you that you then worked with. Do not talk yourself out of the effort; it was real. Just notice how differently the sentence sits when the gift comes first in the order.
studies.explainEasier: God saved him and the people with him, as a mercy from himself. He cut off the last of the people who called his signs lies and did not believe.

studies.title: Leave Her To Graze
studies.meaning: The third messenger opens with the same sentence as the two before him, and then a sign is produced. The she-camel is attached to God's name, which early scholars explain as an annexation of honour rather than of ownership in any ordinary sense, in the way the sanctuary is called God's house. What follows is not a task but a restraint. Leave her, let her eat on God's earth, and do not touch her with harm. The test being set is a test of leaving something alone.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Thamud lived in the rocky country of the north-west, on the caravan road the Meccans used towards Syria. Their remains were visible to travellers. The Quran never describes how the she-camel came to them. The classical scholars note that the elaborate accounts of her emerging from a rock come from popular and Israelite tradition rather than from anything settled. Ibn Kathir declines to build on them.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to be separate and distinct, the same one behind the word for the space between two things. A proof of this kind makes a distinction visible rather than persuading by argument.
The attachment to the divine name is read by early scholars as one of honour, marking the animal out as set apart, in the same way the sanctuary is called God's house without implying a residence.
A verb of letting go and walking away, the same one used elsewhere in this surah for abandoning inherited gods. The whole instruction is framed as inaction rather than as a duty performed.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Grazing and water were the two things Arabian communities fought over. Both were rationed by custom. A protected pasture was declared and respected. A well had turns, and each herd drank on its day. The Quran elsewhere describes exactly this arrangement being applied to the she-camel, with her drink on one day and theirs on another. The test being set was therefore an ordinary civic arrangement, applied to one animal.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran mentions this she-camel in several surahs and never once describes her. Nothing is said about her size, her colour, or how she came to be there. What is preserved in every telling is only the instruction to leave her alone, and the fact that it was broken. That is a deliberate narrowing, and the early scholars noted it and generally respected it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A sign is given that requires nothing of its witnesses except restraint. That makes the eventual failure hard to explain by hardship. It also shows that a creature can be set apart by being named, not by any property of its own. Nothing in the animal itself is described as remarkable. The parallel with the first refusal in this surah is close. Honour was assigned by command. The offence was refusing to accept an assignment.

crossReferences.why: Sets out the arrangement in detail: her drink on one day and yours on a known day.
Calls the she-camel a test sent to them and instructs the messenger to watch and be patient.
Names her among the signs given, and says signs were withheld because earlier peoples denied them.

studies.applyIt: Find one thing today that you could leave completely alone and normally would not: an argument you could let stand, a message you could not answer, something in someone else's care that you would rather adjust. Leave it. Restraint feels like doing nothing and it is not, which is exactly why it makes such a searching test.
studies.explainEasier: God sent Salih to the people of Thamud, and he was one of them. He told them to worship God alone. He showed them a she-camel as a sign, and told them to let her graze and not to harm her.

studies.title: Palaces And Carved Mountains
studies.meaning: The argument from favours is made again, this time with the evidence in view. They were made successors after the community that had just been described as destroyed, and settled in a land where they built two kinds of dwelling: palaces on the open ground and houses cut into rock. Some early scholars read the pair as summer and winter quarters. Then the instruction, which pivots on a rare verb meaning to spread ruin while moving about. Remember the favours, and do not go through the land wrecking it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Thamud built the rock-cut facades still standing in the north-west of Arabia, and the caravan road from Medina towards Syria passed directly by them. Meccan traders had seen the carved tombs with their own eyes and the site had a reputation as an unlucky place to camp. The Quran is describing something the audience could visit, which is unusual in a sequence otherwise dealing with distant peoples.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to prepare a lodging for someone before they arrive. The verb implies the place was made ready in advance, which is why it sits inside a list of favours rather than achievements.
The verb for cutting stone or wood into shape, used of sculptors. It names skilled and permanent work, which is precisely the point: what they built was meant to outlast them.
A rare verb for going through a place causing damage as you go. The Quran always pairs it with a word for corrupting, and the image is of harm done in motion rather than in one act.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The rock tombs of the north-west were the most impressive ruins an Arab of the seventh century was likely to see. Carved chambers with pillared fronts stood in the cliffs beside a well-travelled road, and caravans passed them on the way to Syria. Arabs treated the site with unease and stories attached to it. When this ayah describes mountains cut into houses, it is naming something the listeners had walked past.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here for going about causing ruin appears only a handful of times in the Quran, and never on its own. It is always joined to the word for corrupting, so the Book never uses it for damage done by accident. The construction describes people whose passage through a place leaves it worse, as a settled habit.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Building is not criticised. The palaces and the carved houses appear in a list of favours received, not in a list of offences. The instruction that follows is about conduct rather than construction. What the passage refuses is the link people make between having built something permanent and being permanent. The reminder of the community they replaced does that work. Those predecessors had drawn the same conclusion from the same kind of evidence.

crossReferences.why: Asks whether they will be left secure among gardens and springs, carving houses from mountains skilfully.
Says they were carving houses from the mountains in security, and what they earned did not avail them.
Names them as those who cut the rock in the valley, in a list of vanished powers.

studies.applyIt: Walk past a building near you that has outlasted the people who put it up: an old shopfront, a wall, a church or a station. Read the date if there is one. Then work out how long ago that was in lifetimes rather than years. It is a two-minute exercise and it does more than most reflections on impermanence manage in an hour.
studies.explainEasier: God put them in place after the people of Aad and settled them in the land. They built big houses on the flat ground and cut homes into the mountains. He told them to remember his gifts and not to go around wrecking the earth.

studies.title: Do You Actually Know
studies.meaning: The elite put a question to the people they had kept beneath them, and the Arabic of that second description matters: it does not say the weak, it says those who were made weak. The question is a sneer, inviting them to admit they cannot really know. The answer does not take the bait. It says nothing about the man and everything about the message: we believe in what he was sent with. The reply from the other side is then blunt and complete, refusing exactly what was just affirmed.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the social shape is the one the early Muslims lived inside. The first followers in Mecca included slaves, freedmen and men from minor clans. The leading families made the make-up of that group into an argument. They asked whether God would guide such people ahead of them. The Quran repeats this pattern in community after community. That suggests the dynamic rather than the personalities is the subject.

keyTerms.note: A passive form, so weakness is something done to them rather than a quality they have. The Quran uses this word for the oppressed throughout, and the grammar quietly assigns responsibility for their condition.

The mirror of the first word and in the active voice. One group did something to itself; the other had something done to it, and the two verbs are built on the same pattern to make the contrast audible.
A passive participle rather than a title. The question asks whether he is a sent one, which is a question about his commission, and the answer given deliberately shifts to what was sent instead.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Standing in an Arabian town was not only wealth. It was the right to be listened to. A man of a strong clan could dismiss a client's opinion without argument, and the client had no forum in which to press it. What happens in this exchange is unusual and would have been noticed. Men of no standing are answering the assembly directly, and they are not backing down.
studies.didYouKnow: The answer does not respond to the question that was asked. They were asked whether they knew a particular man was sent. They reply that they believe in what he was sent with. The classical scholars note the redirection. The questioners wanted a claim about a person that could be disputed, and were given a statement about a message instead.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Faith is located in content rather than in personal loyalty. That distinction has long consequences. A commitment attached to a man rises and falls with him. A commitment to what he brought can be examined, and it survives him. The passage also shows the socially powerless taking the firmer position. It does not present this as a reversal or a surprise, which is itself a claim about where such positions come from.

crossReferences.why: Continues this dispute into the hereafter, with the same two groups and the same two verbs.
Objects to an earlier messenger that the lowest of the people are the ones who follow him.
Separates the message from the messenger explicitly, asking whether faith would turn back at his death.

studies.applyIt: Notice whether your confidence in something you believe rests on the thing itself or on the person who told you. Both feel identical from inside. A quick test: imagine that person turning out badly, and see whether the belief moves. If it does, you have found something worth understanding on its own terms this month.
studies.explainEasier: The proud leaders asked the people they had kept down whether they really knew Salih was sent by his Lord. Those people said they believed in what he brought. The proud ones said they refused to believe any of it.

studies.title: They Hamstrung The Camel
studies.meaning: The verb used is specific. It means to cut the leg tendons, the standard way of bringing down a large animal, and it is a deliberate, close act rather than a killing at a distance. Three things are then reported in order: the deed, the insolence towards their Lord's command, and the challenge. Bring what you promise. The answer comes in one short ayah, and the last word describes bodies fallen forward and still. The whole reversal takes fewer words than the challenge did.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing the third account in the surah's sequence. The audience knew the site and its reputation, so this was not a distant legend to them. No occasion of revelation is reported. The Quran gives the punishment here as a violent shaking. It names it differently in other surahs. The classical scholars square the two as different aspects of one event, not as competing reports.

keyTerms.note: The precise verb for severing the leg tendons of a camel so it collapses. It describes a butcher's act done at arm's length, which is why the word carries a coldness that a general word for killing would not.
From a root meaning dry, hard and past bending, used of a stick too stiff to shape. Insolence in this vocabulary is a hardening rather than an outburst.

From a verb used of a bird crouching flat to the ground and not moving. It describes posture rather than death, which is why translations reach for lifeless bodies without finding an exact equivalent.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Hamstringing a camel was a recognised act with a recognised meaning. It was how you destroyed an enemy's wealth without stealing it. It was done in spite. A camel was a family's transport, milk and capital at once. So the act was understood as a declaration rather than a theft. Doing it to an animal everyone had agreed to protect was a public statement that the agreement was over.
studies.didYouKnow: Elsewhere the Quran says a single man did this. It describes one of them being called, and doing the deed. Here the verb is plural and the whole community is named. The classical scholars explain the difference by saying an act one person carries out with everyone else's consent is attributed to all of them. They treat the two accounts as one.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage attaches the outcome to a broken restraint rather than to disbelief in the abstract. What is destroyed is an animal. What is broken is an agreement about leaving it alone. That keeps the whole episode at the scale of ordinary conduct. It also shows a demand for proof being answered exactly as it was made. They asked for the promised thing to be brought, and it arrived. The Quran presents that without comment.

crossReferences.why: Names one man as the one who called out and did it, then describes the single cry that followed.
Gives the whole account in five short lines, ending on the community being levelled together.
Says they preferred blindness to guidance, and names the punishment with a different word.

studies.applyIt: Think about a small agreement you are part of that everyone keeps by simply not doing something: a quiet carriage, a shared kitchen, a queue. Notice how the whole arrangement depends on restraint and how quickly one person can end it. Then keep yours today with more attention than usual. That is the entire mechanism this passage is describing.
studies.explainEasier: They cut the camel down and went against what their Lord had told them. They told Salih to bring the punishment he kept warning about. The earth shook, and they were left lying still in their homes.

studies.title: You Did Not Like Advisers
studies.meaning: A speech is made to a town that the previous ayah has already described as still. Early scholars differ over how to place it, some reading it as spoken as he departed and others as a formal discharge of what he owed them, and either way the words are addressed past the dead to the reader. Two claims are made and both are about completion: I conveyed the message, and I counselled you. Then the diagnosis, which is not that they failed to understand. They did not like advisers.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) faced a situation of the same shape in the city. The Quran told him again and again that his job ended with delivery, not with results. That principle is put here in an ancient messenger's mouth. It comes after everything has already been lost, which is the hardest possible setting for it. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to reach a destination. The verb is about arrival rather than effort, so the claim is that the message got to them, not merely that he tried to deliver it.
From a root for what is pure and unmixed, and for stitching a garment tight with no gaps. Counsel of this kind has no thread of the counsellor's own interest running through it.

The ordinary verb for loving. The verdict is affective rather than intellectual, which is why the ayah does not say they misunderstood or disbelieved the advice, only that they had no liking for the people who gave it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Advice in a tribal society was a delicate transaction. To counsel a man was to imply he had got something wrong. Doing so in public could be taken as an insult that required an answer. This is why the good counsellor was so highly praised in poetry and so rarely welcome in practice. The complaint at the end of this ayah names a social difficulty everyone listening had felt from both sides.
studies.didYouKnow: The root for sincere counsel runs through this surah more than through any other part of the Quran, and it is spoken by different figures. The deceiver in the Garden uses it of himself while lying. Three separate messengers use it of themselves while telling the truth. The word never changes; only who is saying it does.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Responsibility is defined by delivery rather than by outcome. That is one of the Quran's steadiest positions. It is also a considerable relief to anyone who has tried to help. The closing diagnosis pushes further. Suppose refusal is a matter of dislike rather than disagreement. Then no better argument would have changed it. The messengers in this surah are shown running out of things to say, not running out of reasons.

crossReferences.why: States the limit plainly: the messenger's duty is only the delivering, and God knows what is concealed.
The next messenger in this surah says almost the same words over another ruined town.
Says he cannot guide whom he loves, since guidance belongs to God alone.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone who told you something true that you did not want to hear, and whom you have quietly avoided since. That avoidance is what this ayah is describing. You do not have to act on the advice. Just get back in touch this week for an ordinary reason, and see whether the discomfort was ever really about them.
studies.explainEasier: He turned away from them and spoke. He said he had passed on his Lord's message and had given them honest advice. But they did not like people who gave advice.

studies.title: Their Only Answer
studies.meaning: This messenger is introduced differently from the three before him. Each of those was called the brother of his people. This one is simply named. The classical scholars note that he came to a community he was not descended from. The charge he brings is stated. The word for excess at its close is a general one. It names a people who go past every limit, not one failing. Then comes the response. The ayah is careful to say it was their only answer. Not an argument. An expulsion.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Quran locates these cities on the road between Arabia and Syria. It says elsewhere that its audience passed the site by morning and by night, so the ruins were part of the landscape they travelled. No occasion of revelation is reported. In this surah the account is cut down to five ayat, while surahs 11, 15 and 26 give the visitors, the negotiation and the escape at length.

keyTerms.note: Definite here rather than indefinite, so a particular thing already understood. The root means exceeding all measure, and the Quran uses the same noun of very different conduct in other passages.

keyTerms.gloss: people who go past all bounds
keyTerms.note: From a root for wastefulness and overstepping, used of spending beyond need and of any excess. The summary charge is breadth of transgression rather than one specific act.
A reflexive form of the verb for purifying. It is spoken as an accusation, and the word chosen is one the Quran elsewhere uses with approval, so the insult states a compliment without meaning to.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Expulsion from a town was a real sentence with real results. Outside the settlement there was no water you had rights to. There was no protection, and no standing in any dispute. Communities used exile rather than killing because it was slower. It left the outcome to the desert. To answer a warning by turning the warner out was a decision about whether he lived, not just a brush-off.
studies.didYouKnow: This messenger is the only one in the surah's sequence not introduced as the brother of his people. The three before him and the one after are each described that way. He is not. The classical scholars link this to his having come from elsewhere. The pattern is visible in the Arabic, and no comment is made on it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The community's answer is the part the ayah frames. It records no counter-argument at all. There is only a decision to remove the people raising the question. And the reason given for removing them is that they keep themselves clean. That flips the usual direction of moral language. Restraint is named as the offence, stated as though no one could bear it. The Quran leaves the sentence standing without comment. That is the sharpest way to present it.

crossReferences.why: Tells the audience they pass the ruins of these towns in the morning and at night.
Gives the same episode at length, including his distress and his appeal for some support.
Records the same expulsion demand in nearly identical words, calling them people who keep clean.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time someone's carefulness is used against them: called precious, uptight, holier than you. Whether or not you share their standard, the move being made is the one in this ayah, and it is worth recognising. If it is happening in a room you are in, you do not have to defend them. Just decline to join in.
studies.explainEasier: Lot told his people to stop what they were doing. They did not argue with him. They just said to throw him and his family out of town for being too clean.

studies.title: Except For His Wife
studies.meaning: The rescue is stated with an exception. The word describing her position carries a real double meaning in Arabic. Its root covers both staying behind and passing away. The early scholars record readings along both lines and do not force a choice. The Quran elsewhere is clear that she did not share his stand. Then the ruin, described only as a rain. No substance is named here, though other surahs supply one. The ayah closes by turning to the reader with one command: look.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Quran's audience travelled the road these ruins lay on, and other passages tell them so plainly. No occasion of revelation is reported for the passage. In this surah the account takes five ayat because the sequence, not the story, is the subject. The closing instruction to look at the outcome is a formula the surah uses more than once, and it addresses one listener rather than a group.

keyTerms.note: The root means both to remain and to pass away, so the word can name those left behind or those who perished with the rest. Classical commentators record both senses and do not insist on one.
The Quran uses this form of the verb almost always for punishment, while a related form is used for ordinary rain. The choice of form does the work that naming the substance would otherwise do.
From the root for a heel and for what follows behind. An outcome in this vocabulary is what comes after and treads on the heels of what preceded it, which makes it a consequence rather than an event.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Household loyalty was assumed absolutely in that society. A wife belonged to her husband's protection. A man's household stood or fell with him. That is why this exception would have sounded strange rather than merely sad. The Quran makes the point directly elsewhere. It uses this woman and one other as examples that closeness to a righteous man secures nothing on its own.
studies.didYouKnow: The final clause steps out of the story and speaks to one person. It uses a singular command telling them to look. This surah uses the device again and again, and it works like a camera turning to face the audience. What is asked for is not sympathy or fear. It is watching a pattern the sequence has now shown four times.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Closeness is denied any saving power. The exception is recorded without explanation and without softening. It sits inside a sentence that is otherwise about rescue. The Quran turns that into a general principle elsewhere. The passage also sets its two halves in a fixed order: rescue first, ruin second. That is the order the surah has kept throughout. The ones who were saved are always named before the ones who were not.

crossReferences.why: Names two wives of righteous men as examples, saying their husbands availed them nothing.
Supplies what this account withholds, describing stones of baked clay sent down in succession.
Gives the same exception, adding that the household was to be delivered and she was to remain.

studies.applyIt: Ask whether any part of your religious confidence rests on somebody else: a devout parent, a knowledgeable friend, a community you belong to. Those are real supports and worth keeping. But name one thing you know or do that would still be there if they were not. If nothing comes to mind, that is the useful result of the exercise.
studies.explainEasier: God saved Lot and his family, but not his wife. She was among those who stayed behind. Then a rain came down on the town and ruined it. The verse tells the reader to look at how it ended.

studies.title: Give The Full Measure
studies.meaning: The fourth messenger opens with the same sentence as the others. Then his own subject arrives. That is unusual in this sequence. Give the measure and the weight in full, and do not shortchange people in their things. Two instruments are named. Dry goods were measured by volume and everything else by balance, so the pair covers the whole of trade. Then comes the wider order not to corrupt the land after it has been set right. That assumes the land was in good order to begin with.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Midian lay in the north-west of Arabia near the head of the Red Sea. It sat on the route between the peninsula and Syria, and it lived on the traffic passing through. The Quraysh ran the same kind of economy on the same road. This is the only messenger in the surah's sequence whose message names a specific trade matter, and the match with Mecca's own business would not have been lost on the audience.

keyTerms.note: Two different instruments. Grain and dates were sold by a measured container, everything else by weight against stones, so naming both covers every transaction a person in that market could make.
A verb for reducing what is owed rather than for stealing outright. The Quran uses the related noun for the paltry price Joseph was sold at, so the word names a loss inflicted through a transaction.

From the root for soundness and repair. The phrase assumes the land was already in working order, which makes corruption an interference with something functioning rather than a failure to improve it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A market in Arabia ran on containers and stones. Grain went into a wooden measure. Silver and goods went on a hand balance against known weights. Both could be quietly wrong. A shallow measure or a light stone was invisible in a single sale and hugely profitable over a season. Buyers with any experience carried their own weights, which tells you how common the problem was.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran gives a whole short surah to this subject. It opens with woe to those who take full measure from people and give less in return. The classical scholars link the two passages closely. The pairing shows the Book treating a matter that looks small and technical as serious enough for a chapter of its own.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage runs worship and honest dealing together in one speech. The order to serve God alone and the order to fill the measure come from the same man in the same breath. Nothing marks one as religion and the other as ethics. What follows makes the link plain. Shortchanging is described as corrupting land that had been set right. That raises a market practice to the level of damage done to the world.

crossReferences.why: A whole surah opens on this exact practice, taking full measure and giving short in return.
Places the balance in the created order itself and instructs against transgressing in it.
Repeats the instruction and calls it better and finer in outcome.

studies.applyIt: Look at one place where you give slightly less than you are paid for and nobody would notice. The last twenty minutes of a working day. A job done to the standard that will just pass. Do that one thing properly this week. The passage treats the unseen margin as the whole subject. It is the only part of your work nobody but you can inspect.
studies.explainEasier: Shuaib told his town to weigh and measure things honestly. He told them not to give people less than they paid for. He told them not to ruin a land that was already in good shape. He said this was better for them.

studies.title: Do Not Sit On Every Road
studies.meaning: Three things are named in one instruction. Sitting on the roads. Threatening. Turning anyone who believes away from God's path, while trying to make that path look crooked. The classical scholars read the roads two ways: as the trade routes where travellers could be waylaid, and as the approaches by which someone might come to the message. The Arabic supports both, and the two readings back each other up. Then a favour is recalled, and it is a matter of numbers: you were few, and He made you many.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Midian sat on a route that carried goods between Arabia and Syria. Reports kept by the early scholars describe its people as taxing travellers as well as turning them from the messenger. In Mecca the same thing was happening in a different form, with pilgrims warned off before they could hear the recitation. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah.

keyTerms.note: The verb for sitting down, used of an ambush set beside a road. It appears earlier in this very surah in a vow to sit on the straight path, which makes the instruction here a warning against a familiar role.
A noun for a deviation from straightness. What is being described is not blocking the road but bending it, so travellers who follow it faithfully still arrive somewhere else.

An intensive form of the verb for increasing in number. The favour recalled is population itself, which for a community living on a trade route was the difference between holding a position and losing it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Every trade route had its choke points. Every merchant knew which stretches meant paying someone. Some communities lived respectably on tolls. Others lived on the threat of what happened if the toll went unpaid. The line between the two was not always visible from outside. A town sitting on a road had a permanent temptation attached to its geography, and this instruction addresses it directly.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used in this prohibition and the noun for path are the same pair the adversary spoke earlier in this surah. He vowed to sit for people on the straight path. The Quran does not connect them out loud. It simply hands the same two words to human beings a few dozen ayat later, this time as something they are told not to do.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Getting in the way is named as a wrong of its own, separate from disbelief. A person may refuse the message and stop there. What is named here is the further work of standing between other people and it. Bending the path rather than barring it is the sharper part. A road with a bend in it still looks like a road, and everyone travelling it believes they are going where it said.

crossReferences.why: Describes the wrongdoers with the identical phrase, hindering from God's path and seeking it crooked.
Names those who prefer this life, hinder from God's path, and seek to make it crooked.
Praises the Book sent down with no crookedness in it, using the same rare noun.

studies.applyIt: Ask whether you stand between anyone and something good for them. It is rarely deliberate. It looks like the joke that makes a person's seriousness awkward, or the plan that quietly needs them not to change. Pick one relationship and check. Getting out of the way is easier than helping and it is what this ayah actually asks for.
studies.explainEasier: Shuaib told his people to stop sitting by the roads. They were scaring travellers away from God's path. He also reminded them of a gift. They were once only a few, and God made them many.

studies.title: Until God Judges Between Us
studies.meaning: The community has split, and the messenger describes the split without assigning blame in the sentence. One group believed, one did not. What he says next is addressed to everybody: be patient. The Arabic verb is plural and the instruction is given to both parties at once, and the judgement he points to is said to be between us, a phrase that includes him alongside the people refusing him. He does not claim the verdict in advance. He names who holds it and stops there.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The community in Mecca was split in exactly this way at the time. The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was told again and again to endure rather than to press. Families were divided, and both sides lived in the same small city with no way to separate. No occasion of revelation is reported for this ayah. It is the last thing this messenger says before the threat of expulsion is made against him.

keyTerms.note: From the root for going around something. It names a body of people in motion rather than a fixed faction, and using it twice in one sentence makes the division sound provisional rather than settled.
From a root meaning to bind or restrain, used of tethering an animal. Patience here is holding a position under pressure rather than accepting an outcome, and the verb is addressed to both parties.

The root also gives the word for the bit placed in a horse's mouth, since judging is restraining. A judgement in this vocabulary settles a dispute by holding both parties, not only by declaring one right.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: There was no court in Arabia. Disputes went to an arbitrator both sides agreed to accept. He was often a man from a neutral clan, or a keeper of a shrine. The whole system rested on the parties agreeing in advance to be bound. Everything in this sentence would have sounded ordinary to the first listeners. Two parties, a named arbitrator, and an order to wait for the ruling without acting in the meantime.
studies.didYouKnow: The Arabic says judge between us, using a form that includes the speaker with the people refusing him. He does not say between you and me, or between you and God. The classical scholars note that this phrasing turns down the role of prosecutor. He places himself as a party to the case, not as the one bringing it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets out a way of living with religious disagreement that stays unresolved. It does not pretend the difference away, and it does not settle it by force. Both sides are told to endure. The verdict is placed with someone who is not in the room. That leaves the disagreement standing and takes away the rush to end it. It is a hard posture to hold, and the one the Quran keeps recommending to a minority under pressure.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same instruction to the Prophet: follow what is revealed and be patient until God judges.
Turns the same idea into a prayer, asking the one who knows the unseen to judge between His servants.
Instructs saying that God will gather us and to Him is the destination, with no argument between us.

studies.applyIt: Think of a disagreement you keep reopening with someone who is not going to change. Try treating it as filed rather than lost. You are not conceding the point and you are not agreeing to differ. You are declining to litigate it again this month. Notice how much of the relationship becomes available once that one conversation is set down.
studies.explainEasier: Shuaib said that some of his people believed him and some did not. He told both groups to wait and be patient. God would judge between them in the end. God is the best judge.

studies.title: Or You Will Return
studies.meaning: The threat is specific. Leave the town, or come back to our way. The classical scholars notice a difficulty in the wording. The messenger had never been in their way, so he had nothing to return to. They read the verb either loosely, as covering the whole group he is named with, or as aimed at the believers among them who had been. The shape of the offer is not in dispute. Belonging is the lever. The reply is a question rather than a refusal: even if we are unwilling.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The pressure described was the pressure the early community lived under. Expulsion from a clan meant losing protection entirely. The Quraysh used exactly this instrument, including a boycott that cut a whole branch of the family off from trade and marriage. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah. The match between the two situations is left for the reader to see.

keyTerms.note: Doubly emphatic in Arabic, with an oath particle and a heavy ending. The construction is the one used for a vow, so the sentence is not a warning about what might happen but a commitment to make it happen.
A word for the road a community walks, covering religion, custom and social order together. Leaving it in that setting meant leaving everything the word contained, not only a set of beliefs.

From the root for what is disliked and imposed against inclination. The reply asks whether the demand still stands with this word attached, which exposes what compelled adherence would actually amount to.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A town in that world was not a place you could simply leave and rejoin elsewhere. Your water rights, your trade contacts, your standing in a dispute and your children's marriage prospects were all attached to it. Expulsion was the heaviest penalty short of violence. It was preferred because it looked less brutal while leaving the outcome to chance.
studies.didYouKnow: The answer given is not a refusal but a question. In Arabic it is three words. Rather than saying they will not return, the reply asks whether the demand is meant to apply even to people who do not want it. That hands the problem with forced belief back to the people making the demand, and requires them to answer it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Belonging and belief are pulled apart. The threat assumes they are the same thing. It assumes a person can be returned to a religion the way he is returned to a town. The reply exposes that assumption by asking what such a return would consist of. The Quran states the principle directly elsewhere. Here it shows the same conclusion arriving in the middle of an argument, from someone with no power to enforce anything.

crossReferences.why: States the principle this exchange dramatises, that there is no compulsion in religion.
Gives the same threat from other communities to their messengers, expulsion or return to our way.
Asks whether the Prophet would compel people to believe, when God did not make everyone believe.

studies.applyIt: Notice where you use belonging as a lever, even gently: the tone that tells someone they are drifting from the group, the invitation that quietly stops arriving. Most families and workplaces run on some of this. Pick one person you have been pulling and stop pulling for a month. See what they choose when the cost of choosing goes down.
studies.explainEasier: The proud leaders of the town told Shuaib to leave. They said he and his followers could stay only if they went back to their old ways. He asked if they would force him, even when he did not want it.

studies.title: Decide Between Us In Truth
studies.meaning: The answer to the threat of expulsion runs through five moves in one sentence. Returning would itself be a lie told about God. Return is not ours to make, unless God wills it. The early scholars read that as a reservation about the future, not an opening they are entertaining. His knowledge takes in everything. On Him we rely. And then a prayer. It uses a verb that means to open, and southern Arabian usage used it for giving a verdict, so the request is for the matter to be opened and settled.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The believers in the city faced exactly this pressure, and the Quran repeatedly gives them speech to hold rather than instructions to fight. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah. It comes as the last word of this messenger before the account of what happened to the town, and it is notable that the speech asks for a decision rather than for rescue or for the punishment of anyone.

keyTerms.note: A reservation attached to a firm refusal. The early scholars read it as a refusal to guarantee one's own future rather than as doubt, since no person holds their own heart's next position.
From a root meaning to appoint an agent to act for you. Reliance in this vocabulary is a delegation of the outcome, not an abandonment of effort, since one still instructs the agent.
The ordinary verb for opening. In southern Arabian usage it also meant to judge, and a judge was called an opener, so the prayer asks for something shut to be opened and decided.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arbitration was arranged by consent. The arbitrator was usually paid, housed and courted by both sides. A man with no clan behind him could rarely get a hearing at all. The whole system depended on someone strong enough to enforce the ruling. To appeal past every available arbitrator to God directly was the move of someone who had run out of human help and knew it.
studies.didYouKnow: This is one of the densest single ayat in the surah. One unbroken sentence holds a refusal, a reason, and a reservation about the future. It also holds a statement about God's knowledge, a declaration of reliance, and a prayer with a name of God attached. The classical scholars treat it as a model of how a hard answer can be given with no threat in it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Reliance is shown as something that follows a decision rather than replacing one. The refusal is made first, plainly. Only then is the outcome handed over. The reservation attached is the more searching part. Even while refusing, they will not claim to know what they will be tomorrow. That keeps confidence about your own faith from turning into another form of the pride the surah has been describing.

crossReferences.why: Instructs attaching the same reservation to any statement about what one will do tomorrow.
Gives the same reliance in the same setting, messengers answering a threat with patience and trust.
Uses the same verb for judging, asking the one who gathers all to open between us in truth.

studies.applyIt: Next time you say what you will definitely do, or definitely never do, add the reservation this ayah adds. Not out loud, unless you want to. Just internally: if God wills. It costs nothing, it does not weaken the decision, and it quietly removes the claim to own a future you have never once controlled.
studies.explainEasier: Shuaib said he would be lying about God if he went back to their old religion. He said God had saved them from it. Then he asked God to judge between his people and him.

studies.title: It Was They Who Lost
studies.meaning: One word travels through this passage and comes back changed. The notables warn their people that following the messenger will make them losers. The town is then struck, and the closing ayah returns the word to the people who threw it, twice in one sentence. The repetition is not a stylistic accident; Arabic reserves this kind of doubling for emphasis a reader is meant to hear. In between sits a line saying it was as though they had never lived richly there, which uses a word for dwelling built from the root for wealth.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The argument the notables use here is the argument the Quraysh used in Mecca: this will cost you, look at the people who have already joined, consider your trade. It was a warning about ruin delivered in commercial terms to people whose lives were commercial. No occasion of revelation is reported. This closes the last of the surah's four Arabian and near-Arabian accounts before the narrative moves to Egypt.

keyTerms.note: A trading word for those whose venture came back short. Its use as a threat and then as a verdict is the hinge of the passage, since the same term measures both what they warned of and what happened.
