From the root for wealth and self-sufficiency, the verb means to live somewhere in comfort. The phrase says it was as though they had never been well off there, not merely as though they had never been there.
From a root for trembling and shuddering, used of the earth and of a heart. It names the movement rather than the cause, which is why other surahs can describe the same event with a different word.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Commercial words filled Arabian speech. Men spoke of a good deed as a profitable trade and a wasted life as a bad season. Poets used the language of debt and settlement for honour. When the notables call the believers losers, they are not reaching for a metaphor. They are using the plainest word their society had for a person who had made a bad decision with everything they owned.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah describing what happened to this town is word for word the same as the one describing the fate of a different community earlier in the same surah. Not similar. Identical. The Quran does not remark on the repeat. It simply gives the same sentence twice, so a reader moving through the sequence hears an outcome they have already heard.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage handles the question of who is really taking the risk. Both sides in the argument agree that a wrong choice here is ruinous. They differ only on which choice that is. That is a truer picture of religious disagreement than one where a careless party faces a careful one. What settles it in the story is not the strength of either argument. It is an event, and the Quran presents that as the only thing that ever does settle it.

crossReferences.why: The ayah repeated verbatim here, describing an earlier community struck in the same terms.
The parallel ending, which names a single cry instead of a quake and repeats the same closing line.
Gives the same account in two ayat, with the same warning about measure and the same outcome.

studies.applyIt: Notice who is telling you that a good decision will cost you, and what they have at stake in your not making it. Often nothing dishonest is going on; people warn sincerely out of their own fears. But name the interest anyway, once, quietly. It does not make the warning wrong, and it stops you from mistaking their fear for information.
studies.explainEasier: The leaders warned people that following Shuaib would make them losers. Then an earthquake hit the town. The ones who turned Shuaib away were the real losers in the end.

studies.title: How Should I Grieve
studies.meaning: The whole weight of this ayah sits in its last clause. It is a question about feeling, not a statement about duty. The verb for grieving comes from a root that also gives the word for a healer and for comfort. So the grief being named is the kind that attends someone else's harm. The early scholars do not read the question as hardness. They read it as a man letting go of a sorrow he no longer has anywhere to put. Everything that could be said has been said, and the people it was said to are gone.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was told again and again not to grieve himself to death over people who refused. The instruction came often enough that the Quran clearly treated the danger as real. No occasion of revelation is reported for this ayah. It closes the last of the surah's Arabian accounts, and it is the second of two nearly identical farewell speeches in this stretch of the surah.

keyTerms.note: From a root that also produces the words for consoling and for a physician who mends. The grief named is bound up with wanting to repair someone, which is why it attaches to a messenger rather than to an opponent.
Plural, so more than one delivery over time. The word records repetition, which matters for the claim being made: he is not saying he spoke once but that he kept speaking.
A verb for turning the body away and departing. Elsewhere in this surah the same verb describes people turning from a message, so the messenger's departure uses the vocabulary of their refusal.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Grief in Arabia was a public performance with rules. Women keened and poets composed elegies. A man's standing partly rested on whom he mourned and how openly. Mourning people who had rejected you and were not your dead sat outside the whole system. There was no form for it. What this ayah names is a private sorrow with no social outlet, and that is the sort most likely to become unbearable.
studies.didYouKnow: Two messengers in this surah give a departing speech, and the first halves are almost the same words. The second halves diverge sharply. One ends by naming what was wrong with the people, that they had no liking for advisers. This one ends by asking a question about the speaker's own heart, which is the only place in the sequence where a messenger examines himself.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage takes seriously the cost of caring about people who will not be helped. It does not tell the reader that such grief is wrong, and it does not describe it as being switched off. It stages a question instead, asked after the work is finished, which leaves the emotion intact while removing the obligation that fed it. That distinction, between what you owe and what you feel, runs through the Quran's treatment of every messenger.

crossReferences.why: Asks whether the Prophet will destroy himself with grief if they do not believe this account.
Tells him not to let his soul go out in regrets over them, since God knows what they do.
Opens a surah by noting he may be killing himself with grief that they will not believe.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone you have worried about for years with no change. Ask what you actually still owe them, as a list of specific actions. Then do those. Everything past that list is grief with no task attached. It is worth naming as grief, rather than carrying it as an unfinished duty.
studies.explainEasier: Shuaib walked away from his town. He told them he had passed on the messages from his Lord and had given them good advice. Then he asked why he should feel sad for people who would not listen.

studies.title: So That They Might Turn
studies.meaning: A rule is stated with no exceptions. No prophet was ever sent to a town without its people being taken by hardship and distress. The early scholars separate the two words. They read the first of trouble from outside, like poverty or conflict, and the second of harm to the body. Then comes the stated purpose. The verb is the one for lowering yourself to ask. Hardship is described as aimed at a posture, not at a punishment, and the particle attached leaves the result genuinely open.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The early community was under real pressure, and the surrounding city read that pressure as evidence the message was false. This ayah reverses the reading, treating difficulty as a normal accompaniment of prophecy rather than a verdict on it. No occasion of revelation is reported. The passage steps back from the four narratives just given and states the pattern they share in general terms.

keyTerms.note: From a root for force and severity, used of war and want. The early scholars generally read it of difficulty striking from outside a person: poverty, conflict, the failure of a season.

From the root for damage and injury. The early scholars read it of harm reaching the body itself, such as illness. Together the two words cover what can go wrong around a person and what can go wrong inside them.
From a root meaning lowliness and smallness. The verb describes making yourself small in order to ask, and the same root appears earlier in this surah in the instruction on how to call upon God.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian religion was largely a matter of trade and season. You went to the gods when the rains failed, when a child sickened, or before a raid. The approach was made in the posture the word here describes: crouched, small, asking. Nobody needed to be taught how to do it. What the ayah describes is not a strange behaviour but a familiar one. The question is only what occasions bring it out, and towards whom it is directed.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for humbling oneself here is built on the same root as a noun used earlier in this surah. There the reader is told to call upon their Lord humbly and in secret. So the surah names the posture as an instruction in one place and as the purpose of hardship in another. One root connects a command and a consequence.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Difficulty is given a purpose that is neither punishment nor a test of endurance. It is described as aimed at one posture, the posture of asking. That turns hardship into an invitation that arrives in a painful form. The particle that introduces the purpose is one of hope, not certainty. So the ayah stops short of promising the outcome. Suffering is given a direction without being given a promise.

crossReferences.why: States the same rule for earlier communities and adds that their hearts hardened instead of softening.
Gives the instruction that uses the same root, to call upon your Lord humbly and in secret.
Notes that they were seized by punishment and still did not lower themselves to their Lord.

studies.applyIt: Think about the last time you prayed with your whole attention, and what had just happened. For most people the honest answer involves something going wrong. Try one deliberate asking today with nothing wrong. No crisis. No request that matters much. It is surprisingly hard, and the difficulty is the information.
studies.explainEasier: God says he never sent a prophet to a town without its people meeting hard times. Money ran short and bodies got sick. The point was to make people humble, so they would turn and ask him for help.

studies.title: Then We Gave Them Ease
studies.meaning: The second stage is the dangerous one. Hardship is exchanged for good conditions. They grow and multiply. Then they say something that sounds like wisdom: hard times and ease touched our fathers too. The early scholars read this as the clever refusal rather than the crude one. It is not a denial that anything happened. It is a way of making it natural. Fortune turns, it always has, and so nothing is being said to anyone. Then the seizure, sudden and unnoticed, which is what that reading leaves a person open to.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The city had grown from a settlement around a well into the trading and religious centre of western Arabia. That happened within living memory of its grandfathers. The Quraysh explained their position by family line, trading skill and the sanctuary's prestige, all of which were true. No occasion of revelation is reported. The passage completes a two-stage description begun in the ayah before: hardship first, then relief.

keyTerms.note: A verb for substituting one thing for another in the same position. The good conditions are described as occupying the space the hardship had, which keeps both stages inside a single arrangement.

From a root for abundant growth, which also yields the words for pardon and for effacing. Early Arabic dictionary writers connect the senses through the idea of something spreading over and covering what was there.
A noun used adverbially for something arriving with no approach. The Quran attaches it to the final Hour repeatedly, and the word carries the specific quality of a thing that gave no notice.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian life ran on real cycles. A drought year was followed by a green one. A tribe that lost a battle recovered over a generation, and everyone had seen fortunes turn twice. The observation these people make is therefore accurate. What the ayah addresses is not a false claim about the world. It is a true one used to conclude that nothing further needs looking at, which is a different and harder error.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used for their increase comes from the same root as the Arabic word for pardon and for wiping something away. Early Arabic dictionary writers explain the link through the idea of growth that covers a thing over. Plants cover ground. Hair grows over a scar. In this root, the vocabulary of plenty and of erasing is one vocabulary.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Ease is presented as a more searching condition than hardship. Difficulty at least produces a posture of asking. Comfort produces an explanation, and the explanation offered here is not stupid. That is the point. The passage suggests that what closes a person off is often a reasonable account of their own life, arrived at honestly. It leaves no obvious place for a warning to enter, and nothing that feels like a refusal.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same sequence, doors of everything opened until they rejoiced, then a sudden seizure.
Notes that they and their fathers were given long enjoyment until the age grew long upon them.
Names the two misreadings directly, honour when given ease and humiliation when provision is measured.

studies.applyIt: Take the most reasonable explanation you have for why your life is going well or badly, and check whether it is doing a second job. Reasonable accounts are often true and also close a question. Ask yourself what you would have to consider if that explanation were only half the story. Ten minutes, and no conclusion required.
studies.explainEasier: After the hard times, God gave the people good times instead. They grew in number and got comfortable. They said that good and bad days come to everyone. Then trouble caught them all at once, when they were not looking.

studies.title: Blessings From Sky And Earth
studies.meaning: The sentence is built as something that did not happen. Had they believed and guarded themselves, blessings would have been opened upon them from the sky and from the earth. The classical scholars read that pair plainly, as rain above and growth below. The verb is the one for opening a door or a gate. That makes provision sound like something held behind a barrier rather than made. Then the actual outcome. The reason attached is not their disbelief in the abstract but what they had been earning.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The audience lived in a valley where nothing grew. They understood provision as something that arrived, not something the ground made. No occasion of revelation is reported. This ayah sits between the description of how communities are handled and the questions that follow about feeling safe. It supplies the choice the whole sequence has kept unspoken: these outcomes were not the only ones on offer.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to kneel and settle, as a camel does, and connected to a pool where water gathers and stays. A blessing in this vocabulary is good that comes to rest rather than good that passes through.
The verb for opening a gate or a lock. Provision is pictured as already present and withheld behind something, which is a different picture from one in which it has to be produced.

The commercial verb for acquiring through work. Attaching it to the seizure makes the outcome a wage rather than a verdict, and its continuous form makes it the product of a practice rather than an incident.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca imported almost everything it ate. The valley grew nothing. Wealth came in on the backs of animals from Yemen and Syria, which is why the word for a gate opening would have felt exactly right. Elsewhere in Arabia a good year meant rain arriving on the highlands and grass appearing where there had been stone. Both halves of this ayah's promise, from above and from below, described things people had watched arrive.
studies.didYouKnow: The Arabic here uses the form kept for something contrary to what actually happened. It says this would have been so, and was not. The Quran does not use it often. Its appearance here means the ayah is not stating a general rule about wealth. It names a particular history that these communities did not have.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A link is drawn between what a community is like inside and how it fares outside. It is drawn carefully. The passage speaks of towns rather than persons. That keeps it from becoming a rule that good people prosper, a claim the Quran denies elsewhere by showing prophets in hardship. What is offered is a statement about whole peoples over long stretches of time. And it is stated as a road not taken, not as a machine.

crossReferences.why: Promises rain in abundance, wealth and children to a community that seeks its Lord's forgiveness.
Says that upholding the revelations would have brought them provision from above and beneath their feet.
Attaches provision from unexpected directions to guarding oneself, at the level of a person.

studies.applyIt: Think of one collective you belong to: a family, a team, a neighbourhood. Ask what would actually be different about it if everyone in it were slightly more honest for a month. Not a fantasy, a specific difference. Then supply your share of it. The passage speaks about towns rather than individuals, and that is where your part is small enough to do.
studies.explainEasier: God says these towns could have had a different end. If they had believed and done right, he would have opened up good things from the sky and the earth. Instead they called the truth a lie. So he took hold of them.

studies.title: Do They Feel Secure
studies.meaning: Three questions in a row, each built on the same verb. The first names night and sleep. The second names mid-morning and play, so the two hours cover a whole day and the two activities cover a whole life. The third asks about something else. The early scholars are careful with the word used there. They explain it as God's hidden arranging in answer to their own scheming, not as deception, since the Quran uses it of both parties in the same breath elsewhere. The closing clause makes felt security itself the failure.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, addressed straight to the audience after four accounts of vanished towns. The Quraysh saw their position as backed by the sanctuary, and there was a settled confidence in the city that nothing would touch it. No occasion of revelation is reported. These questions are the point where the surah stops telling about other people and turns the whole sequence towards the listeners.

keyTerms.note: Built on the root that also produces the words for faith, safety and the trustworthy. The Arabic therefore places felt security and belief one step apart, which is what makes the closing verdict so pointed.
The part of the day after full sunrise when work is under way and nobody is expecting anything. Paired with night, the two words cover the hours a person is least braced for something.
The early scholars explain this as requital arranged unseen in answer to the scheming of others, and the Quran regularly uses the word of both sides at once. It is not attributed to God as deception.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Both times named here are the times a settlement was least defended. Raiders struck sleeping camps before dawn. Mid-morning was when a town was full of its own business, gates open and everyone at work. A merchant city ran on the assumption that neither would happen. That assumption was the security the ayah is asking about, and it was rebuilt every morning without anyone deciding to.
studies.didYouKnow: The first of these questions uses the same word for a night raid that appeared near the start of this surah. There it described towns struck while their people slept. The audience is being asked, in that same vocabulary, whether they feel safe from what the opening ayat described happening to somebody else.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The Quran's balance of fear and hope is stated here from one side only, and that is deliberate. Elsewhere it is despairing of God's mercy that is named as the failure of those who have gone astray. Here it is feeling safe. The two are given as a matched pair across the Book. The effect is to rule out both settled dread and settled confidence. That leaves a person with neither of the two positions that would let them stop paying attention.

crossReferences.why: Gives the opposite failure, that none despairs of God's comfort except a people who disbelieve.
The opening of this surah, where towns are struck by night or during the midday rest.
Asks the same question of those who plot evil, naming several ways a seizure might come.

studies.applyIt: Notice where your sense of safety actually comes from today. Not what you would say if asked, but what you would miss if it went: an income, a diagnosis that came back clear, a person who is well. Name one. You are not being asked to stop relying on it. Just to know that you were, and that you had not noticed.
studies.explainEasier: The verses ask if people feel safe from God while they sleep at night. They ask the same about the daytime, while they are busy playing. Only people who lose out feel safe from God's plan.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: Those Who Inherit The Land
studies.meaning: The question is addressed to a specific group: people who came into a place after its previous occupants were gone. Has it not become clear to them, the ayah asks, that the same could be done to them for their own wrongs. Then a second clause about hearts being sealed so that hearing stops. The classical scholars are careful about the order here. The following ayah states that they refused what they had already denied before, which places the sealing after a settled refusal rather than before any choice.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Arabs held territory that had belonged to others and knew it; the peninsula's history was a record of tribes displacing tribes, and the ruins of vanished peoples stood on the trade routes. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah. It comes at the close of the surah's long sequence, at the moment the argument turns from what happened to earlier communities to what follows from it for whoever is listening.

keyTerms.note: The verb for receiving property from the dead. Applied to land and to peoples, it makes present occupation a form of succession, which carries the fact of the predecessor inside the description of the tenant.
From the root for impressing a stamp into clay or wax. The same root gives the Arabic word for a person's ingrained nature, so the image is of a shape becoming fixed rather than a lid being shut.
The ordinary verb for hearing, denied. Nothing is said about their ears; what stops is reception, which the Quran regularly distinguishes from the physical act throughout its descriptions of refusal.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian genealogy was also a property record. A tribe recited who had held a well before them and how it had changed hands, and children learned the list. Nobody imagined their grazing had always been theirs. This is why the address here lands where it does: it does not have to argue that the audience are successors, since they would have told you so themselves and been proud of it.
studies.didYouKnow: The image behind the sealing of hearts comes from a merchant's seal. He pressed it into wax or clay to close a shipment. The same root produced the everyday Arabic word for a person's character. So the Book's vocabulary for a heart that no longer takes anything in is also its vocabulary for a settled temper.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage is careful about order, and the care matters. A sealed heart is described in the setting of people who have already refused again and again. The next ayah says so plainly. That keeps the language from describing a condition imposed before anyone chose anything. What the image conveys is that refusal, repeated, stops being a decision and becomes a shape. The Quran uses the words of hardening and setting rather than of prevention.

crossReferences.why: The following ayah, which states they would not believe what they had already denied before.
Explains the covering on a heart as rust laid down by what a person has been earning.
Uses the same image of a seal on hearts and hearing, with a covering on the eyes.

studies.applyIt: Think of a criticism you have heard so often that you no longer register it. That numbness is the process this ayah describes, at the ordinary scale where it is still reversible. Ask the person who last raised it to say it once more, and this time write it down instead of answering. Writing keeps you from hearing it the practised way.
studies.explainEasier: God asks the people who take over a land after the old people are gone to notice something. He could do the same to them for their own wrongs. He could seal up their hearts so they stop hearing.

studies.title: We Found No Covenant
studies.meaning: The sequence is closed and named. These towns, and We recount to you some of their tidings, with a partitive that admits only part has been given. Then a clause the early scholars read in two ways: they would not believe in what they had denied before, either the message at its first hearing or something older still, which the surah returns to later. The second ayah gives the verdict, and it is not about intelligence or even about belief. Most of them were found to have no covenant they kept.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Oaths and treaties were the load-bearing structure of Arabian society, and a reputation for keeping them was the most valuable thing a clan owned. To sum up four vanished communities by saying that most of their people could not be relied on to hold to an agreement was to condemn them in the terms the audience took most seriously. No occasion of revelation is reported.

keyTerms.note: Not ordinary news. This noun is used of reports that carry consequence, the kind that change what a hearer does, which is why the Quran uses it of the great announcement in other surahs.
The word covers a treaty, a promise and an entrusted responsibility. Saying most of them were found without one means not that none was made but that none was kept once made.
From a root used of a ripe date splitting its skin. The image is of something leaving the covering that held it, so the word names departure from bounds rather than any particular offence.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a society with no courts and almost no writing, a deal was held in place by memory and name. Treaties were recited in public. Some were hung in the sanctuary. A man who broke one had it recited against him in poetry for the rest of his life. Keeping your word was not a private virtue there. It was the frame everything rested on, and a town that lost it could no longer organise anything.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran calls what it has just given only some of their tidings, using a word that means part of. Four communities have been described across forty ayat, and the summary states plainly that this was a selection. The classical scholars note that the Book repeatedly signals what it is holding back. That is unusual in old storytelling. It is part of how the Book keeps attention on the pattern rather than the plot.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The last verdict is about character, not about doctrine. What is named is a failure to keep their word: they could not hold to a thing once undertaken. That is offered as the summary of everything the sequence has described. It suggests the refusals in these stories were not really about the arguments. They were about a settled refusal to be bound. That explains why better evidence never made a difference in any of them.

crossReferences.why: Later in this surah, a covenant taken from all humanity, which some early scholars read as the earlier denial.
Describes those who keep God's covenant and do not break the compact, as the positive counterpart.
States that the covenant will be asked about, in a list of ordinary responsibilities.

studies.applyIt: Look at one commitment you made and have quietly let lapse: a standing arrangement, a promise to call, a payment plan. Either restore it this week or tell the other person plainly that you are ending it. Both are honest. What the passage describes is the third option, which is leaving it undischarged and saying nothing.
studies.explainEasier: God says these towns had messengers come to them with clear signs. The people would not believe what they had already turned down. God also says that most of them did not keep their promises.

studies.title: I Am A Messenger
studies.meaning: The longest narrative in the surah opens with almost nothing. He was raised up after them, sent with signs to a named ruler and his notables, and they dealt unjustly with the signs. No birth, no river, no burning bush, no flight into the desert. Then the first sentence he speaks, which is a bare statement of position: I am a messenger from the Lord of all worlds. The early scholars note that he opens by claiming a role rather than by making a demand, which is the reverse of how one might approach a throne.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and this account occupies more of the surah than any other. The Quran uses the ruler's title as though it were a name and never supplies another, in contrast with the Joseph narrative, where the ruler of Egypt is called the king throughout. The audience knew Egypt as a wealthy northern power on the far end of a trade route, and its antiquity was proverbial. No occasion of revelation is reported.

keyTerms.note: The verb is the one the Quran also uses for raising the dead. Sending a messenger and raising a body are named with a single word, which puts a prophet's arrival in the vocabulary of an event that interrupts.
The same word used for the tribal assemblies of the earlier accounts. An empire's court and a desert town's elders receive one description, which quietly places them in the same category.
An unusual construction. The early scholars read it as wronging themselves by their treatment of the signs, or as doing injustice to the signs, and the Arabic accommodates both without resolving it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Egypt was the great power at the end of the northern road. Arabs knew it as a place of grain, linen and enormous stone. Its rulers were remembered as absolute in a way no Arabian chief could be. A tribal leader governed by consent and could be abandoned. A man walking into that court alone with a claim about God would have struck the audience as either mad or carrying something they could not see.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran uses two different titles for the rulers of Egypt in its two Egyptian narratives. In the Joseph account the ruler is called the king throughout. In this account, set generations later, he is called Pharaoh throughout, and the Book never mixes them. The distinction is maintained consistently across every passage in which either story appears.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The opening sentence sets the shape of everything that follows. He does not introduce himself by name, by family, or by the wrong he has come about. He states a commission and its source. Everything else proceeds from that. This makes the meeting about authority rather than about grievance, from the first word. It also explains why the ruler's answer, when it comes, is a challenge about credentials rather than a defence of what he does.

crossReferences.why: Gives the commissioning this ayah skips, including his fear and the request for his brother.
Compresses the same mission into three lines, with the invitation to be purified.
Supplies the background of the oppression that makes the later demand intelligible.

studies.applyIt: Think about how you introduce yourself when something difficult needs saying. Most people lead with credentials, or with the grievance, or with an apology. Try leading with the thing itself, in one sentence, and let everything else come afterwards if it is needed. It is shorter than you expect and it changes what the conversation is about.
studies.explainEasier: After those towns, God sent Moses with signs to Pharaoh and his leading men. They treated the signs badly. Moses told Pharaoh that he was a messenger sent by the Lord of all the worlds.

studies.title: Only The Truth About God
studies.meaning: The first thing established in front of a throne is a restriction on the speaker's own mouth. It is binding upon me that I say nothing about God except the truth. The classical readers differ slightly over one particle in the opening phrase and the sense comes out the same either way. Only after that constraint is stated does anything else follow: evidence has come, and a demand attached to it. Send the Children of Israel with me. The demand is political and it arrives second, resting on the sentence before it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the parallel with the situation in the city was direct. The Quraysh accused the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) of composing what he recited. The Quran answers again and again by describing the limits a messenger speaks under. No occasion of revelation is reported for this ayah. The demand it ends with is the first time in the surah that a messenger asks for something concrete rather than for belief.

keyTerms.note: From the root for truth and for what is due. The word means both worthy and obligated, so the claim is that truthfulness about God is owed rather than chosen, and the speaker states it against himself.

Indefinite, so a proof rather than the proof. The same word appeared in the mouths of two earlier messengers in this surah, which links the confrontation with an empire to confrontations in small towns.
The imperative of the same verb used for sending a messenger. He asks the ruler to send a people using the word for what God did to him, which places the two acts of sending side by side.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Envoys in that world spoke under a discipline everyone understood. A man carrying terms between tribes was not free to improve them. He could not soften them or add his own view. A messenger who changed what he had been given was worse than useless, because nothing he brought could be trusted afterwards. Opening with a statement about the limits on your own speech was the ordinary way of showing what kind of person was talking.
studies.didYouKnow: This surah gives the confrontation in two sentences. Surah 20 gives the same meeting at length. It includes an instruction the messengers get beforehand that does not appear here: to speak to him gently, in the hope that he might take heed. The two accounts together show the Quran spreading details of one episode across different surahs.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The order of the sentences carries the argument. A limit on speech comes first. Then the evidence. Then the demand. So the political request rests on a claim about honesty rather than on power or on justice alone. This is the Quran's regular pattern for prophetic speech. What a messenger may say is limited before anything he asks for is stated. That limit is presented as the ground of his trustworthiness.

crossReferences.why: Has the Prophet reply that he cannot alter the recitation of his own accord, on the same principle.
States what would follow if he attributed sayings to God that were not given to him.
Gives the instruction absent here, to go to him and speak gently, that he might take heed.

studies.applyIt: Try a day of not repeating anything you cannot personally vouch for. No forwarded claims. No I heard that. No probably. It sounds easy and it is not; most conversation runs on borrowed material. The discipline this ayah describes is narrower still, since it concerns claims about God. A day of the wider version makes the narrower one clear.
studies.explainEasier: Moses told Pharaoh that he would only say true things about God. He said he had brought clear proof from Pharaoh's Lord. Then he asked Pharaoh to let the Children of Israel leave with him.

studies.title: A Learned Magician
studies.meaning: The challenge is issued and answered without a word wasted. A staff is thrown and becomes a serpent; a hand is drawn out and is white to those looking. Other surahs describe the same snake with different words, large in one place and quick in another, which the early scholars take as two aspects of one thing rather than a discrepancy. The whiteness is specified elsewhere as being without any disease. Then the court's verdict, and it is not a denial. They accept that something happened and file it under expertise.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Quraysh handled the recitation the same way, calling it the work of a poet, a soothsayer or a man taught by someone, all of which are explanations rather than denials. Egypt had a genuine reputation for this kind of skill in the ancient world, so the court's verdict was the professional judgement of people who knew the field. No occasion of revelation is reported for the passage.

keyTerms.note: The most ordinary object a traveller carried, used for leaning, driving animals and knocking leaves down for a flock. Another surah has him list its uses himself, which makes what happens to it here more startling.

This word names a large snake, while other tellings use words for a small, quick one. The early scholars read the difference as describing size in one place and movement in another, not as competing reports.

The second word is an intensive form meaning deeply learned, and the Quran uses it of God elsewhere. Applied here it is a compliment about technique, which is precisely how the verdict avoids the question.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabia had its own practitioners, and the audience knew the category well. Men who tied knots and blew on them, who read omens, who were paid to affect an outcome. Every tribe could name one. The verdict passed by the court was therefore not exotic to Meccan ears. It was the verdict Mecca itself was passing on the recitation at the time this surah was revealed.
studies.didYouKnow: The two signs given are the most personal objects available. A man's own walking stick and his own hand. Nothing is summoned from outside and nothing is borrowed. The classical scholars note the contrast with what a court would expect from a claimant, which is a display of armies, wealth or spectacle. The Quran gives neither in any of its tellings.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The verdict shows how a sign can be received without being received. Nothing is disputed about what happened. A category is supplied that keeps the event from meaning anything, and the category is a respectful one. This is the Quran's usual account of how evidence fails. Not by being refuted, but by being filed. Once a thing is filed, the question it raised is no longer available to be asked.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same two signs at their first appearance, with the staff's uses named by him.
States that they knew in themselves the signs were true, and rejected them out of injustice and pride.
Records the same manoeuvre in Mecca, calling the recitation nothing but transmitted magic.

studies.applyIt: Watch for the moment you file something instead of considering it: that is just anxiety, they are only saying that because, this is a phase. Filing is fast and it feels like understanding. Pick one thing you have already filed this week and reopen it for ten minutes without reaching for the label. Most of the time nothing changes, and occasionally something does.
studies.explainEasier: Pharaoh asked Moses to show a sign. Moses threw down his staff and it turned into a snake. He pulled out his hand and it was shining white. The leaders said he was just a clever magician.

studies.title: Is There A Reward
studies.meaning: The claim is turned into a threat about territory. He wants to drive you out of your land. That converts a question about God into a question about safety, and puts the whole court on one side of it. The early scholars differ over the next clause. It is either the ruler asking his council for advice or the council still speaking, and either reading leaves a man of supreme power taking counsel. The plan is to delay and to call people in. Then the professionals arrive, and their first sentence is about the fee.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Quraysh made the same move against the message. They argued that it would divide families, unsettle the sanctuary and damage the standing of the city, which turned a dispute about God into a matter of survival for everyone. No occasion of revelation is reported for the passage. It begins the longest episode in the surah, and the professionals brought in here will end it in a way nobody in the scene expects.

keyTerms.note: From a verb meaning to defer or hold something in suspense. The advice is not to answer the claim but to delay it, which buys time to change the terms on which it will be heard.
From the root the Quran uses for the assembling of all people on the final Day. The word for the officials sent to summon magicians is the word for what will one day summon everyone.
The ordinary word for a worker's pay, used across the Quran for reward with God. Here it is the first thing said in the presence of power, before any question about what is being contested.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabs paid for services of this kind and haggled over them like any other. A diviner was engaged for a fee, a poet was paid to compose a satire against a rival tribe, and the price was settled before the work. Nobody would have found the question improper. What the passage sets up is a group of men who enter for money and who will, within a few ayat, be offered everything and refuse it.
studies.didYouKnow: The men sent out to summon the magicians are named with one word. It is built on the root the Quran uses for the gathering of all people at the resurrection. The same term names the officials riding out to the cities. It also names the gathering of everyone who has ever lived. The surah makes no comment on the shared vocabulary.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage shows how a claim gets defused without being answered. It is recast as a threat to a group's interests. At that point disagreeing with it costs something, and nobody has to look at it. The detail about the fee does a second job. It fixes exactly where these men start, which is the only way the reader can measure how far they travel by the end of the episode.

crossReferences.why: The parallel account, which adds the magicians' question about whether they will be brought near.
Gives the same argument about expulsion from the land, put by the magicians to each other.
Records him fearing that Moses will change their religion or bring corruption to the land.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time a disagreement is reframed as a threat to your group. It is one of the most effective moves in ordinary life and it usually happens without anyone deciding to make it. When you spot it, try asking the original question again, out loud, in its plain form. That is all. Half the time nobody has heard it yet.
studies.explainEasier: Pharaoh told his people that Moses wanted to drive them out of their land. His men told him to wait. They said to send for the best magicians in the country. The magicians came and asked what they would be paid.

studies.title: They Bewitched The Eyes
studies.meaning: The fee is confirmed and a second offer added: you will be among those brought near, which is the Quran's own phrase elsewhere for those brought near to God. Then the professionals put a choice to Moses, and he gives them the first throw. What follows is described with care. They bewitched the eyes of the people and struck dread into them, so the object of the working is the perception of the audience rather than the ropes themselves. Another surah says the same thing in different words, that it merely seemed to be moving.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The recitation in Mecca was being called magic by people who did not dispute its effect, only its source. So an episode about a contest between a sign and a technique had immediate bite. No occasion of revelation is reported for the passage. The choice offered to Moses, and his answer, are given in every telling, which suggests the detail was thought worth keeping.

keyTerms.note: The Quran uses this exact word elsewhere for those brought near to God. Here a ruler offers nearness to himself in the same term, which is the whole of what he has to give.
The object of the verb is the eyes of the onlookers, not the objects thrown. The early scholars take this precisely: what was worked on was seeing, so nothing in the ropes themselves had changed.

keyTerms.gloss: and they struck dread into them
keyTerms.note: From a root for awe and fear. The verb form implies they sought to produce the fear rather than merely causing it, so intimidation is named as part of the technique and not a side effect.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabia had its own practitioners and everyone knew what they did. They tied knots and blew on them, read the flight of birds, and were consulted before journeys and marriages. Their authority rested on an audience's willingness to see what they were told to see, and a crowd was part of the equipment. What this ayah describes was therefore not foreign to the listeners. It was a Thursday at a fair.
studies.didYouKnow: Two surahs describe this moment and both put the effect in what people saw, not in the objects. One says the eyes of the people were worked on. The other says the ropes seemed, through their working, to be moving. Neither says the ropes became anything, and the classical scholars build their whole account of the episode on that agreement.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage draws a line between changing what is there and changing what is seen. A technique that works on an audience can be overwhelming. It can produce real terror while leaving the world untouched. That is why the answer to it, when it comes, does not need to be more impressive. It only needs to be real. That distinction is what the whole contest turns on, and it is stated before the contest is decided.

crossReferences.why: Says their ropes and staffs seemed to him, through their working, to be moving quickly.
Uses the same word for those brought near, describing them in the gardens of bliss.
Has him declare that what they brought is magic, and that God will render it void.

studies.applyIt: Think of something that recently frightened you into a decision. Ask whether the fear came from what was actually the case or from how it was presented: the headline, the tone, the number given without a comparison. You may reach the same decision. But separate the two once, deliberately, and see whether it holds.
studies.explainEasier: Pharaoh promised the magicians a reward and a place close to him. They let Moses choose who would throw first, and he told them to go. When they threw, they tricked people's eyes and made them afraid.

studies.title: Then The Magicians Fell
studies.meaning: The instruction comes as an inspiration and it is one word: throw. What follows is described with a verb for gulping something down, and the object swallowed is not the ropes but what they were fabricating, which keeps the whole matter at the level of the false thing rather than the physical one. Truth fell into place; what they had been doing came to nothing. Then the last sentence of the contest, and its grammar is the point. The magicians were cast down prostrate. They did not throw themselves; the passive says they were thrown.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. This is the moment the surah has been building towards across its longest story, and it turns on the reaction of professionals rather than of the ruler. In Mecca the message was winning over people who had every reason to refuse it, including men of standing. The pattern of an expert changing sides in public would have been familiar. No occasion of revelation is reported.

keyTerms.note: A verb for gulping something down quickly and completely, used of snatching food. It leaves nothing behind, which matters because the contest ends with no remaining object for anyone to examine.
From a root meaning to turn a thing away from its proper state. What is swallowed is named as their inversion rather than as their ropes, so the object destroyed is the falsehood itself.
The passive of the verb for throwing, the same one that has run through the whole scene. After all the throwing, the last thing thrown is the throwers, and the grammar gives them no part in it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Public contests settled things in Arabia. Poets duelled at the seasonal fairs before crowds who judged on the spot, and a man who lost in front of everyone lost his standing with his verses. Reputations were made and destroyed in an afternoon. What made such contests binding was that the audience saw the result together, which is why nobody could later dispute it, and it is the setting this whole episode assumes.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for throwing runs through this whole passage like a thread. A staff is thrown. The professionals ask who will throw first, and they throw. The staff is thrown again. The passage ends with the magicians themselves being thrown down in prostration, in the passive voice. The Arabic uses one root for all of it, and the last use is the one they did not perform.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The men best placed to judge are the ones who change position. The Quran makes their expertise the reason rather than an obstacle. They alone in that crowd knew exactly what could and could not be done by technique. So they were the only people present who could tell that what they were watching was not one. Their prostration is described as something that happened to them. That is the Book's usual way of describing conviction that arrives all at once.

crossReferences.why: The parallel telling, which adds that a worker never succeeds wherever he comes from.
Gives the same collapse, with the magicians falling prostrate and declaring faith in the Lord of the worlds.
States the principle behind the outcome, that God establishes the truth by His words and voids falsehood.

studies.applyIt: Think of the person best qualified to disagree with something you believe. Find out what they actually say, in their own words. Not a summary from someone who already agrees with you. Experts change their minds more often than amateurs do, because they can see what would count against them. That is worth borrowing rather than resenting.
studies.explainEasier: God told Moses to throw his staff. It swallowed up the fake things the magicians had made. The truth won and their work came to nothing. Then the magicians fell down and said they believed in the Lord of the Worlds.

studies.title: Before I Gave Permission
studies.meaning: The declaration is completed with a second ayah naming whose Lord. The early scholars read the addition as deliberate. Without it, a ruler who had claimed the highest position for himself could have taken the first sentence as pointing to him. The response that follows makes two moves. It claims that belief needs a licence from the throne. And it recycles the accusation used earlier, calling the conversion a plot to drive out the city's people. The same charge is now aimed at men who arrived that morning as employees.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Converts in the city were being accused of disloyalty rather than of error. Families treated a change of conviction as an act against them. No occasion of revelation is reported for this passage. Its placement is exact. The charge of plotting comes only after the contest has been decided in public, when no argument about the outcome is left and something else has to be found.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to give ear and then to allow. The claim is that conviction runs through an office, so that a person's inner assent is something a throne can license or withhold.
A word for arrangement carried out unseen. Applying it to men who were summoned that day by his own officials makes the accusation impossible, which is a mark of how little else was available.

The specification added in the second ayah. The early scholars read it as closing a gap, since without a name attached the phrase Lord of the worlds could have been claimed by the man they were standing in front of.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Belief in Arabia was a tribal possession, not a private matter. A clan's gods, its alliances and its honour came as one inheritance. A member who took up something else was understood to have walked out of the clan itself. He had not simply changed his mind about a question. Accusations against converts in Mecca took exactly this form. Not that they were wrong, but that they had broken with their own people.
studies.didYouKnow: The charge of plotting to drive out the city's people is the same sentence used earlier in this episode against Moses himself. It was invented then to make a claim about God sound like a threat to the country. Here it is reused within a few ayat against a different group, with no change to the wording.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage isolates a claim that political power makes about religion. The claim is that assent is something it can authorise. Everything else in the exchange follows from it. The outrage is not that they believe something false but that they believed without leave. The Quran lets the sentence stand exposed rather than arguing with it. The reply that comes in the next ayat does not dispute the power, only its reach.

crossReferences.why: Records the claim that made the addition necessary, that he was their lord most high.
The parallel version of the same accusation, naming Moses as the one who taught them their craft.
Has him tell his council that he shows them only what he sees and guides them only rightly.

studies.applyIt: Notice whether anyone in your life needs to approve of a conclusion before you feel able to hold it. Everyone has someone. It is not always wrong; deference to people who know more is sensible. But identify the person, and then check whether their authority actually covers the question you are deferring to them on.
studies.explainEasier: The magicians said they believed in the Lord of Moses and Aaron. Pharaoh was angry that they had believed without asking him first. He said it was a secret plan to drive the people out of the city.

studies.title: To Our Lord We Return
studies.meaning: The threat is detailed and public. It names a specific mutilation followed by execution, and it is delivered with the most emphatic construction Arabic has. The answer is five words. It contains no defiance, no plea, no bargaining and no counter-argument. Only a statement about where they are going. The early scholars notice the verb they choose. It is built on the same root as the word used a few ayat earlier for their being turned back in defeat. The word that described their humiliation is picked up and made into a destination.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and this exchange was among the passages the early community in Mecca lived on. Several of them were being held and pressed to renounce, and some did not survive it. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayat themselves. Within the surah's structure, the reply here answers the ruler's claim in the previous ayah that belief runs through his permission, by pointing past him to what his authority does not reach.

keyTerms.note: A phrase specifying alternation, one hand and the opposite foot. Its precision is part of the threat, since a punishment described in detail is more frightening than one left general.
Doubly emphatic in Arabic, with an oath particle and a heavy ending. The construction is the form used for a vow, so the sentence commits the speaker rather than merely warning the hearer.
From the root for overturning and returning. The same root described their defeat a few ayat earlier, so the word for what was done to them becomes the word for where they are going.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabs valued composure in the face of death above almost anything. The last words of a man facing execution were remembered and recited. There was a whole genre of the death-speech, usually a boast about family line or an unfinished feud. To an audience trained on that genre, the striking thing about this reply is that it contains no boast at all. It does not even mention the man threatening them.
studies.didYouKnow: The answer is one short sentence. It names no grievance, makes no appeal and does not address the person speaking to them. The classical scholars note that it also contains no request. Set beside almost every other reply in this surah, it is remarkable for how little it asks for, given the circumstances in which it is spoken.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reply works by moving the question rather than by answering it. A threat of death assumes that death is the far limit of what can be done to a person. The sentence quietly declines that assumption without arguing about it. This is the Quran's usual move against force. Not a claim that the man threatening lacks power, but a statement that his power ends somewhere he cannot see.

crossReferences.why: Gives their fuller reply, that they will not prefer him over the clear signs that have come.
Records the same answer in different words: no harm, we are returning to our Lord.
Describes another group killed for believing, and names the only fault held against them.

studies.applyIt: Think of the worst outcome you are quietly afraid of. Write it down in one plain sentence, without softening it. Then write what would still be true afterwards. Most fears lose a surprising amount of their grip once they are stated at their full size rather than circled around, and this passage is a very short example of that being done aloud.
studies.explainEasier: Pharaoh threatened to cut off their hands and feet and then put them to death. The magicians answered with one short sentence. They said they were going back to their Lord.

studies.title: Pour Patience Upon Us
studies.meaning: First a diagnosis of the charge against them, stated as a question that is not really one: you resent us for nothing except that we believed the signs when they came. The clause about timing is doing work, since they believed at the moment the evidence arrived rather than before or after. Then the speech turns away from the ruler entirely and becomes a prayer, and its two requests are unexpected. Not rescue and not vindication. Patience, asked for as something poured out, and death in a state of submission.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The same prayer, word for word in its first half, appears elsewhere in the Quran on the lips of a small force facing a much larger one, which suggests it was already understood as the petition for a situation with no way out. No occasion of revelation is reported here. It is the last thing the magicians say in the surah, and the narrative moves on without reporting what happened to them.

keyTerms.note: From a root joining disapproval and punishment, so the verb means to find fault and act on it together. It names the ruler's response as personal resentment rather than as judgement or policy.

The verb for emptying a vessel completely over something. Patience is asked for as a liquid poured from outside rather than as a quality summoned from within, which is a specific request about where it comes from.
The participle from the verb meaning to hand something over intact. They ask to die in the state of having handed themselves over, which is a request about a condition rather than about an outcome.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Water was poured, not turned on. It came from a skin or a jar, tipped until it was empty. The verb used here for that action was one of the most ordinary in the language. Asking for patience to be poured out was therefore a homely image rather than a lofty one. It carried the sense of a container fully emptied over something dry, with nothing held back.
studies.didYouKnow: The exact request, our Lord, pour patience upon us, appears in one other place in the Quran. There it is spoken by a small band about to face a much larger army. The two settings could hardly be more different, and the Book gives them the same words. That is why the phrase became one of the most widely used prayers in Muslim practice.
studies.theologicalSignificance: What they ask for is exactly what is still open to them. Rescue would change the setting. Patience changes what they can bear inside it. Dying while handed over to God names the only end they can still want. The prayer therefore models a rare kind of asking. It has measured the situation honestly, then asks for the thing that is still possible.

crossReferences.why: The same request, word for word, from a small force facing a much larger one.
Joseph's prayer at the height of his fortune asks for the same ending, to be taken in submission.
Gives a matching supplication asking for firmness of foot and help against a disbelieving people.

studies.applyIt: Take a situation you cannot change and notice what you have been praying for about it. Most of us keep asking for the circumstance to move. Try asking, once, for the capacity instead: not that this ends, but that I can be in it well. It is a different request and it is answerable, which the first one may not be.
studies.explainEasier: The magicians told Pharaoh why he was angry. He was punishing them only for believing the signs when they came. Then they turned to God. They asked him to pour patience on them and to let them die with their hearts given to him.

studies.title: We Have Power Over Them
studies.meaning: The court presses the ruler. The charge they bring is corruption in the land, which is the word the Quran uses elsewhere of his own conduct. They add that he is being abandoned along with his gods. The early scholars find that phrase striking, given his claims about himself, and some record another reading that would make it his worship rather than his deities. His answer brings back an old policy against the children. It ends on a statement of dominance in the present tense.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Quran describes an earlier phase of the same policy elsewhere, so the announcement here is a return to something already done rather than something new. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah. In the surah's sequence it comes right after the magicians' prayer. A scene of people preparing to die well is followed at once by the machinery that produced the danger.

keyTerms.note: The verb for letting something go, used twice in this ayah. The council frames inaction as a decision, which is how pressure is usually applied to a ruler who has not yet chosen.

A plural, which sits oddly beside his claims about his own status. Classical readers record an alternative pointing of the word that would render it his worship, and the early scholars note both without deciding.
From a root meaning to subdue by force so completely that no resistance remains. One of the names of God is formed from it, which makes its use here about human power over people pointed.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabia had no body able to do this. A chief who tried to kill the sons of a clan would have faced blood vengeance from every relative they had. The whole system of protection existed to make such a thing impossible. What the ayah describes was truly foreign to its first hearers. It would have landed as the special horror of a state. A state can do what no tribe could.
studies.didYouKnow: The accusation the council brings against Moses is corruption in the land. The Quran uses that same expression of the ruler himself in another surah, describing him as one of the corrupters. So the charge is made with words already applied to the person it is being made to. The surah offers no comment on the reversal.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage records the ordinary mechanics by which cruelty gets approved. A council raises the danger. A policy is announced as a response to it. The whole thing is closed with a claim about what can be done rather than about what is right. Nothing in the exchange requires anyone to believe the accusation. It requires only that the question be treated as one of safety, which the earlier ayat had already arranged.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same policy in an earlier phase and names him plainly as one of the corrupters.
Records the identical order given again later, and says the scheming of the deniers goes astray.
Recalls the whole affliction to the descendants as the great trial they were delivered from.

studies.applyIt: Watch for the sentence that turns a disagreement into a danger: they want to destroy what we have, if we do nothing now. It is the oldest move in the passage and it works because it makes caution feel like betrayal. When you hear it, ask for the specific harm and the evidence for it. Usually the answer is thinner than the tone.
studies.explainEasier: Pharaoh's chiefs asked him if he would let Moses and his people spoil the land and leave his gods. He answered that he would kill their sons and let their women live. He said he had full power over them.

studies.title: The Earth Belongs To God
studies.meaning: The answer to a threat of extermination is two verbs and a fact. Seek help in God, and be patient, with no strategy offered and no promise of rescue. Then the fact, and its qualifier is where the early scholars dwell: the earth belongs to God, who gives it in inheritance to whomever He wills of His servants. Not to you automatically. The closing clause supplies the condition, and it is a moral one rather than an inherited one. The outcome belongs to those who guard themselves.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, spoken to a community with no power to resist and told by their own leader that none was coming. The early Muslims in the city were in the same position. They had no numbers, no weapons and no protectors, and were told again and again to endure rather than to organise. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah. It is the only advice given to the oppressed in this whole episode.

keyTerms.note: A form meaning to request assistance rather than to receive it. The same verb appears in the opening surah, in the sentence recited in every prayer, so the instruction is one the reader already performs daily.
The verb for passing property to an heir. It makes the earth something handed on rather than seized, and the phrase that follows specifies the giver's choice rather than any heir's entitlement.

From the root meaning to place a shield between yourself and harm. The outcome is attached to a quality that anyone may have rather than to a lineage, which is why the promise carries no group's name.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Land in Arabia changed hands constantly and everyone knew it. A tribe held a valley because another had been driven from it. The same valley would pass on again within a few generations. Nobody claimed lasting title from anything but present strength. To say the ground belongs to God, and is handed on at His choosing, was to take a familiar kind of change and give it a different owner.
studies.didYouKnow: The words attached to the promise keep it from becoming a right. God bequeaths the earth to whomever He wills of His servants. Another surah finishes the thought by saying that the righteous among His servants will inherit it. The classical scholars read the two together. Neither passage ties the promise to a people by name.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The advice given to people facing being wiped out contains no promise that they will survive. It offers a posture: help sought and patience held. Then a statement about ownership that cuts the power threatening them down to size, without saying it will go. The last clause is the sharpest part. It means the community being addressed has no automatic claim on the outcome either. Their conduct stays a variable, not a formality.

crossReferences.why: Completes the thought, that the righteous among God's servants will inherit the earth.
Uses the same verb for seeking help, in the sentence recited in every unit of prayer.
Promises succession in the land to those who believe and act rightly, with conditions attached.

studies.applyIt: In the next situation you cannot control, try separating what you are asking for from what you are doing. Ask for help, plainly and in your own words. Then do the small next thing that is actually yours. The passage gives no strategy at all, and that omission is deliberate: it leaves only the two moves that are always available.
studies.explainEasier: Moses told his people to ask God for help and to be patient. He said the earth belongs to God. God gives it to whichever of his servants he chooses. The good end belongs to people who do right.

studies.title: Then He Will See
studies.meaning: The people of Moses come to him worn down, and their complaint lands on him. We were harmed before you came, they say, and we are harmed still. He does not tell them they are wrong. What he offers is a maybe rather than a promise: perhaps your Lord will destroy your enemy and leave the land in your hands. Then he adds the words that change the whole shape of it, 'then He will see how you behave.' The rescue they are waiting for has a test waiting on the far side.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, and the believers there were worn thin. Some of them said so to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) himself, asking how long help would take. The answers given in those years keep doing the same thing. They encourage, then warn about what people become once life gets easier. Early scholars report no particular occasion for this verse. The next line turns to the other side, to the hardship God sent on the ones holding the power.

keyTerms.note: The particle of hope and expectation. It stops the sentence short of a promise, which is why the reply can be honest about a future the speaker does not control while still pointing at it.
From the root for following behind and taking another's place. Succession in this vocabulary always implies a predecessor who was removed, so the word contains its own warning to whoever receives it.
Literally the years, used idiomatically for years of drought, as the Joseph account uses the same word for a run of hard seasons. Arabic names the famine by the time it occupies.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabs kept time by what happened in it. A year was named for its event: the year of the elephant, the year of the flood. A long drought was called simply the years, with nothing else added. A tribe's history was a list of seasons that had gone wrong, remembered out loud. So when this verse says God took Pharaoh's people with the years, it is naming disaster the way they already named it.
studies.didYouKnow: Most words of comfort stop at the good news, and this one does not. God's reply names the enemy destroyed and the land handed over, then adds in the same breath that He will watch what they do with it. The promise and the test arrive together. The Quran does this wherever it describes a people being handed power.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God gives hope here without inflating it. The word He chooses holds the sentence just short of a guarantee, so nobody is being flattered. And the relief on offer is treated as a beginning, not an ending. That is the steady view of it: holding power is a riskier place to stand than lacking it. Comfort asks something of you that hardship never did, and God says so at the very moment He makes the promise.

crossReferences.why: Promises succession in the land on the same terms, and warns those who disbelieve afterwards.
States plainly that later generations were made successors in the land to see how they would act.
Names humanity as successors on the earth, raised in ranks, in order to be tested by what was given.

studies.applyIt: Think of a hard thing you are waiting to be over, then ask what you plan to do in the first week after it ends. Not a plan for the relief itself, a plan for the day after. Most of us never think that far, which is why relief so often leaves nothing behind. Write one line of it down tonight.
studies.explainEasier: The people told Moses they had suffered both before and after he came. He said their Lord might destroy their enemy and put them in charge of the land. Then God would watch how they behaved.

studies.title: This Is Ours
studies.meaning: Watch the same people handle two kinds of news. When something good lands, they say this is ours, as though their own worth had produced it. When something bad lands, they pin it on Moses and the people with him. The verb for that comes from the Arabic word for a bird, because omens were read from the way birds flew. The reply does not deny that something is attached to them. It says their bird is with God, which early scholars took to mean their own record, held by Him and caused by no man.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, where reading the world for omens was ordinary life. A traveller would startle a bird before setting out and turn back if it flew the wrong way. The habit was common enough to grow a vocabulary of its own. Early scholars report no particular occasion for this verse. In Mecca the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was blamed for whatever went wrong in the city, in exactly the pattern described here.

keyTerms.gloss: they took it as an omen
keyTerms.note: Built on the word for a bird, because Arabs divined by watching which way one flew. The verb means to read a bad sign into something, and its whole grammar assumes the practice.
The same word turned around. Early scholars read it here as what is fastened to a person, their record or what is decreed for them, and another chapter describes it as tied around each neck.
Definite and general, covering anything that goes well. The claim made about it, that it is ours, is a claim of desert, which is the exact thing the following clause relocates.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Bird divination ran right across Arabia. You startled a bird, watched which way it went, and read your answer: to the right meant go, to the left meant stay home. Caravans changed their plans on it. The habit soaked so far into the language that the ordinary Arabic word for luck is the word for a bird. This verse speaks straight into that vocabulary.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran takes the word for an omen and hands it back with a new owner. Elsewhere it says every person's bird has been tied to their own neck, meaning the record of what they did travels with them. The Book spends less effort calling omens false than it does moving them. Not a sign read off the sky, but an account already fastened to the one reading.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The lopsidedness is the whole subject. Good gets claimed as merit, bad gets handed to an outsider, and both moves guard the same thing, which is how a person feels about themselves. God refuses the second without granting the first. Nothing went wrong because an inconvenient man walked into the room, and nothing went right because you had it coming. Two mistakes, one root, and naming that root is the kindness here.

crossReferences.why: Says each person's bird has been fastened to their neck, and their record produced open on the Day.
Addresses the identical habit, good attributed to God and evil blamed on the messenger.
Records messengers being called an evil omen and answering that their omen is with themselves.

studies.applyIt: Watch your own explanations for a single day. When something goes well, notice whether you reach for your own skill. When something goes badly, notice whether you reach for a person to blame. Both reflexes are fast, and neither one feels like a decision. Correct nothing today; just count how often each of them fires.
studies.explainEasier: When good things came, the people said they had earned them. When bad things came, they blamed Moses and the people with him. The verse says their share is really with God, and most of them do not know it.

studies.title: Whatever Sign You Bring
studies.meaning: The verdict is in before any evidence arrives. Whatever sign you bring us to bewitch us with, they tell Moses, we will not believe you. The word they use for whatever turns up nowhere else in the Quran, and it sweeps every possible case off the table in advance. Then five things are sent anyway: the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood. Each is a piece of the ordinary world. They are called signs set apart, which early scholars read as arriving one at a time, with gaps in between.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, where the Quraysh had taken the same stand. They listed the signs they would accept, then waved away whatever came, and the Quran says elsewhere they would not have believed even if an angel had come down. Early scholars report no particular occasion for these verses. The five are given here in a single line. Other traditions fill them out, while the Quran says nothing about how any of them worked.

keyTerms.note: A conditional word that does not occur elsewhere in the Quran. It sweeps every possible case into the sentence in advance, which is exactly what the speakers are doing with the evidence.

The early scholars differ over the exact creature, offering lice, ticks, small locusts and grain weevils. They record the range without settling it, since the Arabic word had regional variation even then.

From the root for a joint between bones, and for separating things at their natural divisions. The signs are described as articulated, arriving one at a time rather than as a single undifferentiated disaster.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Every item on that list was a normal Arabian disaster. Locusts came in clouds and stripped a season in a day. A flash flood could fill a dry valley within the hour, and vermin ruined stored grain slowly, over weeks. None of it was exotic. These were the exact things a farmer or a merchant lay awake over, so the list read like a year in which everything that could go wrong did.
studies.didYouKnow: Nothing on that list breaks the rules of nature. Water, insects, frogs and blood are the world's own parts, arriving out of measure. The Quran usually argues from creation the same way, pointing at rain and crops rather than at wonders. Here the same familiar material is turned around and used as a warning.
studies.theologicalSignificance: There is a limit on what evidence can do, and this passage draws it. A person who has already decided is not short of facts. Handing them more changes nothing, which is why God so often speaks to the will rather than the mind. The word chosen for these signs matters too: they came spaced out and separate. Every arrival was a fresh chance to think again, so the refusal had to be made all over again each time.

crossReferences.why: States that even angels descending and the dead speaking would not have brought them to believe.
Says those against whom the word is realised will not believe even if every sign comes to them.
Explains that signs were withheld because earlier peoples denied them when they were sent.

studies.applyIt: Pick something you hold strongly and ask what would change your mind about it. If the honest answer is nothing, that is worth knowing, whether or not the belief is true. Write down one specific thing that would count against it. You are not agreeing to give anything up. You are checking that the position still touches the world.
