studies.explainEasier: The people told Moses that no sign would ever make them believe. So God sent them floods, locusts, lice, frogs and blood. Each one was a clear sign. They were too proud to listen, and they kept doing wrong.

studies.title: Pray To Your Lord
studies.meaning: The plea only ever comes once the blow has landed, and every word of it is placed with care. They ask Moses to pray, which admits that his prayer works. They say your Lord, not ours, in the very sentence where they want His help. They lean on the covenant God made with him, borrowing a bond they will not enter themselves. And they attach two promises to the asking: we will believe, and we will let your people go. The next verse reports both dropped the moment the pressure lifted.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca. The scene describes a pattern the Quran holds up to its own listeners as well: people who pray hard in a storm at sea and forget the moment they reach dry land. Early scholars report no particular occasion for this verse. In the story it comes after the five signs, and the Arabic makes the whole thing a loop rather than one night. Affliction, plea, promise, relief, and the promise abandoned.

keyTerms.note: A word for something repellent, used in the Quran for punishment and for defilement. It names the quality of the thing rather than its mechanism, which is why the same word covers several different visitations here.
The possessive is doing a great deal of work. In the very sentence asking for His intervention they will not say our Lord, which keeps the relationship at arm's length while requesting its benefits.

keyTerms.gloss: by what He covenanted with you
keyTerms.note: An appeal to a standing arrangement between God and the messenger. They ask him to draw on a relationship they have refused, which makes the request an attempt to use a door they will not walk through.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: When the rain failed in Arabia, people went to whoever was thought to have standing with heaven. A holy man, the keeper of a shrine, sometimes a stranger with a reputation. He was asked to pray, and gifts were sent along with the request. Nobody had to believe anything to make the approach; it was a trade. The plea here would have sounded entirely familiar, right down to the promise forgotten afterwards.
studies.didYouKnow: One small word in their plea is the one early scholars keep coming back to. They say call upon your Lord, in the second person, at the exact moment they need Him most. Nothing in the request admits any bond of their own. The Quran keeps that wording rather than smoothing it into a general appeal.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Here is prayer used as a tool instead of entered as a bond. What they ask for is real, and God grants it. That is the hard part. The relief arrives and changes nothing in them. A request made from outside a relationship leaves you standing exactly where you were. It is why the Quran so often measures sincerity by what happens after an answer, rather than by how hard the asking sounded.

crossReferences.why: Describes calling sincerely in a storm at sea and turning away at once on reaching land.
Says that when harm touches you at sea, everyone you call on is lost except Him, and then you turn away.
Gives this exact scene again, with the same plea and the same breaking of the undertaking.

studies.applyIt: Think of the last thing you prayed hard for and were given. Then ask what you said you would do, and whether you did it. Most people find there was something and that it quietly lapsed. Pick it up again this week, even in a smaller form. Answered prayers leave a debt, and it is the easiest kind to forget.
studies.explainEasier: Every time a plague hit them, they asked Moses to pray to his Lord. They said that if he took the plague away, they would believe him. They also said they would let the Children of Israel go.

studies.title: They Broke Their Word
studies.meaning: The relief comes with a clause attached: for a term they were going to reach anyway. The reprieve is real, and it has an edge on it, fixed before they ever asked. Then the breaking, told with a verb that means to unpick a thread you spun yourself. What follows is not a change of policy but a settlement. And the reason is doubled. They called the signs false, and they paid no attention to them, which are two different failures set side by side.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca. The chapter has now shown this loop several times: pressure, appeal, relief, the appeal forgotten. Early scholars report no particular occasion here. In Mecca the Quran kept describing people who called on God in a storm at sea and dropped the call on dry land. So the pattern was handed to listeners who could test it against their own week, not only against a story about Egypt.

keyTerms.note: From a root for untwisting a rope or thread that has been spun. To break a promise in this vocabulary is to undo work you did yourself, which puts the damage on the side of the one who breaks it.
The commercial word for a due date. The relief is issued with an expiry already written into it, which makes the whole episode a postponement rather than a reversal of anything.
An unusual word for a body of water. The Quran keeps it almost entirely for this one story, and uses the ordinary word for sea two verses later, when the same water is crossed.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Spinning was household work, done by women in every home, and one spun thread stood for hours of it. To unpick it was plain waste, and everyone knew that. The Quran elsewhere builds a whole image out of the folly. A crowd who watched wool turn into thread every day heard a broken promise just as this verb has it: not a failure to act, but the choice to undo what you had made.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran uses two different words for water in this stretch. The one here, where the drowning happens, turns up almost nowhere else in the whole Book outside this story. Two verses later, when the same water is crossed safely, it uses the ordinary Arabic word for a sea. The vocabulary shifts with what the water is doing.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two failures are named as the cause, and they are not the same kind of thing. Calling the signs false is a judgement, made on purpose. Being heedless is an absence, never looking at all. Putting them together means God does not treat inattention as the lighter case. Someone who denied nothing because they never looked lands in the same sentence as someone who looked and said no.

crossReferences.why: States the principle behind the verb: whoever breaks a pledge breaks it only against himself.
Builds an image out of the same folly, one who unravels her yarn after spinning it strongly.
Describes the identical cycle at sea, sincere calling followed by immediate forgetting on land.

studies.applyIt: Think of a promise you made to yourself in a hard week and dropped once the week ended. Not a moral failing, just the ordinary shape of relief. Pick it up in its smallest version today, while nothing is wrong. Promises made under pressure rarely survive the pressure lifting unless you renew them in the calm.
studies.explainEasier: When God took the plague away, they broke their promise. They had been given time, and they used it up. In the end they were drowned in the sea, because they turned the signs down and paid them no attention.

studies.title: Because They Endured
studies.meaning: The people the verse calls kept weak are the ones who end up inheriting. The land is named by its easts and its wests, both plural, which early scholars read as the whole of it rather than two edges. And the reason the promise came true is given in three words: because they were patient. Not because of who they were. Then the other side of the ledger. The verb for what was pulled down is the one used for raising trellises and tall buildings, so ruin is told in the language of building up.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca. Early scholars differ over which land is meant. Some name Syria and Palestine, others read it as Egypt itself, and the sources keep both without settling it. No particular occasion is reported for this verse. Where it sits matters. The chapter has just described a drowning and moves straight into inheritance, so both halves of one event arrive in a single sentence with a hinge in the middle.

keyTerms.note: A passive in the continuous tense, so the weakness is described as something done to them and still ongoing at the time of speaking. The grammar denies that the condition was theirs to begin with.

The cause given for the whole outcome, in three words. Patience is named as the reason rather than lineage or promise, which attaches the fulfilment to something a person does rather than something they are.
From a root for a trellis raised over vines, and the same root that gives the Arabic word for a throne. Early scholars read it as their gardens or their tall buildings, and keep both.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabs measured what a people had achieved by what they had raised. Wells dug, forts built, trellised gardens at an oasis kept alive across generations. These were the things that outlived a man and kept his name alive. Poets praised them, and enemies knocked them down first. So describing an empire's fall as the flattening of what it had raised named the loss in the terms this audience felt hardest.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for what was destroyed shares a root with the Arabic word for a throne. Its plain meaning is the light frame raised over a vine to hold it up. So the ruin of a great empire is carried by a word a farmer would use about his own garden.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reason attached to the promise is what carries the weight. Inheriting the land is credited to patience. That makes the promise lean on conduct rather than on birth, and it does not come to a people as a right. The Quran keeps that condition every time it repeats the promise. It also means what changed here was not merely who held the power. This is the finish of something said long before, and the waiting was part of it.

crossReferences.why: States the intention behind this reversal, to favour those kept weak and make them the inheritors.
Gives the same outcome, gardens, springs and treasures passed to the Children of Israel.
Attaches inheritance of the earth to the righteous among God's servants, keeping the condition.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you are enduring with no visible progress. Ask what would count as the thing you are waiting for, in one concrete sentence, then put the sentence away. This verse credits an outcome to patience that must have felt, for most of its length, like nothing happening at all. Knowing what you wait for makes waiting a different activity.
studies.explainEasier: God gave the land to the people who had been treated badly. He had promised this, and it came true because they were patient. What Pharaoh and his people had built was pulled down.

studies.title: Make Us A God
studies.meaning: The request comes right after the crossing, and that is the detail early scholars keep returning to. They have just walked through water that opened for them, and the first thing they want is an image, because they have passed a people who have one. The comparison is the whole argument: as they have gods. Nobody claims the images work. The verb they use is the plain one for making a thing, so what they ask for is manufacture. Moses answers by naming their condition rather than the request.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, where carved images were the normal furniture of religion. Every clan kept them, and travellers set one up wherever they camped. Early scholars report no particular occasion for this verse. The chapter puts the episode straight after a rescue, so the reader can see how short the gap was. Nothing is done to soften the sequence.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to remain attached to something and not leave it, the same root behind the practice of secluding oneself in a place of worship. Devotion in this word is described as staying put.
The word for a figure shaped by hand, distinct from another Arabic term for an unworked stone set up for worship. It names something made by a craftsman, which is what the request asks for.

The ordinary verb for making or appointing a thing. What is requested is manufacture rather than revelation, which is why the answer is about their state of understanding rather than about the object.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian religion was portable, and people compared. A household kept an image, a tribe kept a bigger one at its shrine, and a family leaving on a journey carried a stone from home to set up at each stop. Which god you had was tied to who you were. A group with none was visibly missing what everyone else had. The request in this verse is about that gap, not about belief.
studies.didYouKnow: They ask for a god to be made for them, and a few verses later they make one themselves, without asking anybody. What they wanted handed over, they end up melting out of the ornaments they carried away from Egypt. The chapter sets the request and its answer within ten verses of each other and never points it out.
studies.theologicalSignificance: What drives the request is comparison, not conviction. They never argue that the images work; they notice that other people have them and want the same. That puts a whole category of religious behaviour down to not wanting to stand out, which is harder to spot in yourself than doubt or greed. Moses does not argue the case either. He names the state that produced the request, which is simply not knowing.

crossReferences.why: The same people, ten verses later, making from their ornaments the very thing they had asked for here.
Gives the calf episode at length, including the account of how it was made and who made it.
Names the same reasoning in another form: we follow what we found our forebears doing.

studies.applyIt: Ask what you have taken up in the last two years because the people around you had it. Not objects only; opinions, ambitions, ways of spending an evening. Pick one and ask whether you would have arrived there alone. You may well keep it. But knowing which of your commitments came by comparison changes how tightly you need to hold them.
studies.explainEasier: God brought the Children of Israel safely across the sea. Soon after, they passed people who prayed to carved statues. They asked Moses to make them a god like that. He told them they did not know what they were saying.

studies.title: Shall I Seek Another
studies.meaning: Moses passes two verdicts on the people his own community had just been admiring. What they are caught up in is shattered, a word built on a root for breaking something into pieces. What they do is empty. Neither word says the images are weak; both say the business has no substance in the first place. Then his reply, put as a question rather than a flat refusal. The reason he gives is a favour already received, which early scholars read as gifts given to that generation, not a standing rank.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca. The Quraysh kept many figures at the sanctuary while still acknowledging one supreme God. The Quran's quarrel with them was never about whether the one exists, but about whether the extras were needed. Early scholars report no particular occasion for these verses. The reply here folds that whole argument into a single question about looking elsewhere.

keyTerms.note: An intensive passive from a root meaning to break into fragments. The Quran uses nouns from the same root for utter destruction elsewhere, so the verdict is not that it fails but that it is already in pieces.
The standard Arabic term for what has no reality behind it, the opposite of the word for truth. It describes emptiness rather than error, so the works are not called wrong so much as not there.
From the root for surplus and bounty. The early scholars read it of the specific favours given to that generation, and the Quran attaches conditions to such preference wherever it names one.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The images at Arabian shrines were kept, dressed and fed by families, and the job passed from father to son. A great deal of work went into the upkeep. So calling the whole arrangement broken and empty was talking about a working trade, with real staff and real income. It was not a far-off judgement, and everyone listening could name the homes it would hurt.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for their ruin is not a forecast. It is an intensive form from a root the Quran uses for total destruction, and it describes something already smashed rather than something due to break. So the sentence reports a present condition. That is how it can be said of people who were visibly doing well.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reply roots single-hearted devotion in gratitude rather than in argument. It does not say the other objects fail to work. It asks why you would look elsewhere when everything you already hold came from one source. That makes sincerity a matter of honest accounting rather than of strong feeling. It also explains why the Quran keeps returning to long lists of favours; those passages are doing the work of an argument.

crossReferences.why: Answers the same instinct: go-betweens are sought only to bring a person nearer to God.
Asks whether any protector other than God should be taken, when He feeds and is not fed.
Says those called upon besides Him cannot remove harm and themselves seek a means of nearness.

studies.applyIt: List the three things your life most depends on. Then trace each one back until you run out of causes you can name. The reply in this verse is not an argument so much as an act of tracing, and it works only if you actually do it rather than agree in advance how it would come out.
studies.explainEasier: Moses said that what those people were doing was already broken and empty. He asked why he should look for another god for them. God had given them more than anyone else.

studies.title: In That Was A Trial
studies.meaning: God turns to the descendants of the people He rescued and asks them to hold one event in mind. The verb for what Pharaoh's men did to them is the one used for driving animals out to graze. The picture is of a people put out to feed on the worst of punishment. It is a bitter image and a deliberate one. The words at the end are where early scholars part ways. The word for trial covers hardship and favour alike, so the great test is read either as the cruelty or as the rescue. Both readings are kept.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca. This sentence turns up three times in the Quran with small changes, addressed each time to the Children of Israel, which suggests it worked as a set formula for recalling the rescue that made them a people. Early scholars report no particular occasion here. In this chapter it sits just before the appointment at the mountain, so a reminder of what they escaped comes before the account of what they were given.

keyTerms.note: The verb for driving livestock out to graze, and for setting a price on goods. Using it of punishment pictures people being pastured on suffering, which is why translations reach for subjected or afflicted.

A word that covers testing by hardship and testing by favour without distinction. Early scholars divide over which is meant here, and the Quran uses it in both senses within a few chapters of each other.
A particle introducing a past event held up for recall. The Quran uses it to open its reminders, and Arabic idiom supplies the imperative to remember without the word appearing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Memory was the only archive these people had. A tribe was whatever it could still recite, and what stopped being recited stopped existing within a generation or two. Family lines, battles and years of famine stayed alive because someone repeated them at gatherings. A family that let its account lapse lost its claims along with it. So an order to remember was an order to keep something in circulation, not simply to feel it.
studies.didYouKnow: The same sentence appears three times across the Quran with a single word changed. Two of them use an ordinary verb for killing. The third uses a verb that means slaughtering. Everything else in the formula stays exactly as it was. That is how the Book handles its repeated passages: one deliberate change, and nothing said about it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The double sense in that last word is not a flaw. If the trial is the cruelty, then suffering is given a purpose without ever being called good. If the trial is the rescue, then relief is named as a test, on the view that comfort undoes people more reliably than pressure does. The Quran's own usage supports both. Leaving it open means the verse tells you something true whichever of the two you are living in.

crossReferences.why: The same sentence in chapter 2, with a verb meaning slaughtering rather than plain killing.
The third instance, framed as an instruction to remember the favour of God upon them.
States the double sense of the word directly, that people are tried with evil and with good.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing you came out of and no longer think about: an illness, a job, a stretch you would not repeat. Tell someone the short version this week, or write four sentences about it. Memory that is never spoken thins out, and what this verse asks for is exactly that, keeping an account in circulation.
studies.explainEasier: God reminded the people how He saved them from Pharaoh's men. Those men had hurt them badly. They killed their sons and let their women live. All of that was a great test from their Lord.

studies.title: Take My Place Among Them
studies.meaning: The appointment is given twice over: thirty nights completed with ten, and then again as a total of forty. Early scholars read the repeating as weight on the completing, not a change of plan. What follows is a handover in three parts. Take my place. Put things right. Do not walk the road of those who spread ruin. The third is a warning from one prophet to another, and early scholars generally read it as watchfulness about the people rather than suspicion about the brother who is being told.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca. Early scholars offer several answers for which months the thirty and the ten fell in, and they pass them on as reports rather than settled fact. No occasion of revelation is attached to this verse. Within the chapter the handover matters. It shows who was holding responsibility while the mountain episode ran, which is what makes the calf story that follows a story about a community rather than about an empty room.

keyTerms.note: From the root for a fixed time. The same word names the places and times set for the rites of pilgrimage, so it carries the sense of an arrangement made in advance and binding on the one who arrives.

From the root behind the words for succession and for a deputy. To take someone's place in this vocabulary means to stand where they stood and carry what they carried, not merely to hold a position open.

From the root for soundness and repair, and the exact opposite of the word used in the next clause. The instruction is not to maintain but to mend, which assumes there is already something needing it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A chief leaving his people named a deputy in front of witnesses. The orders were given aloud, so everyone knew how far the power ran. Arguments over what a deputy had been allowed to do were among the commonest quarrels a tribe could have. What is recorded here follows that shape exactly: a named successor, one thing to do, one limit, all said out loud before the leaving.
studies.didYouKnow: Forty is the Quran's number for a stretch of preparation that has to be finished. Here it is nights on a mountain. Elsewhere it is the years a generation spent wandering. Elsewhere again it is the age at which a person comes into full maturity. The Book never remarks on the pattern, yet it uses the number the same way all three times.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A duty is handed over with terms rather than assumed. The three parts cover the post, the work and the danger, and the danger is named out loud to the most reliable man available. That says something about how leadership is understood here. The safeguard is not the character of the person you appoint. It is the clarity of what you told him, said in front of witnesses and left on the record.

crossReferences.why: Picks up the account at the mountain and reveals what had happened among the people meanwhile.
Names the same forty nights and states plainly what the people did during the absence.
Records the original request for this brother as a helper and a share in the task.

studies.applyIt: Next time you hand something over, say the three parts out loud: what the person now holds, what you want improved rather than merely kept going, and the one thing you are worried about. Most handovers give only the first. The third feels awkward, and it is the one that heads off the argument you would otherwise have later.
studies.explainEasier: God set a time of thirty nights for Moses, then added ten more, making forty. Before he left, Moses told his brother Aaron to take his place. He told him to set things right and not to follow people who cause trouble.

studies.title: You Will Not See Me
studies.meaning: Speech has already been granted, and now sight is asked for. The request is not treated as out of line. The answer is a plain no, and then a demonstration instead of an explanation: look at the mountain. When the disclosure comes, the mountain is levelled and Moses drops senseless, and the case is closed without a word of argument. What he says on coming round is a turning back to God. Early scholars read his last phrase as first among his people, or first to hold what he had just been shown.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca. This verse has been among the most discussed in the Quran since the earliest days. Early scholars broadly agree that the request was about seeing God in this life, and that the answer refused it for this life. They treat the asking itself as something a prophet may do. No particular occasion is reported. The verse sits at the centre of the chapter's longest story, between the rescue at the sea and the calf.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to become clear or uncovered, used of polishing metal until it shows and of a morning that reveals what darkness hid. The verb names an unveiling without describing what was unveiled.

A word for something flattened completely rather than broken into pieces. The Quran uses the same term for what happens to the earth on the final Day, so the mountain receives what the whole world receives.
From the root for a thunderbolt. It names being felled by something overwhelming rather than fainting from weakness, and the related noun in the Quran describes the cry that ends a community.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mountains were the Arabian picture of permanence. Poets swore by them and used them as the measure of what never moves. They stood for anything you could lean on without thinking about it. Tribes placed themselves on the map by them, generation after generation. So a mountain flattened named the collapse of the one thing in that landscape nobody had ever seen change. That is the work the demonstration is doing.
studies.didYouKnow: The verse hands over what was granted before it names what was refused. His Lord spoke to him, and only then does the request for sight arrive and get its answer. Early scholars notice the order. Hearing has already happened. Losing one thing is never treated here as losing the other, which is why the next verse opens with a title rather than a telling-off.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The showing answers the request in a way that words could not. Nothing is said about why the sight is impossible. A mountain is shown what a man asked to be shown, and scale settles the question where argument would not. What he says on coming round is worth noticing as well. It is not disappointment but a turning back. The asking is treated as something to step away from, with no hint that it had been forbidden.

crossReferences.why: States the general principle: vision does not comprehend Him, and He comprehends all vision.
Says a mountain would be seen humbled and split apart if this Quran were sent down upon it.
Names the distinction granted here, that God spoke to Moses directly in speech.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you have asked God for that has not come the way you wanted. Notice whether the silence has made you back away from everything else you were given at the same time. This verse keeps the speaking and the refusal in one sentence, and the man in it does the same. That separation is available to you.
studies.explainEasier: Moses asked God to let him see Him. God said he would not see Him, and told him to watch the mountain instead. When God showed Himself to the mountain, it crumbled and Moses fell down. When he woke, he turned back to God.

studies.title: Take What I Have Given
studies.meaning: A refusal is followed at once by a title. Two things are named as the ground of the choosing, and they come as a pair: My messages and My speech. The second is what the tradition has always taken as the distinguishing gift, since being addressed directly is not reported of every prophet. Then the instruction, in two halves. Take what you have been given, and be one of the thankful. Nothing at all is said about what was withheld. The response asked for concerns what is already in his hands.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca. The Quran says elsewhere that God spoke to Moses in direct speech, and the title the tradition gives him comes from that. Early scholars report no particular occasion for this verse. Where it sits is the whole point. It comes right after the request that was refused, so a passage that could have ended in disappointment closes by naming what is already held.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to take the clear part of something, as one skims what has settled. Choosing in this vocabulary is selection of what is purest rather than preference among equals.

The ordinary word for speech, attached here as a distinct gift alongside the messages. The Quran names this elsewhere as something given to him specifically, and the tradition's title for him comes from it.
The active participle, so a settled disposition rather than an act. He is told to be among a group, which makes thankfulness a company one joins rather than a response one produces on an occasion.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Gifts in Arabia set up relationships, and they were meant to be acknowledged in public. A man given a camel or a horse by a chief praised the giver in front of others. A gift taken without thanks was an insult, and it could break an alliance. So thankfulness was a social act with visible content, not a private warmth. That is how this instruction would have landed.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for choosing here comes from a root for the clear part that rises to the top of a liquid. Related Arabic words name the choicest portion of anything. The Quran uses this same verb of several prophets and of the family lines it names. It always carries the sense of something picked out of many, rather than a merit spotted and rewarded.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The instruction meets a very particular danger. A refusal can rearrange a person's whole attention around the thing withheld. What is offered instead is an inventory: take what you were given, and join the thankful. That moves the exchange off the missing item and onto the ones in hand. And God gives this as the reply to an unanswered prayer, not as general advice about being content.

crossReferences.why: States plainly the distinction named here, that God spoke to Moses in direct speech.
Gives the principle behind the instruction, that thankfulness increases what has been given.
Uses the same idea of preference given to a people, in a reminder addressed to their descendants.

studies.applyIt: Write down the thing you most wanted this year and did not get. Underneath it, list what you did get in the same months. Do not compare the two or draw a conclusion from them. Just have both lists in front of you at once. That is the verse's method, an inventory set beside a refusal, and a reader left to look at the page.
studies.explainEasier: God told Moses He had chosen him above everyone else. He had given him His messages and had spoken to him. He told Moses to take what he was given and to be thankful.

studies.title: Take The Best Of It
studies.meaning: What was written on the tablets is described with two words that sit oddly together: one that moves a person, one that lays things out in detail. Then the instruction, take it with strength, using a word for a firm grip. The words at the end are where early scholars part ways. Tell your people to take the best of it: either the finer of two allowed options, pardon over payback and patience over reply, or all of it, because all of it is best. Both readings are old, and neither shuts the other out.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca. The Quran never says what the tablets were made of or how many there were. Early scholars note that the details reported about them come from Israelite tradition rather than from anything settled. No particular occasion is reported for this verse. It follows straight on from the naming of what was given, so the record comes after the title, and the closing promise about the home of the wrongdoers turns the passage forward.

keyTerms.note: The plural of an ordinary word for a plank or flat board. The Quran uses the same word for the timbers of a ship and, in the singular, for the preserved tablet, so it covers a range from carpentry upward.
From a root for counsel that softens a hearer and moves them to change. It names the effect rather than the content, which is why it is paired here with a second word describing information.
A superlative with a possessive ending. The early scholars read it either as choosing the finer option among what is permitted, or as taking the whole because every part of it is best.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Writing existed in Arabia, and it was rare. A handful of men in Mecca could write, and contracts were sometimes set down on a page. Because nearly everything else was carried in memory, a written page held enormous weight. To hear of a revelation written out and handed over as an object was to hear of something that would last. Reciting, however carefully kept up, did not look like that.
studies.didYouKnow: One plain Arabic word for a flat board does three jobs in the Quran. It names the planks of the ship built before the flood. It names the tablets given at the mountain. And it names the guarded tablet on which the Book itself is said to be written. A carpenter's word covers a hull, a scripture, and something in the unseen.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Pairing a word that moves a person with a word that informs them describes a revelation working on two levels at once, and neither collapses into the other. The instruction to hold it with strength assumes a grip that can loosen. Either reading of the closing words leaves you with judgement to do. Even taking all of it means knowing which part speaks to the situation in front of you today.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word for a tablet, describing the Quran as in a preserved one.
Applies the same word to the planks of the ship carried through the flood.
Gives the same instruction to this community, to follow the best of what was sent down.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you know you should do and ask what the best version of it looks like, rather than the acceptable one. The gap is usually small: a message sent instead of thought about, an apology without the qualifier on the end. Do the better version once today. That is the whole of what this instruction asks, at the scale you actually meet it.
studies.explainEasier: God wrote things for Moses on tablets. They held advice and a clear account of everything. God told him to hold on to them firmly. He also told him to tell his people to take the best of what was in them.

studies.title: Every Sign They See
studies.meaning: Three conditions run one after another, and together they describe a settled direction rather than a run of mistakes. Every sign is seen and not believed. The road of sound judgement is seen and not taken. The road of wandering off is seen and taken. The word for sound judgement means the maturity that lets a person handle their own affairs, and its opposite means losing the way. The reason at the end repeats, word for word, one given ten verses earlier, and it names denial and heedlessness together.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca. The Quraysh objection to the message was tangled up with their standing in the city. The Quran keeps describing their refusal as a matter of self-importance rather than of evidence. Early scholars report no particular occasion for this verse. It stands between the account of the tablets and the account of the calf, drawing a general point out of one story before the chapter goes back to the next part.

keyTerms.note: The same reflexive verb used of the first refusal at the start of this chapter. The grammar carries the falseness inside the word, since it means treating oneself as great rather than being so.

The word for the maturity at which a person can be trusted with their own affairs. It names competence in living rather than correctness of belief, which is a more practical idea than guidance in the abstract.
Its standard opposite in Arabic, naming the state of one who wanders with no direction. Another chapter places the two words together in a single famous sentence about clarity.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Roads in Arabia were choices, not surfaces. A traveller at a junction picked between routes on a guide's advice, and the wrong one could mean days without water. Everyone knew what it was to see the right way and be talked out of it, or to follow a track because it was easier underfoot. So the language of two roads was literal long before it was moral.
studies.didYouKnow: The reason at the end of this verse is identical, word for word, to the one that closes a verse ten places earlier in the same chapter. There it explains a drowning. The Quran repeats the whole phrase without altering anything. The same two failures, denial and heedlessness, are given as the cause in two very different settings.
studies.theologicalSignificance: These three conditions describe something argument cannot reach, because seeing is not what is missing in any of them. The cause named is making yourself great without any right to. That puts the trouble in a posture rather than in a belief. The order is careful too. The denial is given as the reason for the turning away, not the other way round, which keeps this from being about people who never had a chance.

crossReferences.why: Places the same two words together, saying that right direction has become clear from error.
Ends with the identical reason clause, applied there to a completely different community.
Describes hearts and sight being turned about, as they refused to believe the first time.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you know is better for you and have not started, where the reason is not doubt. Usually it is a small dignity: it would mean admitting you were wrong, or being a beginner in front of people. Name that dignity out loud. It is nearly always smaller than what it is costing you, and saying it makes that visible.
studies.explainEasier: God says He will turn proud people away from His signs. They can see every sign and still not believe. They can see the right road and not take it. They can see the wrong road and take it.

studies.title: Their Works Came To Nothing
studies.meaning: Two denials are named together: the signs, and the meeting that comes after death. The outcome uses a verb early Arabic dictionary writers explain from grazing. An animal eats too much of a certain plant, swells, and dies of it. The same verb describes works that grow impressively and are worth nothing. Nothing here says the deeds were few or badly done. Then a question closes the verse, and it rules out any added penalty. They receive what they were doing, and not a thing beyond it.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca. The Quraysh did real acts of generosity. They fed pilgrims, kept the sanctuary, honoured their oaths, and they counted all of it as their standing before God. The Quran does not deny the acts; it asks what the acts were pointed at. Early scholars report no particular occasion for this verse. It comes in a run of general statements set between two stages of one story.

keyTerms.note: Early Arabic dictionary writers explain the verb from an animal that grazes greedily on a plant, swells up and dies. It describes something that looks like abundance and is in fact the shape of a loss.
The ordinary noun for an encounter. Naming the hereafter as a meeting rather than a place makes what is denied a personal appointment rather than a doctrine about geography.
From the root for settling an account and paying what is due. The question at the end uses it to rule out anything extra, so the outcome is described as an exact settlement rather than a sentence.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Herdsmen knew which plants bloated a beast, and they knew a swollen animal was not a fat one. For a day or two a growing herd and a dying herd looked the same, and underneath they were nothing alike. That is the picture this verb carries. To people who lived off their animals, it named a specific and familiar kind of ruinous good appearance.
studies.didYouKnow: The word the Quran uses for the hereafter in this verse is simply the word for a meeting. The Book keeps describing what comes after death as an appointment kept or missed, rather than a place you enter. So denying it is phrased throughout as denying an encounter with someone, not a location.
studies.theologicalSignificance: This separates how much a person does from what it is all aimed at. Deeds do not vanish because they were too few. They are described as swelling and coming to nothing, which is about direction, not volume. The closing question keeps you from reading any spite into it. Nothing is added on top. What is described is an account settled at its real value, which is a demanding kind of fairness.

crossReferences.why: Describes deeds turned into scattered dust, a matching image for effort that had nothing behind it.
Names those whose striving in this life was lost while they reckoned they were doing well.
Compares the deeds of the disbelievers to a mirage a thirsty man takes for water.

studies.applyIt: Look at the thing you have put the most hours into this year and ask what it is finally for. Not the immediate purpose, the one after that. If you cannot get past two answers, that is worth sitting with. This verse is not asking you to do less. It is asking you to know where the effort points.
studies.explainEasier: Some people say no to God's signs and to the meeting after death. Their good works come to nothing. They will get back exactly what they did, and nothing more.

studies.title: A Body That Lowed
studies.meaning: The description gives the object nothing. It was made from their own ornaments, and what it was is a body with a lowing sound, using a word the Quran keeps for shapes without life. Nothing is said about it moving or doing anything at all. Then two questions, and they are the two tests that matter in this story. Did they not see that it does not speak to them, and does not guide them to any road. Those are exactly the two things the Lord they had just left behind had done.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca. The episode is given here in five verses, while another chapter supplies the account of who made the calf and how. No particular occasion is reported. Where it sits in this chapter is the point. The request for a made god was voiced only ten verses earlier, right after the crossing of the sea. Here the people answer their own request during a forty-night absence.

keyTerms.note: The jewellery they were carrying, which they had brought out of Egypt with them. The material of the object is named first, before anything about its form, which keeps its origin in view throughout.

The Quran uses this word for forms that lack life or ordinary need. Choosing it here denies animation before any question about the object is raised, so the description settles the matter in one word.
The specific noun for the sound a cow makes. The verse grants it a noise and nothing else, and the two questions that follow ask about speech and direction, which a noise is not.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Gold in that world was worn rather than banked. A family's wealth hung on its women and moved with them, which is why a fleeing people carried their capital as jewellery. So melting it down was not an act of piety funded from a treasury. It was a whole community spending its entire portable estate, all at once, on an object that made a sound.
studies.didYouKnow: The two tests named here answer straight back to two things said of God a few verses earlier in this same chapter. He had spoken, at the mountain. He had guided them, through the sea. The calf is measured against exactly those two and fails both. The chapter lays the verses out so the comparison is there without ever being stated.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument is not that the object was weak but that it was mute. Speech and direction are named as the two things that make a relationship possible: one addresses you, the other takes you somewhere. Whatever offers neither cannot be in a relationship with anybody. That test travels. It applies to anything a person builds a life around, and most of those things do not speak either.

crossReferences.why: The parallel account, which asks the same question, seeing that it returned them no word.
The request made ten verses earlier for a god to be made for them, using the same verb.
Abraham asks the same kind of question of objects that neither benefit nor harm those who serve them.

studies.applyIt: Put the two tests to something you organise your week around. Does it say anything back to you, and does it take you somewhere. Plenty of good things fail one and pass the other. What this verse watches for is the thing that fails both and still holds the centre of a life, which is easier to acquire than anyone expects.
studies.explainEasier: While Moses was away, his people made a calf out of their gold. It was only a shape that made a sound like a cow. It could not talk to them or show them the way. They were wrong to take it.

studies.title: When It Fell Into Their Hands
studies.meaning: The Arabic for their remorse turns up nowhere else in the Book, and it literally says the regret was dropped into their hands. Grammarians have talked about it for centuries as regret so physical you feel it in the body. Two things happen at once, the regret and the seeing, and the seeing comes second. Only after the feeling lands do they recognise what they had done. What they say then is almost word for word what the first human beings said, with two verbs swapped around.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca. This expression entered Arabic largely through this verse. Early Arabic dictionary writers cite it as an idiom the Quran handed to the language. No particular occasion is reported. Inside the chapter the passage sits between the making of the calf and the return from the mountain. So the community's remorse is on the record before anybody arrives to confront them with what they did.

keyTerms.gloss: it was dropped into their hands
keyTerms.note: A passive construction found only here in the Quran. Early Arabic dictionary writers explain it as the bodily feel of remorse, the sinking that arrives before any thought about it, and Arabic keeps the idiom to this day.
The verb for losing one's road. It is placed after the feeling rather than before it, so the passage describes people who felt something was wrong and only then worked out what.
An emphatic conditional used for a case treated as serious rather than hypothetical. The sentence it opens states an outcome without asking to be spared it, which is what makes the plea unusual.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabic had a whole vocabulary of gesture for regret. Biting the hand, striking one palm against the other, letting the hands fall open. Poets used these instead of naming the feeling, because an audience read the body before it read the word. The idiom here belongs to that set, which is why it works without any abstract noun for regret in the sentence.
studies.didYouKnow: The plea here is the same sentence the first human beings spoke earlier in this very chapter, with the two central verbs in reverse order. There it runs forgiveness then mercy, said straight to God. Here it runs mercy then forgiveness, said about Him. The words at the end match exactly.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Recognition arrives after the feeling rather than producing it, which turns around the order most of us assume. The passage also hands a whole community the same words as the first parents. A shared act of idolatry and one private slip get the same form of answer. And nothing in the plea bargains, explains, or asks to be let off. It states a dependence and a consequence, then stops.

crossReferences.why: The same plea earlier in this chapter, with the words for forgiveness and mercy in the other order.
Gives what happened before this moment, the people refusing to leave the calf until Moses returned.
Shows the same gesture of regret, a man biting his hands over what he chose.

studies.applyIt: Notice where you feel regret before you can name it. The tightening when a certain message arrives. The reluctance to open one particular drawer. That signal is usually right and usually ignored for weeks. Follow one of them this week to whatever it is attached to, and decide nothing until you have found what it was pointing at.
studies.explainEasier: Later the people felt very sorry and saw that they had gone wrong. They said that if their Lord did not show them mercy and forgive them, they would be losers.

studies.title: Son Of My Mother
studies.meaning: Two words describe the state Moses comes back in. Early scholars note that the second covers fury and grief both, so the Arabic does not make you choose. What happens next is told plainly, with nothing softened. He casts down the tablets and takes his brother by the head, pulling him close. The reply is where the verse turns. Aaron names their shared mother rather than their father, reaching for the tenderest bond he has. Then he asks two things: not to be made a spectacle for enemies, and not to be counted among the wrongdoers.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca. The Quran gives this scene in two chapters and neither one says the tablets broke. One says they were cast down. The other says they were taken up again once the anger settled. The details about breakage in the commentaries come from Israelite tradition, and the early authorities say so plainly. No particular occasion is reported for this verse.

keyTerms.note: The early scholars record both senses for this word and it carries them together here. Anger and grief share a form in Arabic because they share an occasion, which is caring about something that has been damaged.
They shared both parents, so naming the mother is a choice. Arabic uses the maternal bond where an appeal needs tenderness rather than authority, and the vocative form here is unusually intimate.
From a root naming the specific pleasure taken in an enemy's misfortune. English has no single word for it. The request is not to be spared harm but not to become the occasion of that pleasure.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Brothers in Arabia were expected to hold together without exception. A quarrel between them in public was a gift to a rival clan. Half-brothers by different mothers were common where men married more than once, so the phrase son of my mother marked the closest tie there was. It owed nothing to inheritance or clan politics. It was the phrase you used when you needed to be heard as family.
studies.didYouKnow: The tablets are thrown down here and picked up again four verses later, once the anger settles. Neither passage says they broke, or that a word of them was lost. Early scholars note that the accounts of breakage come from Israelite tradition rather than from the Book, and Ibn Kathir treats them as reports rather than settled fact.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A prophet is recorded in overwhelming anger and nobody tidies it away. What we are shown instead is the exchange finishing: the brother speaks, the appeal lands, and the next verse is a prayer for them both. That sequence is the point. Anger does not disqualify a man here, and the repair happens in the next breath rather than being put off or narrated away.

crossReferences.why: The parallel account, where the same plea mentions the beard and the fear of causing division.
The immediate answer, a prayer asking forgiveness for himself first and then his brother.
Shows the other end of a sibling rupture, forgiveness given without any account being settled.

studies.applyIt: If you are in the middle of something with a sibling or a close relative, try the move Aaron makes here. Do not defend the facts first. Name the relationship, then say what you are actually afraid of. It takes one sentence, and it changes what the other person is answering, which is the only part you control.
studies.explainEasier: Moses came back angry and sad. He asked his people what they had done while he was gone. He threw down the tablets and took hold of his brother's head. Aaron said the people had been too strong for him.

studies.title: Forgive Me And My Brother
studies.meaning: The order is the striking thing here. He asks forgiveness for himself before his brother, though he is the one who has just seized the other by the head, and his brother is the one who was overpowered. Early scholars keep returning to that sequence. Then the second request uses a verb of entering, so mercy is asked for as a space to be let into rather than a quality to receive. The last words build a superlative from one root used twice, naming God the most merciful of all who show mercy.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, and the words come straight after the confrontation between the two brothers. No particular occasion is reported. The same closing phrase turns up elsewhere in the Quran as the last words of Job's plea after long affliction, and in the Joseph story at a moment of deep grief. So the chapter is reaching for a formula the Book keeps for people with nothing left to argue with.

keyTerms.note: The self comes first in the sentence, before the brother. The classical scholars note the order and read it as a man beginning where the responsibility is nearest before extending the prayer outward.
A verb of entering, so mercy is asked for as a place with an inside rather than as something handed over. The Quran uses the same construction elsewhere for entering God's servants and His garden.
A superlative formed from the root repeated twice. It does not say God is merciful and others are not; it places Him at the top of a scale that includes every merciful being.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Shelter in Arabia was entered, not handed out. A man in danger went to a stronger house and asked to be taken in. Once he was let in, that household stood behind him against everyone else. The words were said aloud and witnessed. So asking to be let into mercy carried the whole picture. Not a gift passed through the door, but a threshold crossed, with everything on the far side of it.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase that closes this prayer shows up at only a handful of points in the Quran, and every time it is in the mouth of someone at the end of what they can bear. Job uses it after long affliction. It appears in the Joseph story at a moment of grief. The Book holds it back and never spreads it across ordinary requests.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The prayer sets an order that runs against instinct. A man who has just been in the right, or acted from a motive he could defend, asks first for himself. That treats even justified anger as something to bring for forgiveness rather than to argue for. And he asks for the two of them in one breath, so the prayer mends the break inside itself before a word is said about mending it.

crossReferences.why: Job's petition ends with the same phrase, after describing affliction without asking for anything specific.
Jacob uses the same words when he has run out of grounds for confidence in anyone else.
Abraham's prayer asks forgiveness for himself, his parents and the believers, in a widening order.

studies.applyIt: The next time you have been wronged and also lost your temper, try praying for yourself first. Not because your grievance was empty. Because starting with the part that is yours is the only place a repair can begin, and it drops the need to settle who was more at fault before anything moves.
studies.explainEasier: Moses prayed for himself and his brother. He asked God to forgive them both and to take them into His mercy. He said God is the most merciful of all.

studies.title: Then Repented Afterwards
studies.meaning: Two verses sit side by side, and they do not pull against each other. The first names what came to those who took the calf: anger from their Lord, and lowliness in this life. Then it widens to cover anyone who makes things up. The second gives the other track: those who did wrong, turned back after it, and believed. The Arabic for after that appears twice in that short verse, once for their turning and once for God's answer. His answer follows their move exactly as their move followed the wrong.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca. The Quran often puts a statement of consequence right beside a statement of mercy, and neither is allowed to cancel the other. No particular occasion is reported for these verses. Where they sit in the chapter matters. The community has already been shown regretting, a few verses earlier, so the reader meets the open door after watching people arrive at it.

keyTerms.note: From a root for being made small and submissive, used of a path worn down by feet. It names a public condition in this life, placed alongside a consequence that belongs to the next.
From the root for cutting leather to a pattern. The general rule is stated of fabricators rather than of that one community, which lifts the verse out of a single episode into a class of conduct.

The same phrase occurs twice in the second verse, first of their turning and then of God's response. The repetition makes the answer follow their move in exactly the way their move followed the wrong.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Coming back from disgrace was possible in Arabia, but slow and public. A man who had broken faith won his standing back by conduct people watched for years. The tribe decided when the account was closed, not the man himself. Set against that, forgiveness given the moment someone turns back was startling. There was no waiting time and no judge in between, and the crowd had nothing to match it.
studies.didYouKnow: The second of these two verses lays out three stages in order: doing wrong, turning back after it, then believing. The Arabic repeats the phrase after that for God's answer. So one short sentence carries the phrase twice, marking both hinges of the sequence. Early scholars treat the doubling as deliberate rather than as filler.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Together these two verses refuse a choice most religious writing forces on a reader. Consequence is stated plainly, with no hedging. Mercy is stated right after it, also with no hedging. The Book never tells you which of the two is yours. That leaves both live at once, which is the actual condition a person is in, and it is why warnings and promises keep appearing here side by side.

crossReferences.why: States the same offer, forgiveness for whoever turns back, believes and acts rightly, then stays guided.
Puts the offer at its widest, addressed to those who exceeded all bounds against themselves.
Adds the further stage, that God exchanges bad deeds for good ones for those who turn and act.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you have decided is past forgiving in yourself. Notice that the decision was yours and no one else made it. You do not have to feel differently about it today. Just see that you have been holding a verdict you were never in a position to issue. Set it down for a week and watch what changes.
studies.explainEasier: The people who took the calf brought anger on themselves and shame in this life. But God also says something else. If people do wrong and then turn back and believe, their Lord will forgive them.

studies.title: When The Anger Fell Silent
studies.meaning: The Arabic makes the anger the subject of the sentence and says it fell silent from him. Not that he mastered it or set it aside; it stopped speaking. Early scholars keep coming back to that image, because it describes anger as a voice that had been talking inside a man and then went quiet, leaving him able to act. Only then does he pick the tablets up. What is written on them is named as two things, guidance and mercy, and the people who receive it are marked out by what they hold in awe: their Lord.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, closing the episode of the return from the mountain. No particular occasion is reported for this verse. The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) met provocations of a similar kind in the city, and the counsel given to him through those years was always about holding back rather than answering. This verse belongs to that register.

keyTerms.note: The ordinary verb for a person ceasing to speak, with anger as its subject. Arabic treats the anger as something that had been talking, and the verse records the moment it stopped rather than the moment he chose.
From a root meaning to copy something from one place to another. The word implies a text transferred rather than composed, which matters for what the tablets are being said to contain.

A verb for reverent fear, distinct from ordinary fright. Arabic places its object before it in this verse, which is a way of saying that it is their Lord specifically whom they hold in awe and nobody else.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian culture prized fierce anger and the strength to hold it, and had a word for each. A man of forbearance was praised in poetry as highly as a brave one, and having both was the ideal. What everyone understood was the timing. Nothing useful was settled while the anger was still speaking, and the wise man was the one who waited for the quiet, not the one who never felt the heat.
studies.didYouKnow: Nobody calms anybody down in this sentence. Anger is the grammatical subject, the verb is the ordinary one for falling silent, and the man is the one it falls silent from. Early scholars note that the wording never says he crushed it. It describes a state passing, which is what anger actually does when nothing is said into it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things sit on either side of a pause. Before it, fury and a physical act. After it, a revelation picked back up and called guidance and mercy. Nothing condemns the interval, and nothing is lost across it. The whole claim here is about order: the same man, the same tablets, and a different capacity to hold them, separated only by the anger going quiet.

crossReferences.why: Describes those who restrain anger and pardon people, in a list of what the God-conscious are like.
Names those who forgive when they are angry, placing the forgiving inside the anger rather than after it.
Instructs repelling with what is better, so that an enemy becomes as though a close friend.

studies.applyIt: Set one rule for yourself this week: nothing decided, sent or said while the anger is still talking. Not crushed, not resolved, only postponed until it goes quiet. Then look at the matter again. Most people find that about half of what they would have said turns out to be the anger talking rather than themselves.
studies.explainEasier: When the anger in Moses went quiet, he picked the tablets up again. What was written on them was guidance and mercy. It was for people who hold their Lord in awe.

studies.title: For What The Foolish Did
studies.meaning: Seventy men are chosen, and a tremor takes them. The prayer that follows is one of the boldest in the Quran. It opens with a protest dressed as an observation: had You willed, You could have destroyed them earlier, and me along with them. Then the question about being held liable together. For the offenders he uses the very word a rejecting people had once thrown at a messenger in this same chapter. Then he reframes the whole thing as a testing, and only then asks. He speaks as one of them throughout, never stepping outside the people he defends.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca. Early scholars differ over what the seventy were chosen for and what the tremor was. They pass on the range rather than settling it, since the Quran gives neither. No particular occasion is reported. In the chapter the prayer stands as the fullest example of a messenger speaking up for his people, and it comes right before an answer that became one of the Book's most quoted sentences.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning lightness and flimsiness. A rejecting people used this same word against a messenger earlier in this chapter, and here a messenger uses it of his own community, with the words among us attached.
From the root describing gold put into fire to separate it from what is mixed in. Naming the whole affair a testing recasts it as a process that reveals rather than a punishment that ends.
The singular of a word used at the start of this chapter for the false patrons people take beside God. The prayer returns the term to its one rightful holder, which is the ground of the whole appeal.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Being held liable together was Arabian law. If a man of a clan killed, the clan paid. If a clan sheltered a wrongdoer, the whole clan could be raided for it. So a man asking whether the many should suffer for the few was raising something poets and judges argued over in earnest. In ordinary practice the answer was usually yes, which is what this prayer pushes against.
studies.didYouKnow: He never once says they about the people he is defending. The offenders are the foolish among us. The punishment is asked about as will You destroy us. The plea is forgive us and have mercy on us. Across the whole prayer, a man speaking up for a community that had just made an idol keeps himself inside it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Speaking up for others is shown here as standing with them, not pleading from outside. He never sets his own record against theirs. He puts himself in the same sentence as the people at fault and asks for both at once. The prayer also does something rare in the Quran: it argues. The argument is left standing in the text, uncorrected, and that itself says something about what may be brought before God.

crossReferences.why: The answer that follows immediately, widening the request far beyond what was asked for.
Shows Abraham disputing on behalf of a community, and being told to leave off the argument.
Gives another intercession that declines to plead innocence, placing the matter with God entirely.

studies.applyIt: Next time you speak up for a group you belong to that has behaved badly, notice which pronoun you use. Saying they lets you stand outside, and it costs you nothing. Saying we costs something, and it is usually the only version anyone listens to. Try it once this month, in a room where you would rather have distanced yourself.
studies.explainEasier: Moses chose seventy men to meet God with him. A shaking took hold of them. He asked God not to destroy them all for what a few foolish people had done. He asked God to forgive them and show them mercy.

studies.title: My Mercy Encompasses Everything
studies.meaning: They ask for good to be written for them in both worlds, and the answer comes back using the same verb, so you know the request was heard on its own terms. Then two statements that are not built alike. Punishment is described with a will attached: it strikes whom He wills. Mercy is described by its reach, covering everything, with no limit set on it anywhere. Early scholars dwell on that difference. What follows names who the written portion is for, and it never takes back the sentence before it.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, and this is among the most quoted verses in the whole Quran. It arrives as the answer to a prayer made for a community that had just made an idol. It is spoken, in other words, into the least promising moment the chapter has described. No particular occasion is reported. The closing words turn forward, and the next verse carries the naming on.

keyTerms.note: The verb of inscribing something so that it holds. The answer picks up the same verb and says I shall write it, so the reply is framed in the exact vocabulary the request used.
From a verb meaning to return by the road you came. It describes coming back rather than arriving, which fits a petition made on behalf of people who had gone somewhere else and come back.
From the root for breadth and room. The verb is in the perfect tense, so mercy is described as having already taken everything in, not as capable of doing so if occasion arises.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Writing was scarce, and so it was weighty. A debt set down, or a treaty inscribed and hung at the sanctuary, had a permanence that spoken words did not. People asked for things to be written when they wanted them past dispute. The prayer here uses that vocabulary, and the answer grants it in the same word. It would have landed as an undertaking rather than a reassurance.
studies.didYouKnow: The two statements about punishment and mercy are not built the same way, and that is the surprise. The first ties punishment to a will. The second gives mercy an extent, with nothing narrowing it. Early scholars note that the Quran never phrases mercy as smaller than what it applies to, and this is the widest instance in the Book.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A wide statement is followed by a narrower one, and the tradition holds the two together. Neither is allowed to cancel the other. Mercy in this life reaches everything that exists, the believer and the denier alike. What is written for the next life comes with terms attached. That is how this verse can be quoted as widely as it is without turning into a claim that nothing matters. It is also why hope here always arrives paired with something to do.

crossReferences.why: The angels' prayer, which describes God as having encompassed everything in mercy and knowledge.
States that He has prescribed mercy upon Himself, using the same verb of writing.
Applies the same breadth to those who exceeded all bounds, telling them not to despair.

studies.applyIt: Take the line about mercy covering everything and put it against one thing today. Not the world in general. A situation you have written off, or a person, or yourself. Say the sentence with that one thing held in mind. Big statements do nothing until they meet something small, and that meeting takes two minutes.
studies.explainEasier: Moses asked God to write good for them in this life and the next. God said His punishment reaches whoever He wills. He said His mercy covers everything. He will write it for people who do right and give to others.

studies.theme: The Love Between God and the Believer
studies.title: The Burdens And The Shackles
studies.meaning: The naming carries on, now describing a messenger and what following him actually involves. He is called unlettered, which early scholars explain as having picked up no writing, as one is at birth. Then a list of what he does for people, and the last item carries the verse: he lifts off them their burden and the shackles that were on them. The word for shackles shares a root with the word used earlier in this chapter for rancour taken out in the Garden. Four responses follow, and every one is an act rather than an opinion.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca. The Quran says this description was found with the communities holding earlier scripture, and it presents that as a continuity rather than a quarrel. The weight through the whole passage falls on what following amounts to, not on an argument with anyone. No particular occasion is reported for this verse. It completes the answer given to the prayer just before.

keyTerms.note: Built from the word for mother, in the sense of being as one was when born. The early scholars explain it as having acquired no writing, which is why what he brought could not be traced to any book he had read.
A load that binds a person in place, from a root meaning to tie down. The word appears in the closing prayer of the longest chapter, where the community asks not to be made to carry one.
Iron collars, from the same root as the word used earlier in this chapter for rancour drawn out of the chest. Both name something that gets inside and then holds its bearer fast.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Very few people in Mecca could write. The skill was a trade, not a mark of education, so a man who could not write was in the ordinary position. What counted socially was memory. Men were valued for holding poetry, family lines and treaties in their heads. The description in this verse named a normal member of the community rather than marking anyone out as lacking.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for shackles here comes from the same root as a word used earlier in this chapter. There it named the rancour drawn out of the chests of the people of the Garden. Arabic builds both from the idea of something getting inside and holding fast. What is lifted away is named with one root twice in a single chapter, once inside and once outside.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Following is described as a load taken off, not a load added, which is the opposite of what most people expect religion to be. Weights are set down and chains come off. The four responses named afterwards are all things done rather than agreed to: believing, honouring, supporting, and following a light. Closeness is spoken of in actions the whole way through. That is how the Quran usually talks about love.

crossReferences.why: Asks in prayer not to be made to carry the burden that was laid on earlier communities.
Uses the related word for rancour drawn out of the chests, the inward version of the same removal.
States the connection directly, that following him is what God's love for a person runs through.

studies.applyIt: Ask what religion currently feels like to you: something set down, or something added. Both answers are common, and only one of them matches this verse. If yours is the second, find one obligation you invented and have been carrying that nobody actually placed on you, and put it down this week. Then see whether anything real was lost.
studies.explainEasier: The verse speaks about the Prophet who could not read or write. Earlier books told about him. He tells people to do good and keeps them from what is bad. He takes heavy loads and chains off them.

studies.title: To All Of You
studies.meaning: He is told to say something, and it is the widest address in the chapter. Every messenger described in the hundred verses before was sent to his own people, named as their brother and speaking their language. This one is told to say he is sent to all of you together, and the word for all is placed with weight. What grounds the claim is not any standing of his own, but ownership of the heavens and the earth. Then a description early scholars find striking: the Prophet who himself believes in God and His words.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca. The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was speaking to one city, and the scope announced here ran far past anything the Quraysh were arguing about at the time. No particular occasion is reported for this verse. Where it sits, at the end of the chapter's longest story, is deliberate. The run of local missions is finished, and the last of them is described in terms none of the others were.

keyTerms.note: A word for a totality gathered rather than a sum of parts. Its position in the sentence gives it weight, and it is the term that separates this commission from every other one described in the chapter.
Two verbs of the same form, one the opposite of the other. Naming both under one authority is the Quran's usual way of ruling out a division of the world between competing powers.

An unusual thing to say about a prophet. It places him among the believers rather than above them, which is consistent with the Quran's insistence that the one who delivers a message is also under it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian identity was local to the bone. A man was of a clan, inside a tribe, inside a region, and his religion, his protection and his duties all followed those lines. Even the sanctuary at Mecca was run by particular families with particular rights. An address to all people had no precedent in that world. No clan, region or family line was named, and it had no obvious audience either.
studies.didYouKnow: This chapter spends more than a hundred verses on messengers, each described as the brother of his own people. Each was sent to one community, in its own language. Then a single verse orders a message addressed to everyone. The contrast is built purely by placement, and the Book says nothing about the change of scope at the moment it makes it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The universal claim rests on ownership rather than on the messenger. The heavens and the earth belong to one, so a message meant for all people follows from that. And the man carrying it is described as one of those who believe what he carries. That keeps the reach of the message from turning into a claim about the standing of the man announcing it, which is the shape every commission takes here.

crossReferences.why: States the same scope, that he was sent to all people as a bearer of news and a warner.
Describes the sending as a mercy to all the worlds, in one short verse.
Shows the messenger believing in what was sent down to him, alongside the believers, as here.

studies.applyIt: Notice how local your sense of religious belonging is: your community, your language, the way things are done where you live. None of that is wrong. But find one thing this week from a Muslim community very unlike yours, a recitation, a teacher, a practice, and take it seriously for an hour. This verse's scope is worth testing now and then.
studies.explainEasier: The Prophet is told to say that he is God's messenger to all people. The heavens and the earth belong to God. There is no god but Him. He gives life and takes it away.

studies.title: A Community That Guides
studies.meaning: One short verse, and it does something the passages around it do not. After a long account of a community's failures, it says that among those same people is a group who guide by the truth and act justly by it. Nothing is qualified and nothing is taken back.
