The verb for acting justly comes from a root for balancing two things until they are equal, so guiding and weighing share a vocabulary. Early scholars note that the Quran says this of a people it has just shown at their worst.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca. The chapter has spent forty verses on the calf, the tremor and the pleading, and then this sentence arrives with no transition at all. No particular occasion is reported. Later in the same chapter the identical wording is applied to humanity in general rather than to one people. So this verse is one case of something the Book says more widely about every group of human beings.

keyTerms.note: Indefinite, so a community rather than the community. The word covers any body of people with a shared character, and its indefiniteness keeps the statement from being a claim about numbers.

The active verb, so they are described as guiding others rather than as being guided. The Quran distinguishes the two carefully, and here it credits the harder of them to a people it has just criticised.
From a root meaning to make two things equal in weight, which also gives the word for a counterweight on a pack animal. Justice in this vocabulary is an act of balancing rather than a principle held.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabs argued all the time about the character of other tribes, and satire built on it was a known art. A whole people could be written off for what a few of them did, and the insult would be recited for years. Against that habit, this sentence stops in the middle of a long complaint and names a group inside the blamed people as guides. It cut across how the crowd used language.
studies.didYouKnow: This exact wording appears twice in this one chapter. Here it describes a group among the people of Moses. Twenty verses later the same phrase, guiding by the truth and acting justly by it, is applied to those God created, with no people named at all. One sentence does duty for a single community and for humanity at large.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The verse refuses to let a long account of failure harden into a verdict on a people. It arrives without argument and without softening what came before. That is how the Quran usually handles this: it does not withdraw a criticism, it simply declines to widen it to everyone. Pairing guiding with justice matters as well. It makes the mark of such a community what it does for others, not what it holds.

crossReferences.why: Uses the identical wording later in this chapter, applied to those God created rather than one people.
Says plainly that they are not all alike, and describes an upright community among them.
Names a moderate community among them, distinguishing it from those doing evil.

studies.applyIt: Take a group you have a settled bad opinion about and name one person in it you respect. If you cannot, that is a fact about the range of people you know rather than about the group. Either way, do not soften the criticism you hold. Just add the exception, out loud, the next time you make it.
studies.explainEasier: Not everyone among the people of Moses went wrong. The verse says there is a group among them who guide others by the truth. They also act fairly by it.

studies.title: Each Knew Its Drinking Place
studies.meaning: Provision arrives in three forms, and each one comes organised. Twelve springs for twelve groups, with every group knowing which one was theirs, so the water carries an allocation instead of an occasion to fight. Then shade, then food sent down. The verb used here for the water coming out means a first seeping. The account in another chapter uses one meaning a full bursting, and early scholars read the two as stages of a single thing. The closing line puts all the damage on the side of the people.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, spoken to an audience for whom every item here was a live worry: water rights, shade, and food arriving without being grown. No particular occasion is reported for this verse. The passage stands between two general statements about the community. It works as an inventory of what had been supplied, set down just before the account of what was done with it picks up again.

keyTerms.note: A verb for water first breaking through, gently. Another chapter describes the same event with a verb meaning to burst open fully, and early scholars read the two as the beginning and the completion of one event.
A noun of place from the verb to drink. The verse says each group knew theirs, so what is described includes an allocation, which is the part that keeps twelve groups from fighting over water.
From the root for shade, which in Arabic belongs to the vocabulary of relief rather than of darkness. Shade in a desert is not an absence of light but the condition that makes daytime survivable.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Water rights were the sharpest question in Arabian life. Wells were shared out by turns everyone knew, and people fought over them anyway, sometimes over a single day's precedence. Shade was managed too. A tribe camped where a rock or a stand of palms gave it, and travellers rested through the worst hours or died. The three gifts listed here are, in that order, what a desert journey actually took.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran tells this episode in two chapters and changes one verb. Here the springs seep out; in the other account they burst open. Early scholars note that the two verbs catch different moments of one event, the first trickle and the full flow. They read them as fitting together rather than as versions to choose between.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The provision has structure built into it, which is easy to read straight past. Twelve springs matched to twelve groups is not more water than one spring would be. It is water arranged so that receiving it does not turn into a fight. Then the closing formula puts everything that followed on the human side. It says the wrong done reached nobody except the people doing it.

crossReferences.why: The parallel account, using the other verb for the springs and listing the same three provisions.
Names the same food and warns against transgressing in what had been provided.
Describes the striking of the sea with the staff, the other occasion on which the staff opens water.

studies.applyIt: Look at something you share with other people and ask whether the arrangement is clear: whose turn, whose portion, who decides. Most friction over shared things is about allocation, not shortage. Fix one of those this week by saying it aloud instead of assuming it. This verse treats the sharing out as part of the gift itself.
studies.explainEasier: God split the people into twelve groups. Moses struck the rock with his staff and twelve springs came out. Each group knew which spring was theirs. God also gave them clouds for shade and good food to eat.

studies.title: Enter The Gate Bowing
studies.meaning: Four instructions and a promise. Settle here, eat freely, say one particular word, and come through the gate lowered. The word they are told to say means the setting down of a load, so it asks for a burden to be lifted rather than being a formula of any other kind. Early scholars differ over the posture. Some read full prostration, others a bowing of the head, since a gate is hard to enter face down. The promise attached comes doubled: forgiveness, and then an increase for those who do well.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca. This instruction appears in two chapters, and the two versions give the same four elements with the word and the gate in opposite order. Early scholars note the variation without treating it as a discrepancy. No particular occasion is reported. What followed comes in the next verse, where the word they were told to say is exchanged for another.

keyTerms.gloss: a setting down of the load
keyTerms.note: From a verb meaning to unload an animal or put a burden on the ground. The early scholars explain it as asking for the weight of wrongdoing to be taken off, which is how one word can carry a whole request.

A plural participle describing their bearing as they enter. The early scholars read it as full prostration or as bowing the head, noting that a gateway makes the first difficult, and they record both.
From a root joining goodness with beauty, so the word means doing a thing finely rather than merely correctly. The increase promised is attached to that quality rather than to the entering itself.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Entering a town was a formal act, with a bearing attached. A defeated party came in bareheaded and on foot; an honoured guest rode. Anyone at a gate could read a person's standing from how they came through it. There were words for thresholds too, asking leave or calling for protection. The instruction here uses that whole grammar, pairing a word with a posture at the exact point where both were read.
studies.didYouKnow: This instruction appears twice in the Quran with its two central clauses in opposite order. One chapter gives the gate first and then the word. This one gives the word first and then the gate. Everything else is kept, which is how the Book usually repeats a passage: one deliberate change, and no comment on it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Speech is paired with posture here, and neither counts as enough alone. A word is given to say and a bearing to take, and the promise attaches to the two together. That is how the Quran usually describes a turning back: something said, and something done with the body at the same time. The doubled promise then keeps being forgiven separate from being increased, so pardon is not the ceiling of what is offered.

crossReferences.why: The same instruction with the gate and the word given in the opposite order.
Reports what followed, the word replaced by a different one from the one they were given.
Pairs a movement with a request for forgiveness in the same way, in the pilgrimage passages.

studies.applyIt: Think of an apology you owe and have been planning to make in writing. Consider doing it in person instead, or at least by voice. The instruction here attaches a posture to a word. The two together cost something the word on its own does not, and that difference in cost is most of what makes an apology land.
studies.explainEasier: God told them to live in the town and eat what they liked. They were told to say one word asking for their load to be lifted. They were told to go through the gate bowing low.

studies.title: A Word Other Than
studies.meaning: One word was given to say, and a different one was said instead. The verse never reports which. It reports only that a swap took place. Early scholars notice the limit built into the sentence: it names the wrongdoers among them rather than the whole community, and the consequence lands on that same limited group. What comes down arrives from the sky. It is called by a word meaning something repellent, the very term used earlier in this chapter for what was sent on Egypt.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, and the Quran gives this episode twice. Both tellings keep the limit to those who did wrong, one by repeating the phrase and this one by adding a word meaning among them. No particular occasion is reported for it. It follows straight on from the instruction in the verse before, so the reader has just heard what was asked for before hearing what was done with it.

keyTerms.note: The verb for putting one thing in another's place, so the position was kept and the content swapped. Nothing was refused outright, which is what makes the act a substitution rather than a rejection.

A partitive, restricting the subject to a portion of the community. The Quran keeps the restriction in both places where it tells this, and the consequence in the same verse is directed only at that portion.

A word for something repellent, used earlier in this chapter for what was sent upon Egypt. It names the quality of what arrives rather than its form, which is why the Quran gives no description of it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wording mattered in a world with almost no paperwork. The exact words of an oath, a truce or a marriage were what made it binding, and changing a syllable could void the whole thing or start a feud. Witnesses were kept precisely to hold those words. People trained to keep a formula exact would have grasped at once that swapping one word for another counted as an act, not a slip.
studies.didYouKnow: The word they were told to say was one syllable long, a request for a burden to be set down. What the Quran records is not that they refused it. It records that something else was put in its place. Both tellings in the Book withhold the substituted word completely. The reader never learns what was actually said, only that the exchange happened.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A small change in speech is treated here as a serious matter, because the words in question were the whole of what was asked. Where a request has been reduced to one thing, changing that thing is not partial obedience. It is a complete swap. The care the verse takes to limit who it means is just as deliberate. It keeps a community's failure attached to the people who actually committed it.

crossReferences.why: The other telling, which keeps the same restriction to the wrongdoers by repeating the phrase.
The instruction that was given, including the word to say and the posture to enter with.
Describes displacing words from their places, with speech twisted by tongues in another setting.

studies.applyIt: Notice the small substitutions in your own speech this week: I will try instead of I will, someone should instead of I should, we for I when something has gone wrong. Each is a word put in another's place, and each changes what was actually said. Catch one, and put the original word back.
studies.explainEasier: Some of them changed the word they had been told to say. They put a different word in its place. Because of that wrong, God sent down trouble on them from the sky.

studies.title: The Town By The Sea
studies.meaning: The test is set out with unusual care. On the Sabbath the fish came, rising where everyone could see them, and on other days they did not come at all. Early scholars point at the timing: the plenty arrived exactly when it could not be taken. So the hardship was never hunger. It was the sight of plenty just out of reach. The verb for their overstepping means going past a limit, not doing harm in itself, and the closing words call the whole arrangement a test.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca. The verse opens by telling the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) to ask them about the town, so the story was already known to the people being addressed. The Quran never names the town, and early scholars offer several coastal sites, recorded as reports rather than settled fact. The Book keeps that same restraint elsewhere about details it holds back.

keyTerms.note: A phrase meaning right on the shore rather than merely coastal. Three words set out the town's whole livelihood. That is why nothing more needs saying about why fish mattered so much.

A rare plural describing the fish raising themselves at the water's surface. Early scholars explain it as coming visibly and within reach. That detail makes the restraint hard rather than merely inconvenient.

From a root meaning to run past a boundary, used of an animal breaking out of enclosed ground. It names crossing a line rather than any harm in the act itself. That is what a limit-based test consists of.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabia had its own version of this. During the sacred months, raiding stopped. Caravans that would have tempted anyone at other times of year passed by untouched, watched by men who could easily have taken them. Everyone there knew what it was to see something valuable pass under a limit they had accepted. The whole trade of the peninsula rested on that restraint holding for four months a year.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran tells this episode in two chapters and names the town in neither. Early scholars offer several sites along the Red Sea and further north, and they pass them on as reports. The Book holds the name back the same way it holds back the tree in the Garden. It does the same with the man in the parable a few verses later.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The test here was designed rather than accidental, and the verse lets the design show. The plenty was placed exactly where it could not be taken, so the difficulty was arranged on purpose. That says something precise about how the Quran treats testing. A test is not hardship that is simply allowed to happen. It is a setting of things that shows what a limit is really worth to the person keeping it.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same episode in one short verse, with the outcome and none of the circumstances.
Describes another test involving game coming within easy reach, with a restraint attached.
States the principle: what is on the earth was made an ornament to test conduct.

studies.applyIt: Think of the limit you keep that is hardest, and notice when it is hardest. It is almost never when the thing is out of reach. It is when it is right there, easy, and nobody would know. That moment is the whole test, and seeing it as the test rather than as bad luck changes how it feels to stand in it.
studies.explainEasier: A town by the sea was told not to fish on one day each week. On that day the fish came right up to the top of the water. On other days they did not. It was a test.

studies.title: Why Do You Counsel Them
studies.meaning: A group inside the town asks the others why they bother, and the question is not cynical. It assumes the outcome is already settled, so speaking looks like wasted breath. The answer gives two reasons, and they are of different orders. The first is a discharge before their Lord, which does not depend on any result at all. The second comes in with the particle of hope: perhaps they will guard themselves. Early scholars note that the reason depending on success is placed second and given only as a possibility.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca. The believers in the city were speaking to people who had been refusing for years, and whether to keep speaking was a live question for them. No particular occasion is reported for this verse. In the chapter it comes just before the outcome, so the reader hears the argument about whether to speak before learning what happened to each side having it.

keyTerms.note: From a root for speech meant to soften a hearer and move them to change. It names counsel aimed at the heart rather than argument aimed at the mind, which is why the question about futility bites.
A noun for what clears a person of responsibility. The first reason given is therefore about the speakers rather than the hearers, and it holds whether or not anything is achieved.
The particle of hope, which stops the clause short of expectation. Placing it on the second reason keeps the whole answer honest, since the speakers do not claim to think it likely.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Public counsel in a small town was costly and awkward, because everyone knew everyone. Telling a neighbour he was wrong meant living beside him afterwards. Arabs had a word of praise for the man who did it anyway, and a whole store of words for the resentment it drew. The question asked here is whether it is worth the trouble when nothing will change, and that community had surely asked it before.
studies.didYouKnow: The answer never defends the counselling by claiming it will work. It gives a reason that holds whatever the outcome, and only then adds the hope of one, marked with a particle meaning it may be so. Early scholars dwell on that order. It grounds the whole activity in something the speaker controls.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Duty is separated here from results, and that split is what keeps people speaking long after they have stopped expecting change. The verse also takes the objection seriously instead of brushing it off, and it accuses the objectors of nothing. What it shows is a way of carrying on that needs no optimism and does not sink into despair. The two reasons together are what make that possible.

crossReferences.why: Instructs continuing to remind, on the ground that reminding benefits the believers.
Limits the messenger's role to reminding, saying he is not set over them as a controller.
Has a messenger say he intends only reform as far as he is able, with success resting elsewhere.

studies.applyIt: Think of something true you have stopped saying because it never lands. You may well be right that it will not land. Say it once more anyway, briefly and without pressure, then let it go. This verse offers a reason for speaking that does not depend on being heard, which is the only reason that survives long relationships.
studies.explainEasier: Some people asked why anyone should keep warning a town that would not listen. The ones giving the warning said they had two reasons. One was to be clear before God. The other was that the town might still change.

studies.title: Those Who Forbade The Wrong
studies.meaning: Three groups have been described, and only two outcomes are reported. The people who overstepped are seized, and the people who forbade the wrong are saved. The group who asked why anyone bothered appears at neither end. That silence is one of the oldest discussions among the early scholars, and their reports hold a long uncertainty about this group before a view settled. The change announced in the second verse is read by most early authorities as real, while some read it as a likeness of character.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca. Ibn Abbas is reported to have spent a long time uncertain about the fate of the third group before concluding that they were saved. The major commentaries preserve that report as an account of how the question was worked through, not as a ruling handed down. No occasion of revelation is attached to these verses.

keyTerms.note: The deliverance is attached to this description rather than to abstaining. Those saved are named by what they said to others, not by what they refrained from doing themselves, which early scholars note carefully.

A rare adjectival form from the root for hardship and distress. Its unusual shape gives the word an emphasis that the ordinary form would not carry, which is why translations reach for terms like dire.
From a verb used of shooing an animal away. It describes being repelled and made small, and it appears elsewhere in the Quran of a gaze that returns humbled after searching for a flaw.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Silence was the ordinary strategy in a small community. A man who neither joined a wrong nor spoke against it kept his standing with everyone, and Arabian society had nothing that forced him to choose. So whether such a person shares a town's fate was not an abstract question. It was where most people stood most of the time, and everyone knew it.
studies.didYouKnow: Three groups are described in these verses, and only two outcomes are given. The commentary tradition preserves a long-running uncertainty about the group who had asked why anyone was bothering. The reports show the question being weighed for years before a view settled. The Quran itself simply leaves them out of the sentence.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Rescue is attached to speaking, not to holding back, and that raises the bar in an uncomfortable direction. The passage does not say the saved had kept the limit, though they surely had. It says they forbade the wrong. So objecting is itself a way of sharing in a community's fate. That is why the tradition treated the missing third group as a genuinely open question rather than an easy one.

crossReferences.why: Gives the exchange between the two groups that these verses then resolve, or partly resolve.
Names the failure to forbid wrongdoing among one another as what a curse fell upon.
Tells the same outcome briefly and calls it an example for what lay before it and after it.

studies.applyIt: Recall a situation where you neither joined in nor objected. Most of us are in one now. You do not have to make a scene. Say the smallest true thing to one person: I am not comfortable with this. It costs about four seconds, and it moves you out of the group this passage declines to mention.
studies.explainEasier: When the town would not listen, God saved the people who had spoken up against the wrong. The ones who kept breaking the rule were punished. The Quran does not say what happened to the people who stayed quiet.

studies.title: Swift And Yet Forgiving
studies.meaning: The announcement uses a verb meaning to proclaim something so that it is known. What is announced concerns the community this chapter has been describing. The phrase for what will come against them is word for word the phrase used earlier here for what Egypt had done to them. Then the verse closes with two descriptions of God that pull in opposite directions. He is swift in requital, and He is forgiving and merciful. Early scholars read that pairing as deliberate, and the next verse at once marks off the righteous among them from the rest.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, at the close of a long passage about one people and their history. The Quran often attaches this pair of names to its harshest lines, and the same two clauses stand together at the end of another chapter, in this order. No occasion is reported for the verse. The next verse then sets one group apart from another, and early scholars always read the two as one.

keyTerms.note: From the root for giving ear, in a form meaning to proclaim so that it cannot be missed. The verb concerns publication rather than decision, so what is described is a declaration already made.
The same verb used earlier in this chapter for what Egypt did to them, taken from herding and pricing. The Book applies one expression to the oppression suffered and to what is announced here.
Requital here is from a root meaning to follow on the heel, so it names what comes after an act rather than a penalty imposed on it. Swiftness describes the closeness of the following, not haste.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Proclamation was how anything became binding. A herald stood at a gathering, the terms were called out, and from that moment nobody could claim not to have known. Treaties, outlawries and the opening of a market all worked that way. The verb at the start of this verse belongs to that setting. It describes something put on the public record, not a decision reached in private.
studies.didYouKnow: The two names for God that close this verse stand together at the end of another chapter, in the same order and almost the same words. The Quran often places forgiveness and mercy right after a line about paying back. Early scholars treat the pairing as a fixed part of the Book, not a softening tacked on later.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The tradition reads this verse alongside the sentence that follows it, which says plainly that among them are the righteous and among them are others. Neither statement is allowed to swallow the other. The closing pair also keeps the passage from describing a settled fate. Requital and forgiveness are named as belonging to the same one, in the same breath, and nothing is said about which any person will meet.

crossReferences.why: The next verse, which distinguishes the righteous among them from the rest and names both.
Closes with the identical pair of descriptions, swift in requital and yet forgiving and merciful.
States earlier in this chapter that among this same people is a community that guides by truth.

studies.applyIt: When you read a severe passage, get into the habit of reading the clause after it before you decide what it means. This verse ends by naming mercy, and the next one names the righteous among the people just described. Whole readings have been built by stopping one sentence early. The habit of not stopping is cheap to acquire.
studies.explainEasier: God made it known that hard times would keep coming to these people. This would last until the last day. The verse then ends by saying God is quick to repay. It also says He forgives and is kind.

studies.title: Some Of Them Righteous
studies.meaning: The dividing comes first, and the verb is the same one used earlier in this chapter for the twelve tribes. One word does duty for an ordering and for a scattering. Then the sentence the whole passage turns on: among them are the righteous, and among them are those short of that. Nothing is counted. Then the testing, and it comes from both directions, with good things and with bad, which rules out reading either one as a verdict. The purpose given is a returning, brought in with the particle of hope.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca. This verse is where the chapter's long account of one community lands. Early scholars always read it alongside the severe statement just before it, because it is the sentence that stops that passage from becoming a description of a whole people. No particular occasion is reported for it. The chapter then moves on to a general statement about inheritors in the next verse.

keyTerms.note: The same verb used earlier in this chapter for dividing them into twelve tribes. One word covers an orderly arrangement in one place and a scattering across the earth in the other, without changing form.

A phrase meaning below or other than the thing just named. It declines to specify what the second group is, describing them only by their distance from the first, which is a deliberately unfinished description.
Both are named as instruments of testing, in that order. Since the two are given the same role, neither can be read as a report on the standing of whoever receives it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabs generalised about whole peoples constantly, and satire built on the character of a tribe was a recognised art. One line of verse could sum up a tribe, and it stuck for generations. Everyone knew the reputations, and that was the normal way of talking about others. So a sentence that stops to say some of them are righteous and some are not would have sounded like a refusal of the usual idiom.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here for scattering them is the same verb used a few verses earlier. There it describes dividing them into twelve tribes, an orderly arrangement, with water set aside for each group. The Quran uses one word for both. The same act of dividing appears once as provision and once as dispersal.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Testing is described as running in both directions, and that is the verse's most portable claim. If good fortune and bad are both tools, then neither shows where anyone stands, including where you stand yourself. The purpose given is a returning, not a punishment. And the line at the centre keeps the whole passage before it from hardening into a statement about a people as such.

crossReferences.why: Names a community among them that guides by truth, in the same chapter and the same terms.
States plainly that they are not all alike, describing an upright group reciting through the night.
Gives the same principle generally, that people are tested with evil and with good as a trial.

studies.applyIt: Take the last general statement you made about a group of people. Add the qualification this verse adds: some of them, and some of them not. It does not ask you to change your assessment of anything you actually saw. It asks you to stop applying it to people you have not met, which is a smaller thing than it sounds.
studies.explainEasier: God spread these people out into groups all over the earth. Some of them were good and some were not. He tested them with good times and with bad times, so that they would turn back to Him.

studies.title: We Will Be Forgiven
studies.meaning: The word for the generation that followed is the form Arabic keeps for an unworthy successor; one vowel separates it from the near-identical word for a worthy one. They inherited a Book and took the passing goods of this lower world. Then comes the line the whole passage turns on: we will be forgiven. What follows is the sharpest part. If the like comes again, they take it again. The presumption is not a reaction to a slip. It is a standing arrangement that keeps the next one available.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca. The passage is about people who had a scripture, studied it, and used a doctrine drawn from it to keep doing what it addressed. No particular occasion is reported for this verse. It sits where the chapter turns from one community's history to a general statement. And it is followed at once by a description of those who hold the Book firmly, so both possibilities are named.

keyTerms.note: Arabic distinguishes two nearly identical nouns from this root by one vowel, one used for a worthy successor and one for an unworthy one. This verse uses the second, so the assessment sits in the noun itself.
A word for what appears briefly and moves on, used in Arabic for anything incidental rather than substantial. The phrase attaches it to this lower world, so the transience is named twice over.
An intensive form from the root for tying tightly. It names an undertaking made firm rather than a promise given, and the verse says it was taken upon them rather than offered to them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabs had their own version of a teaching that made things easier. The keepers of the sanctuary granted concessions to their own clans, and various customs let a man put off or swap an obligation he found awkward. He could do it and still look like he was keeping it. Everyone knew the move. So this verse does not describe a foreign failing; it describes a very familiar one, done with a scripture instead of a custom.
studies.didYouKnow: The verse notes that they studied what was in the Book, using the ordinary verb for reading something over and over until it is learned. So knowledge was not what was missing. Early scholars dwell on that clause. It removes the usual explanation for such conduct and leaves only the presumption named in the same sentence.
studies.theologicalSignificance: One specific misuse of forgiveness is named here: using it in advance. Turning back after a wrong is the whole subject of the verses a few pages earlier. Here the same expectation is moved to the front, where it becomes a licence. The Quran does not answer by taking forgiveness away. It answers by pointing out that the second taking has already been decided on, which is what a covenant was meant to prevent.

crossReferences.why: Distinguishes turning back soon after a wrong from the turning offered when death arrives.
The next verse, describing those who hold fast to the Book, as the immediate counterpart.
Warns against being deceived about God by the great deceiver, and against worldly life deceiving you.

studies.applyIt: Listen for the moment you decide in advance that something will be all right. Not afterwards, when the regret is real, but before, while the decision is still being made. That sentence is doing work, and it is worth catching once. You do not need to conclude anything about forgiveness. Just notice what the thought was for.
studies.explainEasier: The people who came later were given the same book. They still took what they wanted from this world and said God would forgive them. Then they did it again. The verse asks if they had not promised to hold to the book.

studies.title: Those Who Hold It Firmly
studies.meaning: The counterpart arrives in one sentence: those who hold the Book firmly, using an intensive verb for gripping, and who keep up the prayer. The reward promised is attached to a word meaning those who put things right. Then the mountain, raised over them like an awning. The word chosen for that canopy comes from the root for shade, so the thing hanging above them in threat is named with the vocabulary of shelter. The instruction given underneath it is the same one given to Moses with the tablets.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca. The raising of the mountain is mentioned several times in the Quran, always in a few words, with no account of how long it lasted or how it ended. Early scholars do not go beyond the text. No particular occasion is reported for these verses. The pairing here is deliberate: the generation who presumed on forgiveness is described, and then those who did the opposite.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form of the verb for grasping, so the holding is described as continuous and effortful. It stands against the taking described in the verse before, which used a verb of casual acquisition.
A rare verb for pulling something up forcefully from where it sits. The Quran uses it only here, and its violence is part of what makes the following image so strange.
From the root for shade, and the ordinary word for something spread overhead to shelter people. Naming the suspended mountain with it puts the vocabulary of protection on an object about to fall.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: An awning was the most welcome object in Arabian life. A cloth stretched over poles at a market, the shade side of a tent, a rock ledge at noon: these were where business got done and where a traveller survived the middle of the day. To be under a canopy was to be safe. This verse takes that association and puts a mountain where the cloth would be.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the mountain's shape overhead is built on the root for shade, and in Arabic that root carries relief and welcome rather than darkness or menace. The Quran uses that word for a thing they expected to fall on them. It is the same noun a family would use for the awning they ate their meal beneath.
studies.theologicalSignificance: These two verses set an image against a practice. The instruction under the mountain is to hold what was given with strength, and to remember what is in it. That is exactly what the generation in the verse before failed to do, even while studying it. And the reward named is for those who put things right. So the holding described is not private ownership of a text. It is work done with it.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same raising of the mountain and the same instruction to hold firmly and remember.
Contains the identical instruction given with the tablets, to take what was given with strength.
Mentions the mountain raised over them again, alongside other undertakings taken from them.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing you know from your religion and have never actually put to work. Not a new practice, something you already hold. Use it once this week on a real decision, and see what it does. This verse joins holding to putting right, and a conviction never applied to anything is not yet being held.
studies.explainEasier: Some people hold on to the book and keep up their prayer. God says He will not waste what they have earned. He also reminds them of the day the mountain was raised over their heads. They were told to hold on tight to what they had been given.

studies.title: Am I Not Your Lord
studies.meaning: The descendants are brought out and made to bear witness about themselves, and one question is put to them. Early scholars divide over what is being described. Some read an actual gathering of every human being before they entered the world; others read the nature placed in each person at their making. The tradition keeps both. The answer given is a single Arabic particle used only to contradict a negative, so it does not mean agreement. It denies the denial. And the purpose stated is to close off one excuse.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, and this verse has been among the most discussed in the Quran since the earliest days. Early scholars set out their difference over it plainly, and neither side treats the other as odd. No occasion is reported for it. The verse arrives where the chapter turns from the stories of single peoples to a word about every human being, and what follows carries that widening on.

keyTerms.note: A particle Arabic uses only to contradict a negative question. Had they answered with the ordinary word for yes, grammarians note, it would have agreed with the negation rather than denying it.
The verb for causing someone to bear witness, with themselves as the object of the testimony. They are not asked to observe something else but to give evidence about their own condition.

The excuse ruled out is not ignorance but heedlessness, which is the state of having something available and not attending to it. The Quran uses this word throughout the chapter for the same condition.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Testimony was the backbone of Arabian dispute. Nothing was written down, so an agreement was made binding by witnesses who could be produced years later. The strongest position in any quarrel was to have been there when the words were said. A man who could say I heard it settled the matter. This verse puts every human being in that position about themselves.
studies.didYouKnow: The single word used to answer the question is a particle with no English match. Arabic separates agreeing with a negative question from denying it, and this word does only the second. Grammarians cite this verse as the standard example. Answering with the ordinary word for yes would have conceded that He is not their Lord.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Either reading of the event lands in the same place. Something is put in every human being that comes before argument. The excuse being closed off is not a lack of news. It is the failure to attend to what was already there, which moves the whole question from proof to attention. The witness is also self-given, so nobody is held to a promise somebody else made for them.

crossReferences.why: Describes an original disposition on which people were made, which many read alongside this.
The next verse, which closes off the second excuse, that one's forebears associated others with God.
Recalls a covenant taken with the children of Adam, in the other place they are addressed that way.

studies.applyIt: Ask yourself when you last simply attended to being alive, with no task attached. Ten seconds at a window counts. The excuse this verse closes off is inattention rather than ignorance, so the remedy is not more information. It is a few minutes of the kind of noticing that nothing in an ordinary day asks of you.
studies.explainEasier: Before people were born, God asked them all a question. He asked if He was their Lord, and they said yes. Because of that, no one can say on the last day that they never knew.

studies.title: What Our Fathers Did
studies.meaning: A second excuse is closed, and the chapter has already heard it several times. Our forebears set up partners with God, and we only came after them. The plea that follows is almost word for word a plea made earlier in this chapter, where a prophet spoke for his own people. The difference is instructive. He said the foolish among us, and he asked. This one says the falsifiers, and it pleads descent. The closing line names what all of it is for, and the purpose given is a returning.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, and this was the standing Quraysh defence. Their religion came with their lineage, so it could not be examined without insulting the men who had handed it down. That is why the Quran takes the argument up again and again, from several angles. No particular occasion is reported for these verses. They complete the widening begun just before, which moved from particular communities to every human being.

keyTerms.note: From the root for what has no substance behind it. Calling the forebears by this name inside the excuse is what makes the plea awkward, since it concedes the point while asking not to be held to it.
The same word used in the verse before for the descendants brought out to testify. The excuse uses the very term the testimony was taken from, which is why it cannot succeed on its own ground.

From the root for a joint between bones and for separating things at their natural divisions. Signs articulated this way are given piece by piece, which is what makes each one a separate occasion to reconsider.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In Arabia a man could not disown his ancestors' religion without disowning them, and the poets treated that as the deepest disgrace available. Family lines were recited at every gathering, and a father's name was carried for life. So the excuse here is not laziness. It names a real cost. What the Quran refuses is the next step, that the cost removes the question; it only makes the question expensive.
studies.didYouKnow: The plea here is nearly identical in wording to one made earlier in this chapter by a prophet speaking up for his community after they made a calf. That one was answered with the widest statement of mercy in the Book. This one is ruled out in advance. The difference in the Arabic is which pronoun the speaker uses about the offenders.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two excuses are closed in two verses, and between them they cover most of what people actually say. The first was that nobody told us. The second is that we were handed this. Neither is called false as a description of circumstances. What is denied is that either one transfers the answer. Every person is left holding a question they did not choose to be asked and cannot pass on.

crossReferences.why: The prophet's plea this excuse echoes, made with himself included among the people at fault.
Puts the same appeal to forebears and asks what if they understood nothing and were unguided.
Records the argument at length, that they found their fathers on a way and are following their traces.

studies.applyIt: Name one thing you believe mainly because it came with your family. It may well be true. Spend twenty minutes finding out why it is held, from someone who can explain it rather than merely assert it. You are not testing your parents. You are turning an inheritance into something you can answer for.
studies.explainEasier: People could not say that their grandparents had worshipped other gods. They could not say they were only following along. The verse says that excuse will not work on the last day. God explains His signs clearly so that people will come back to Him.

studies.title: He Slipped Out Of Them
studies.meaning: The instruction is to recite an account, and the man in it is never named. What he was given is stated plainly: Our signs. The verb for what he did with them is the one used of a snake leaving its skin and of a month slipping away, so the signs are pictured as something he was inside and came out of. Then the usual order reverses. Instead of a person chasing an adversary, the adversary follows him. Early scholars read that as the result of the stripping rather than its cause.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca. Early scholars offer several names for the man, some from Israelite tradition and some from Arabia itself, and they record them as reports without settling on any. The Quran holds the name back on purpose, as it holds back the town by the sea and the tree in the Garden. No particular occasion is reported. The next verse supplies the likeness that explains him.

keyTerms.gloss: so he slipped out of them
keyTerms.note: The verb for a skin being stripped from a body and for a snake leaving its own. The Quran also uses it of the sacred months passing away, so it covers both a shedding and a season sliding by.
The order is reversed from what one might expect. The adversary follows the man rather than the man following him, which places the departure first and the pursuit as what it made possible.
From the root used in this chapter for the vow made in the Garden, where the same word described being led off course. The man ends in the category the whole chapter opened by describing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Snakes were common, and their shed skins were a familiar sight in rocky country. Each one was the intact shape of an animal no longer in it. The image was proverbial, and Arabs used the word for anything that had left the form it once filled. Applied to a man and his knowledge, it says what he knew is still there in outline. He is simply not inside it.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here turns up elsewhere in the Quran for the passing of the sacred months. So one word covers a skin shed and a season slipping by, and both senses are gradual. Nothing in the wording suggests a sudden break. That is part of why early scholars describe the man's condition as a departure rather than a decision.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Knowledge is presented as somewhere a person can be inside and can leave, which makes it a place rather than a thing owned. That is an uncomfortable claim, because having been given the signs turns out not to be a state anyone holds for good. The reversal that follows is just as exact: the pursuit comes after the departure. What is described is not a person overcome, but a person who stepped out of cover.

crossReferences.why: The next verse, which gives the likeness explaining what he did and why he could not be raised.
Uses the same verb for the sacred months slipping away, showing its ordinary sense of gradual passing.
Gives a matching image of carrying a book without bearing it, using an animal loaded with volumes.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you once knew well and have quietly stopped living inside: a practice you understood, a subject you cared about, a way you used to treat people. Nothing dramatic happened; you simply came out of it. Step back in for one hour this week. Skins are easier to re-enter than the image suggests.
studies.explainEasier: God gave one man clear signs. Then the man slipped out of them, like a snake leaving its skin. Once he was outside them, Satan came after him. He ended up going the wrong way.

studies.title: It Pants Either Way
studies.meaning: The raising was available and did not happen, and the reason comes in a verb built from the root for permanence. He leaned towards the earth as though he meant to stay in it forever. Then the desire he followed, named with a word whose root means falling. The likeness is exact. A dog pants when it is driven and pants when it is left alone, so the panting comes from inside rather than from what is happening around it. Early scholars dwell on that. It is not a response to pressure but a condition pressure does not alter.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca. The Quran gives this likeness at the end of a long chapter about communities who were shown things and did not change, and it applies the picture to that whole pattern rather than to one man. No particular occasion is reported for this verse. It closes with an instruction to tell the account so that people may think, which is the chapter handing its material to the reader.

keyTerms.note: Built from the root for permanence and eternal remaining. The verb describes leaning towards something as though intending never to leave it, which is why the object of the leaning being the earth is the whole point.

From a root meaning to fall or descend. Arabic names desire with the vocabulary of falling, so the word already contains a direction, and the Quran uses it consistently for wanting that pulls downward.

The specific verb for a dog's open-mouthed breathing. Early scholars note that other animals pant only when driven or exhausted, so naming an animal that pants either way is what makes the likeness work.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Dogs in Arabia were working animals, kept for herding and hunting rather than company, and everyone had watched them. The detail the likeness turns on is one any child there would have noticed without being told. The dog runs and pants. Then it lies in the shade and pants. Nothing in the animal's state tracks what is happening to it, and that is exactly the point.
studies.didYouKnow: The comparison works on a fact of animal behaviour, not on a moral about dogs, and early scholars are explicit about that. It turns on the panting happening either way, under effort and at rest alike. So it names a restlessness that circumstances neither cause nor relieve. Change the animal and the image stops working.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Here is a state in which nothing that happens makes any difference, and it is the most serious condition the chapter has named. Signs were given and then left behind. A raising was possible and was refused. The likeness explains why more evidence would change nothing, since the restlessness it describes is not produced by anything outside. Even so, the closing instruction is to keep telling the account, which leaves the door where the chapter has kept it all along.

crossReferences.why: The verse before, which gives the man this likeness explains and the signs he came out of.
Describes one who takes his own desire as his god, with hearing and heart sealed over.
Asks about the same figure and compares such people to cattle, or further astray than cattle.

studies.applyIt: Notice whether your restlessness actually tracks your circumstances, and test it on a good day rather than a bad one. If the same background hum is there when nothing is wrong, the hum is not about the situation, and no change in the situation will settle it. That is worth knowing before you rearrange anything.
studies.explainEasier: God could have lifted this man up with the signs he was given. Instead he stayed low and followed what he wanted. The verse says he is like a dog that pants whether you chase it or leave it alone.

studies.title: An Evil Likeness
studies.meaning: A verdict lands on the picture just given, and then a clause moves the damage somewhere unexpected: it was their own selves they were wronging. Nothing is said about harm done to anyone else. What comes next states the matter as a pair, and the Arabic is careful. Whom God guides, he is the guided one, with the definite article, so guidance does not simply arrive; it makes the person who he is. Whom He leaves to stray, those are the losers, and the word is commercial again.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca. These verses close the passage about the man who came out of the signs and the likeness of the dog. No particular occasion is reported for them. They work as a summary of everything the chapter has shown across its stories, which is why the language turns from story to statement at exactly this point. The chapter's final section begins just after.

keyTerms.note: A construction of blame in Arabic, used to condemn something by naming its category. The verdict falls on the likeness rather than on individuals, which keeps the assessment attached to a pattern of conduct.
The object is placed before its verb, which in Arabic gives it emphasis. The sentence therefore says it was themselves, and nobody else, that they were wronging all along.
Definite, so not a guided person but the guided one. The construction makes guidance identify the person rather than describe a state they happen to be in at a given moment.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Likenesses were how Arabs argued. A proverb settled a quarrel better than reasoning did, and a good image entered the language and was quoted for years. Poets fought to make them. So closing a comparison by calling it an evil likeness passed judgement in the form the crowd took most seriously. It used their own words of praise and blame against the thing described.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran puts the word for their own selves before its verb here, a word order Arabic keeps for emphasis. The effect is to insist on the target: the wrongdoing had one, and it was the people doing it. The same construction turns up across the Book wherever this point is made.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A hard pairing is set down side by side and neither half is softened. Guidance is credited entirely to God. Loss is described as self-inflicted. The chapter used the same uneven pairing much earlier, for a rescue and a ruin. Holding both at once is uncomfortable, and the Quran does not resolve it here. You are left with responsibility for the loss and no claim on the guidance.

crossReferences.why: States plainly that God does not wrong people at all, but that people wrong themselves.
Says whoever is guided is guided for his own soul, and whoever strays does so against it.
Uses the same pair of clauses about guiding and leaving to stray, in almost identical wording.

studies.applyIt: Take one habit you know is not good for you and describe its cost only in terms of yourself. Not what it does to your family, not what people think. Just the cost to you. Most people find that harder than the other version and more accurate, and it removes the negotiation about whether anyone else really minds.
studies.explainEasier: The verse says it is a bad example when people turn away from God's signs. They are not hurting anyone but themselves. Whoever God guides is on the right path, and whoever He lets go astray has lost.

studies.title: Hearts That Do Not Understand
studies.meaning: Three faculties are listed, and each one is present and unused. They have hearts they do not understand with, eyes they do not see with, ears they do not hear with. The grammar is careful: nothing is missing. What is denied is the use of an instrument that is there. Then the comparison, made twice. First they are like grazing animals, and then it corrects itself to say they are further off the road. The closing word is this chapter's recurring one for inattention.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca. The Quran keeps describing refusal as a failure of reception rather than of information, and this is the fullest statement of that in the chapter. No particular occasion is reported for the verse. It comes near the end, by which point every kind of sign has been described being given and refused. The verse supplies the explanation the stories had been implying.

keyTerms.note: A verb for scattering seed and for bringing creatures out in numbers. It names propagation rather than an act of making, which is why the verse reads as a description of a population rather than of individuals.

From a root meaning to grasp the inner sense of a thing rather than merely to know it. The heart is named as the organ of that grasping, which is the Quran's steady position on where understanding happens.
The word for herd animals kept for milk and meat, not for wild beasts. The comparison names creatures that eat, move and do not consider, which is the specific quality the likeness is reaching for.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Livestock were the measure of everything in Arabia, and people watched them closely all day. A herd follows grass, drinks, lies down, and follows grass again. It does that whether the season is good or the tribe is at war. Nobody thought them stupid. They were creatures fully taken up by whatever stood in front of them, which is exactly what the comparison uses.
studies.didYouKnow: The comparison is made and then immediately revised. They are like grazing animals. Then a particle of correction says: rather, they are further astray. Arabic uses that word to withdraw a statement and put a stronger one in its place. So the verse finds its own comparison too weak, halfway through the sentence.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Faculties are described as given for a purpose, and they are measured by whether the purpose is served. Having the instrument counts for nothing on its own. That explains the whole chapter's account of signs that were seen and changed nothing. The correction added to the comparison matters too. An animal fully taken up by what is in front of it is doing what it was made for. A human being doing the same is not.

crossReferences.why: States the same point directly, that it is not the eyes that go blind but the hearts in the chests.
Makes the same comparison to cattle and the same correction, that they are further astray.
Later in this chapter, the mirror image: objects that lack the faculties these people possess.

studies.applyIt: Pick one faculty and use it properly for ten minutes today. Look at something without photographing it. Listen to someone without getting an answer ready. Read a page without checking anything. The complaint here is not about equipment, and the remedy is at exactly this scale, which is why it is available on a Tuesday.
studies.explainEasier: Some people have hearts but do not understand with them. They have eyes but do not really see, and ears but do not really hear. The verse says they are like farm animals, or even more lost.

studies.title: Call Him By His Names
studies.meaning: Two statements with an instruction between them. The names belong to God, they are called the most beautiful, and what you are asked to do with them is call on Him by them. Early scholars note that the verse neither lists them nor fixes their number. Then a second instruction: leave alone the people who twist the names. That is unusually restrained. No argument is prescribed, only withdrawal, and the outcome is left where it belongs.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca. Early scholars connect this verse with the practice of deriving names for local gods from the divine name itself, which is what the word for distortion is taken to describe. The chapter has spent much of its length on invented religion. Here the same problem is addressed at the level of vocabulary rather than of ritual.

keyTerms.note: A superlative in the feminine, from a root for beauty and for what is good. It qualifies the names as a set, so the beauty is claimed for the whole vocabulary rather than for any single term in it.
The verb covers both calling someone by a name and calling on them for help. The verse uses both senses at once, so naming and asking become a single action rather than two separate ones.
From a root for turning aside, related to the word for a grave niche cut off to one side. It describes bending a name away from its proper direction rather than denying it outright.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Names carried power in Arabia. A person's name announced lineage and often duty, oaths were sworn by names, and poets attacked enemies by twisting theirs. Gods were addressed with strings of titles, and knowing the right form of address was thought to affect whether an appeal was heard. So advice about which names to use was practical, not a matter of style.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran never gives a closed list of these names. The phrase occurs four times, always in the same form. The familiar lists compiled later were drawn from across the whole text by scholars, and no single passage presents them together. The number most often quoted comes from a report rather than from the Quran.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Knowledge of God is given here as words for use, not as information to hold. The instruction is to call, which makes the names tools of connection rather than items of doctrine. The handling of opponents is notably light. Distortion is named as a real fault and then left alone, with no correction demanded. The matter is placed between them and God, not in an argument to be won.

crossReferences.why: Runs a long sequence of the names, closing with the same phrase used here.
Says either name may be used in calling, since the beautiful names belong to Him.
States the same phrase as a single sentence about the one worthy of worship.

studies.applyIt: Pick one of the divine names you rarely think about, and use it once a day this week when you ask for something. Choose it to fit what you are actually asking for. The verse joins naming to asking. Most people default to two or three names, and the difference another one makes is worth noticing.
studies.explainEasier: The most beautiful names belong to God, so call on Him using them. Leave alone the people who twist His names. They will get back what they have earned.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: Drawn On By Degrees
studies.meaning: Four short verses, each doing a different job. The first names a community that guides by truth, using the very words applied earlier in this chapter to one particular people. The second describes a drawing on step by step, from a direction they never notice, which is what the verb literally means. The third adds a lengthening of the rope. Then the turn to the audience: have they not thought about it, since the man they are dismissing is their own companion.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca. The Quraysh explanation for the recitation was that the man producing it was possessed, which was the standard account of anyone who spoke in an unusual register. The answer here reminds them that they had known him all his life, which is an argument from familiarity rather than from evidence. No particular occasion is reported for these verses.

keyTerms.note: Built from the word for a step or rung. It describes bringing someone down a stair so gradually that no single step registers, which is why the verse adds that they will not know the direction it comes from.
From a root for extension in time, related to the word for a long stretch of days. It names giving more rope rather than withholding a consequence, and its object is duration.
The ordinary word for someone you keep company with. The Quran uses it of the Prophet when addressing people who had known him for decades, so the term itself is the argument being made.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A tethered animal given more rope grazes further out and never notices the change. The herdsman lets it out a hand's breadth at a time, and Arabs did this on purpose with animals they wanted to keep calm. The words used in both of these verses belong to that practice. A listener who had let out a rope himself heard a process rather than a threat.
studies.didYouKnow: The wording of the first of these four verses matches a sentence used earlier in this chapter. That earlier one was about one particular community. Here the same words are applied to those God created, with no people named at all. The Quran repeats the phrase without variation, so one description does duty for a single group and for humanity.
studies.theologicalSignificance: This is a danger with no unpleasant symptoms. Being drawn on by degrees and being given length both feel like things going well, which removes the usual signal that something needs attention. Set against that, the community named at the start is defined by two activities. They guide and they do justice. Both are outward and can be checked, which is the Quran's usual answer to the problem of an unreliable inner sense.

crossReferences.why: Uses the identical wording earlier in this chapter, applied to a community among the people of Moses.
Repeats the same two verbs together, drawing on by steps and giving length, in the same order.
Describes doors of everything opened until they rejoiced, and then a sudden seizure.

studies.applyIt: Ask what has been going quietly well for you for a long time, and whether you have looked at it lately. Not out of superstition. Simply because nothing about a comfortable stretch prompts anyone to look. Pick one such area and give it an hour of honest attention this week.
studies.explainEasier: One group of people guides others by the truth and is fair. Those who turn down God's messages get led along slowly, step by step, without noticing. The verse also says the man warning them is not mad.

studies.title: Look Into The Dominion
studies.meaning: The question is an invitation to look. The word for what they are to look into is an intensified form of the ordinary noun for kingship, so it names the deep structure of things rather than their surface. Two objects are joined: that dominion, and whatever God has created of anything, which widens the invitation to take in everything. Then a clause that changes register completely. It asks whether their own term may have drawn near. An enormous view and a personal deadline arrive in one sentence.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca. The Quran's argument in these years leaned heavily on observation, because the audience already accepted a creator and disputed everything that followed from Him. Asking them to look was not a demand for faith. It was a request that they finish an inference they had already begun. No particular occasion is reported. The second verse closes the passage on those left in their overstepping.

keyTerms.note: An intensified form of the ordinary word for kingship, with an ending that adds weight and scope. It names the whole ordering behind what appears, which is why the verb attached to it is one of looking into rather than at.
The particle of possibility again, holding the clause short of a claim. What is raised is not that the term is near but that it may be, which is the only honest form such a statement can take.
A verb for moving without direction, used of someone confused in open country. It differs from the ordinary word for straying by naming the disorientation rather than the wrong road.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Night travel made the sky an instrument, not a view. A guide read the stars for direction and season, and the whole calendar of markets, pilgrimage and rain followed from what was overhead. Looking up was work. The invitation here asks people who already watched the sky every night to look into it once, which is a different verb and a different act.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the dominion here is not the ordinary Arabic term for a kingdom. It carries an intensifying ending that Arabic adds to a small number of nouns to give them scope and grandeur. The Quran uses this form only a few times. Each time it means what lies behind the visible order, not any rule exercised within it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two scales are set in one sentence, and the join is the point. An invitation to consider everything that exists comes first, and a question about how much time you have left comes straight after. Neither works on its own. The vast view without the deadline becomes a pastime; the deadline without the view becomes fear. Held together, they make the kind of attention this chapter has been asking for throughout.

crossReferences.why: Describes Abraham being shown the same deep dominion, using the identical unusual word for it.
Joins looking at the heavens and the earth with remembrance, and calls the result reflection.
Instructs looking at what is in the heavens and the earth, while noting that signs do not suffice alone.

studies.applyIt: Go outside once this week and look up for two minutes with the second question in mind rather than the first. Not how large is this, but how much time do I have. Most people do one or the other. This verse puts them in a single sentence, and holding both for two minutes is the exercise.
studies.explainEasier: The verse asks people to look hard at the sky and the earth and everything God has made. It also asks them to think that their own time may be close. Anyone God leaves to wander has no guide.

studies.title: When Will It Anchor
studies.meaning: They ask when the Hour will drop anchor, using a word for ships, and the answer comes twice in one verse with almost the same wording. Its knowledge is with my Lord. Its knowledge is with God. Between the two comes a description rather than a date: it weighs heavily on the heavens and the earth, and it will come only suddenly. Early scholars differ over the word describing how they ask. Some read it as though he were well informed about it; others as though he were eager for it.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca. The Quraysh asked for a date again and again, and the demand worked as a challenge rather than a question, since an unanswered question could be shown off as a failure. No particular occasion is reported for this verse. The Quran's answer stayed the same throughout those years: it refused the date and insisted on the event. This is the fullest version of that refusal.

keyTerms.note: From a root for a ship coming to rest and for a mountain standing firm. The question asks when the Hour will drop anchor, which pictures it as something already at sea and approaching.
The ordinary verb for being heavy. Applied to the heavens and the earth it says the Hour presses on the whole created order, which is a statement about its magnitude rather than about its timing.
A rare adjective. Early scholars read it as one who has enquired until he knows, or as one who is persistently keen, and both senses fit the sentence, which is why the tradition records the range.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meccan merchants knew ships from the Red Sea ports, even if they rarely sailed themselves. A ship's arrival could not be predicted; you knew it was coming and not which day. The whole trading season turned on waiting for it. The word the questioners use belongs to that world. It already grants the arrival and asks only about the day.
studies.didYouKnow: The same answer is given twice inside one verse, with only the divine name changing. First its knowledge is with my Lord, then its knowledge is with God. The Quran rarely repeats a clause so closely in one verse. Early scholars read the repetition as closing the question rather than as emphasis for its own sake.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The refusal to give a date is not a gap in the message; it is part of it. A known date would turn preparation into scheduling, and the Quran removes that option while insisting the event is real and heavy. What replaces the date is chosen with care. Suddenness is the one feature with practical weight, and it is the only thing about the timing that changes how you live now.

crossReferences.why: Lists knowledge of the Hour among the things held with God alone, beside four other matters.
Records the same question and the same answer, that its knowledge is with God alone.
Asks about its anchoring in the same words and says the messenger is only a warner for whoever fears it.

studies.applyIt: Notice how much of your planning assumes a length of life nobody has promised you. This is not a reason to plan less; the verse does not say that. It is a reason to check whether anything important in your life is waiting for a stage that has no guaranteed arrival. Move one such thing forward this month.
studies.explainEasier: People kept asking when the last hour would come. The answer was that only God knows. It will be heavy for the sky and the earth. It will arrive all of a sudden.

studies.title: I Hold No Power
studies.meaning: He is told to say something that takes a claim away rather than making one. I hold no benefit or harm for myself, except what God wills. Then an argument startling for how ordinary it is: if I knew the unseen I would have gathered much good, and no harm would have touched me. A man with such knowledge would visibly prosper, and his own life is offered as proof that he has none. The role is then given in two words, a warner and a bearer of good news.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca. The demands made of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) included predictions, dates and wonders, and the Quran's answers through these years narrow rather than widen the claims made for him. No particular occasion is reported for this verse. It comes straight after the refusal to name a date, and it explains why that refusal was not an evasion.

keyTerms.note: The verb for owning and having disposal over something. The denial is about capacity rather than willingness, and its object is his own benefit and harm, which is the narrowest possible scope.

A form meaning to seek to increase one's share of something. The word is entirely ordinary and commercial, which is what makes the argument work: anyone with such knowledge would have done exactly this.
Two intensive forms naming the whole of the role. Both are about delivering information in advance, one unwelcome and one welcome, and neither implies any power over what is delivered.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabia had men who claimed exactly what is denied here. Soothsayers were consulted before journeys and marriages, and they were paid for it. A reputation for foreknowledge made a man rich, and everyone knew what such a life looked like. The argument here invites the audience to set that picture beside the man in front of them, which they could check without leaving the city.
studies.didYouKnow: The reasoning here is an argument from plain self-interest, put in the first person about the Prophet himself. Anyone who knew the unseen would have used it to gain more and dodge harm. A life without those gains is offered as proof that he has no such knowledge. The Quran rarely argues this way, and here it does so about its own messenger.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A firm boundary is set around what a messenger is. He is not a source of benefit or protection, and that holds for other people and for himself. The exception ties whatever he does have to God's will, not to his standing. So the message is the whole of what he brings. That is why the Quran can attach so much to following him, and nothing at all to petitioning him.

crossReferences.why: Has him say he holds no harm or right guidance for anyone, and that none could protect him.
Denies knowledge of the unseen and possession of treasuries, and denies being an angel.
Applies the same disclaimer to himself before answering a question about the appointed term.

studies.applyIt: Notice where you are quietly acting as though you knew how something will turn out. The investment, the conversation you are avoiding, the person you have decided will not change. You do not know. Say that plainly about one of them today, and see what becomes possible once the assumed knowledge is set down.
studies.explainEasier: He was told to say that he had no power to help or hurt even himself, unless God wills it. If he knew what was coming, he would have gained a lot. He would have kept all harm away.

studies.title: That He Might Find Rest
studies.meaning: The purpose named for the pair is stillness. The verb comes from the root for dwelling and coming to rest, the same one used earlier in this chapter for settling in the Garden. Companionship is described by the quiet it produces rather than by anything it achieves. Then a pregnancy told in three short movements: a light burden, carried on with, and then heaviness. At that point they call, and the call is a promise. If You give us a sound child, we will be among the thankful.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca. Early scholars divide over this passage, some reading it of the first human pair and others of husbands and wives generally. Both readings are old. Those who read it of the first pair lean on reports the scholars themselves trace to Israelite tradition, and Ibn Kathir treats those with caution. The general reading takes the singular as covering every couple.

keyTerms.note: From the root for stillness and dwelling, the same one behind the word for tranquillity. The purpose named is not company or offspring but the settling of a restlessness, which is a specific claim.

The word for burden covers both a load and a pregnancy. Calling it light names the early stage precisely, when it is real and barely felt, which the following verb about carrying on with it completes.
The verb for becoming weighty, and the exact opposite of the adjective used a clause earlier. The Arabic marks the whole passage of a pregnancy by moving from one word to its antonym.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Childbirth in the Arabia of that day was a real danger, and everyone knew it. Women died, and babies died, and a family counted its living children rather than its births. The prayer here comes at the point where a pregnancy can no longer be hidden.
