It was the plain answer of people who had nothing else to turn to, and every listener knew it as the prayer of their own home.
studies.didYouKnow: The Arabic tracks a pregnancy by moving from one adjective to its opposite. It is first a light burden. Then the verb says she became heavy, built from the antonym of that first word. Two words separated by a single clause carry the whole passage of time, with no months or stages named at all.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The purpose given for marriage is rest rather than work, which is unusual in a holy book and kind towards ordinary life. Then a couple is shown praying at a weak moment and making a promise. The verses that follow describe the promise not being kept. That sequence is what the Quran keeps its eye on, and it matters more than the question of who the couple were.

crossReferences.why: Names the same purpose using the same root, and adds affection and mercy placed between them.
The next verse, which reports what was done once the prayer had been answered.
Describes a pregnancy and its hardship, ending in a prayer of thanks rather than a promise.

studies.applyIt: If you are married, ask whether your household is a place either of you actually rests. Not whether it functions. Rest is the word this verse uses, and it is easy to run a working household in which nobody has been still for a year. Change one thing this week that makes the evening quieter rather than more productive.
studies.explainEasier: God made people from one soul. He made a partner from it, so that each could find rest with the other. When the wife grows heavy with child, they both pray for a healthy baby. They promise to be thankful.

studies.title: Partners In What Was Given
studies.meaning: The gift arrives, and partners are assigned in it. That is the precise wrong being named: not partners in general, but partners in the very thing just granted. Early scholars divide over who is described, some reading the first human pair and others parents in general, and those taking the first reading lean on reports traced to Israelite tradition. Then the verses shift to the plural and argue the case. These are things that create nothing and are themselves created, and they cannot help anyone, including themselves.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca. Arabs commonly tied a newborn's safe arrival to a shrine, a holy figure, or a vow made at a particular place, and names were given that recorded the debt. The Quran addresses that practice without naming anyone, and the argument that follows is general rather than local. No particular occasion is reported for these verses. The plural forms widen the address beyond any one couple.

keyTerms.note: From a root for sharing a property or a herd. What is described is the assigning of a share in something to someone who had no part in producing it, which is why the verse adds the phrase in what He gave them.

A verb of height used in the Quran to place God beyond a description just mentioned. It closes the sentence by stating a distance rather than by refuting the claim, which is the Book's usual move here.
A passive clause set immediately after an active one. The Arabic puts making and being made in the same breath, so the argument is finished by grammar before any reasoning is added to it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Vows tied to childbirth were ordinary across Arabia. A woman who conceived after long waiting might promise a gift at a shrine, or give the child a name that honoured whatever was worshipped there. The whole family saw it as a debt properly paid, and nothing about it felt like a betrayal. That very ordinariness is the state these verses speak into.
studies.didYouKnow: The passage begins in the dual, describing two people, and then moves to the plural for the argument that follows. Early scholars note the shift and divide over what it shows. Some read it as a move from one couple to their descendants. Others read it as a sign that the general sense was meant from the start. Both readings are kept.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The wrong identified here is very specific: a share is assigned in the exact thing that was given. That is a failure of accounting rather than of belief, and it can happen to people who would name God correctly if asked. The argument that follows is just as practical. It tests candidates by what they can do, not by what they are, and it finds they cannot even help themselves.

crossReferences.why: Describes turning to God in distress and then assigning a share to others once relief arrives.
Uses the same argument, that they create nothing and are themselves created, and hold no power.
Shows a person calling on his Lord in distress and then setting up rivals once favoured.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you asked for and received. Now notice who or what gets the credit in the story you tell about it: your timing, a contact, good luck, one person's help. Some of that credit is accurate. Just check whether any of it was quietly moved off the original account, and move it back.
studies.explainEasier: When the healthy baby comes, some parents give part of the credit to something other than God. The verse asks how that can be. Those other things made nothing. They were made themselves, and they cannot even help themselves.

studies.title: It Is The Same Either Way
studies.meaning: Both verses turn on the verb for calling. If you call them to guidance they will not follow, and then a flat statement: it makes no difference whether you call them or keep silent. The second gives the reason, and it is the sharpest sentence in the passage. Those you call upon are servants like yourselves. Then the invitation, put as a test anyone can run. Call them, and let them answer you, if what you say is true.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, addressed to a city whose whole religious economy ran on appeals made at a sanctuary. The Quran's argument is not that the appeals are wrong in principle. It is that those addressed are of the same order as the people addressing them. No particular occasion is reported. These verses close the chapter's argument before its final instructions, and they are cast as a challenge rather than a claim.

keyTerms.note: The same verb used throughout the Quran for supplication. Using it both for calling people to guidance and for calling upon objects lets these two verses turn on one word held in two senses.

The participle for one who says nothing. Its use here is stark, since the verse says the outcome is identical whether or not anything is said, which is the strongest way of describing a call that goes nowhere.
Two words that finish the argument. Whatever is being appealed to is placed in the same category as the person appealing, which removes the difference in standing that any appeal requires.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Appeals in Arabia went upward through a chain of standing. You asked a stronger man because he had something you did not, and the whole system of clients and patrons rested on that gap being real. So being told that the party you were appealing to stood exactly where you stood was not a religious objection to that audience. It was a statement that the deal could not work.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran closes this passage by inviting a test anyone can run: call them, and let them answer you. Early scholars note that the Book argues this way often. It offers a check rather than a proof, and the check costs the challenger nothing and can be tried at once.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Prayer is reasoned about here in terms of who is asked, not who is asking. Sincerity, urgency and repetition make no difference. What matters is whether the one called upon stands anywhere above the caller, which is why silence and speech are said to give the same result. The whole weight of prayer falls on who is being addressed, and that is why the Quran spends far more time on that than on technique.

crossReferences.why: Compares such calling to a man stretching his hands to water that will never reach his mouth.
Says they do not hear the call, and could not answer it if they did, and will disown it later.
Gives the positive counterpart, an invitation to call with a promise of an answer attached.

studies.applyIt: Look at where you take your worries first. For most people it is a person, a search bar, or a plan. None of those is wrong. But notice the order, and try putting a short direct prayer at the front of it once this week, before the other steps rather than after they have failed.
studies.explainEasier: If you call these people to the right path, they will not follow. It makes no difference whether you speak or stay quiet. The things they pray to are servants like them. Ask those things to answer, and see.

studies.title: Feet To Walk With
studies.meaning: Four questions in a row, each naming a faculty and the action it exists for. Feet to walk with, hands to grip with, eyes to see with, ears to hear with. The list mirrors one given a few verses earlier, where human beings were described as having exactly these and not using them. Here the objects lack them altogether. Then the closing challenge, spoken with striking confidence: call your partners, then scheme against me and grant me no respite.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, and the challenge at the end was made in a city where the speaker had no protection beyond his own clan and stood in real danger. Its force came from being issued by a man with nothing to fall back on. No particular occasion is reported for this verse. It closes the chapter's argument about what may be called upon, just before the statement of where the speaker's own protection lies.

keyTerms.note: A verb for taking hold with force, used of a hand closing on something to move or strike it. It names what hands are for in terms of power rather than of dexterity, which fits a list about capability.

An imperative from the root for laying a plan unseen. Inviting people to plot against you is a challenge that only makes sense if you believe their planning has no reach, which is the point being made.
From the root for looking, and therefore for granting a delay. The same verb appeared at the start of this chapter in a request for respite, and here it is a refusal to be granted any.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The images at Arabian shrines were made things, with a maker's marks on them. People washed them, dressed them, carried them on journeys and repaired them when they cracked. Everyone who honoured one had also, at some point, lifted it. So these questions tell the audience nothing they did not know. They only ask them to say out loud what they had handled with their own hands.
studies.didYouKnow: This list is the exact counterpart of one a few verses earlier in the same chapter. There, people are described as having hearts, eyes and ears and not using them. Here, objects are asked whether they have feet, hands, eyes and ears at all. The Quran sets unused faculties beside absent ones inside one chapter and lets the comparison stand.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The test applied is functional the whole way through. Nothing is said about what these objects are made of or who made them. The questions ask only what they can do, and the list covers the most basic powers any living thing has. Set that beside the earlier picture of human beings who have these faculties and do not use them. A harder question follows, and the chapter leaves you holding it.

crossReferences.why: The counterpart list earlier in this chapter, of faculties possessed and left unused.
Abraham asks the same kind of question, whether they benefit or harm those who serve them.
Offers a similar test, that all of them together could not create a fly or retrieve from it.

studies.applyIt: Take the four faculties named here and check which of yours are actually in service today. Feet that go somewhere worth going, hands that hold something worth holding, eyes and ears used on a person rather than a screen. Pick the one that has been idle longest. Use it once, deliberately, before the day ends.
studies.explainEasier: The verse asks whether these things have feet to walk with, hands to hold with, eyes to see with, or ears to hear with. They do not. So they cannot do anything to anyone.

studies.title: My Protector Is God
studies.meaning: The declaration is personal, and it rests on one specific act: my protector is God, who sent down the Book. The bond is identified by what has been given rather than by any general claim, and it widens at once, saying He takes charge of the righteous. Then the contrast, given twice with a small variation. Those you call besides Him cannot help you and cannot help themselves. You may call them to guidance and they do not hear, and you see them looking at you and not seeing.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca. The word used here for a protector is the same one this chapter opened with, where it appeared in a warning against taking such figures besides God. So the argument closes by returning to the term it began with, and then naming the one who may hold it. No particular occasion is reported for these verses. They stand just before the chapter's final instructions.

keyTerms.note: The singular of the word this chapter opened by warning against taking besides God. The whole chapter runs between a prohibition of false patrons and this declaration of the true one.
The verb from the same root, so the sentence uses one root twice: He is my patron, and He acts as patron to the righteous. Protection is described as something exercised rather than merely held.
The ordinary verb for directing the eyes at something, set immediately against a denial of seeing. Arabic can hold both, since one word names the direction of a gaze and the other its result.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A man's patron was the most important fact about him. Protection was declared in public, and it decided whether he could travel, trade, or expect redress if he was harmed. When a patron withdrew it, the man was exposed overnight. The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) lived through exactly that change in Mecca, so the declaration here was made by someone who knew what the word cost.
studies.didYouKnow: The last image describes carved figures with eyes turned towards the viewer, looking and not seeing. Craftsmen shaped and painted them precisely so the gaze would meet a worshipper's, which is what makes the description so exact. The verse does not deny the appearance. It grants the appearance and denies what everyone assumed stood behind it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Protection here is measured by power, not by devotion. The test is whether the one you appeal to can act, and it is applied even to their own case: those who cannot help themselves cannot help anyone. Against that stands a protector known by something already delivered. So the claim rests on an act that has taken place, not on a promise about what is to come.

crossReferences.why: Opens this chapter by warning against following patrons besides Him, using the same word.
Names God as the patron of those who believe, bringing them out of darkness into light.
Asks whether they have taken protectors besides Him, when God is the protector who gives life.

studies.applyIt: Write down who you would call first if something serious went wrong tonight. That list is real and worth having. Then ask what each name on it can actually do, and where their capacity ends. Naming the limit does not diminish anyone. It just makes visible the gap this verse is describing.
studies.explainEasier: The verse says God is the one who protects, because He is the one who sent down the book. The things people pray to instead cannot help them at all. They seem to look at you, but they see nothing.

studies.title: Take What Comes Easily
studies.meaning: Three instructions arrive in one line, and the first is the most discussed. The word can mean pardon, or what is spare and easily given, so early scholars read it as accepting what people readily offer rather than pressing them, and also as forgiving. Then a warning about provocation, with a practical response: take refuge. Then a description of those aware of God. They remember, and then they see clearly, unlike the ones dragged on without ever stopping.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, at the end of a long chapter. That chapter has run through the ruin of earlier peoples and the arguments of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) with his own city. These closing instructions are addressed to him, about how to carry that argument. Early scholars record several reports about the first of them, and each one turns on how a person handles those who will not listen.

keyTerms.note: The root covers both forgiving and surplus. Early scholars take it here as accepting what people offer without pressing them to their limit, which is why the same word can also mean pardon.
Not the uninformed. The word names people who act without restraint, and older poetry uses it for hot-headedness, so avoiding them means declining a fight rather than avoiding the uneducated.
A sudden jab, the word used of driving an animal forward with a point. It names the suggestion as brief and external rather than as a settled state, which is why the response given is immediate.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arab honour culture required an answer to every provocation. Skilled opponents provoked on purpose, knowing an angry man could be steered into a costly quarrel, and poets baited each other in public for exactly that reason. Turning away read as weakness. So the instruction to decline the exchange was not passive advice there. It cut against the main engine of social standing.
studies.didYouKnow: The order to take refuge is followed in the very next verse by a picture of what taking refuge looks like from the inside. A person remembers, and then sees clearly. Early scholars follow that sequence closely. The passage moves from an outward command to an inward view of it working, which is unusual in the Book.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Provocation is treated as something that happens to a person, not as something they are, and that distinction does a great deal of work. The sudden impulse is described as a jab from outside. What is asked for is not suppression but relocation, taking shelter somewhere. And the contrast at the end is not between good people and bad. It is between those who notice and those who are pulled along without ever stopping.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same instruction with a reason, repelling harm with what is better.
Describes the servants of the Merciful answering the ignorant with peace.
Preserves a supplication for refuge from the promptings of devils.

studies.applyIt: The next time you feel the sharp pull to answer something, name it as a jab rather than as your own opinion. Wait until you have finished one slow breath. The passage puts a specific move in that gap. It does not say the provocation was unreal. It says the response is a place you go rather than a thing you win.
studies.explainEasier: God tells the Prophet to take what people give easily. He is to ask for what is right, and to keep away from rude people. If a bad thought jabs at you, ask God to keep you safe.

studies.title: Listen, And Be Silent
studies.meaning: A demand is reported and refused. When no sign appears, the opponents suggest he should simply have made one up. The reply concedes nothing about his own resources: he follows what is revealed, and he does not compose. Then the text names itself as insight, guidance and mercy. The next verse turns to the listener with two instructions, hearing and silence, and attaches an outcome to them that is left as a hope rather than a promise.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, closing the chapter. The demand for a produced sign runs through the whole Meccan period. Early scholars connect the second verse with how people behaved during recitation, though the reports vary; some tie it to the prayer, others to any occasion of hearing. What the two verses share is a shift from arguing about the Quran to describing how it is to be received.

keyTerms.note: A verb for picking something out and gathering it for yourself. The taunt assumes composition, so the choice of word makes the accusation precise: they are asking him to produce, not to transmit.
The plural of a word for inner sight, formed like an instrument. It names the text as something you see by rather than something you look at, which is why the verse pairs it with guidance.
A verb specifically for stopping your own speech in order to hear. It is added after the command to listen, so attention and silence are named separately and each is asked for on its own.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Poetry was heard, not read. Audiences at the fairs listened with a critical ear and broke in freely, and recitation was public and competitive. A listener's noise was itself a verdict. Reports describe opponents at Mecca urging each other to drown the recitation out with talk and clamour. So telling listeners to fall silent met a real tactic, not a matter of manners.
studies.didYouKnow: This is one of the places where the Quran describes how it should be received. The chapter ends two verses later with a prostration, and it is one of the passages at which readers traditionally bow to the ground while reciting. So the call to listen is followed at once by an instruction the body carries out.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Refusing to make a sign on demand defines prophecy by what it leaves out. Invention is not part of the role, and saying so in public costs him the argument in the short term. Then the proof is moved into the text itself, which is called insight rather than evidence. And the call to listen implies something passes over in the hearing that you cannot get by talking about it later.

crossReferences.why: Records the same demand to alter the Quran and the same refusal to change it.
Lists the specific signs demanded of him and the answer given to them.
Describes what happens to believers when the verses are recited to them.

studies.applyIt: The next time you hear the Quran recited, whether you follow the words or not, stop what you are doing for the length of one passage. Give it nothing but attention: no phone, no half-listening. The verse asks for two separate things, hearing and silence, and most of us have lost the habit of the second.
studies.explainEasier: People asked the Prophet to make up a sign of his own. He said he only follows what God sends him. When the Quran is read out, listen and stay quiet, and mercy may come to you.

studies.title: Within Yourself, Not Aloud
studies.meaning: The instruction has five parts, and four of them are about manner rather than content. Remember your Lord inside yourself, humbly, with awe, below the level of a raised voice, morning and evening. The word for humility here shares a root with a verb used earlier in this chapter, one that named what hardship is meant to produce. So the bearing asked for is the one difficulty produces on its own. The closing words warn against the very condition this chapter has been naming all along.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca. Public devotion at the sanctuary was loud and performed in front of others, and the early Muslims prayed while watched and sometimes under pressure. No particular occasion is reported for this verse. It comes near the very end of the chapter, after every argument has been made, and it turns from what to think to how to hold it. That is how the chapter closes.

keyTerms.note: From a root for smallness and lowering oneself. The same root appeared earlier in this chapter as the purpose hardship serves, so what is asked for here is the posture that difficulty otherwise has to produce.
A noun for a quiet, inward apprehension rather than fright. It is placed beside humility as a pair, so what is asked for is a manner with two components rather than one intensified feeling.
A phrase specifying a level rather than silence. Something is being said, and it is being said under the volume that others would hear, which is a description of privacy rather than of soundlessness.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Worship at the sanctuary was loud and communal. Clans chanted their own formulas as they circled, and the noise was part of the occasion, so a person praying silently would have stood out. The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and the early believers often prayed on the outskirts to avoid trouble. The devotion described here leaves no trace at all. Nobody else can watch it or break it up.
studies.didYouKnow: The two times named are the morning and the evening, the hinges of the day rather than its middle. Arabic marks them with a pair of words that appear together across the Quran. The pairing always names the opening and closing of a stretch of activity. It never points to any particular hour inside it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The instruction is almost entirely about manner, which is unusual for a passage about remembrance. Nothing is specified to say. What is specified is where it happens, in what bearing, at what volume, and when. The effect is to describe something that cannot be performed for an audience. The closing words name inattention as the thing guarded against, and that is the condition this whole chapter has diagnosed.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same instruction earlier in this chapter, to call humbly and in secret, using the same root.
Sets the same middle level of voice, neither loud in prayer nor silent, but a way between.
Names what this produces, hearts settling in the remembrance of God.

studies.applyIt: Take thirty seconds at the start and the end of tomorrow, before the phone and after it goes down, and say something to God under your breath. Not a formula, unless you want one. This verse fixes the manner and leaves the words open, and the two times it names are the two nobody else has a claim on.
studies.explainEasier: God tells people to remember Him quietly, inside themselves. He asks for a low voice, not a loud one. He names two times: the morning and the evening. The verse also warns against being one of the people who forget.

studies.title: They Are Not Too Proud
studies.meaning: The surah ends by describing those who are with your Lord, whom the early scholars identify as the angels. Three things are said of them and the first is a denial. They are not too great for His service, which uses the same verb the surah applied to its very first refusal, at the beginning of the chapter. Then they glorify Him, and then, in a clause with its object placed first for emphasis, to Him they bow down. The whole surah closes on the act the whole surah opened by describing being refused.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Angels were part of the religious landscape the audience already accepted, and some Arabs regarded them as daughters of God or as go-betweens whose favour could be sought. The Quran consistently describes them as servants instead, which is what this closing ayah does. No occasion of revelation is reported. It is the last ayah of the surah and the whole chapter turns on it.

keyTerms.note: The same verb used for the first refusal at the opening of this surah, in the same reflexive form. The chapter's last ayah denies of the angels exactly what its first narrative reported of another.
From a root for swimming or moving freely through something. To glorify in this vocabulary is to declare God clear of every deficiency, so the act is a removal rather than an addition.

keyTerms.gloss: and to Him they bow down
keyTerms.note: The object is placed before its verb, which in Arabic restricts it: to Him and to no one else. The chapter's final word is the same verb refused in its opening narrative.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabs honoured go-betweens and expected them to carry a petition upward. Several of the figures at the sanctuary were understood in something like those terms. Approaching a great person through someone with access was simply how anything got done. The closing ayah describes the highest beings as servants who bow. It does not describe them as agents who speak for others. That removed the whole mechanism the audience relied on.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the first place in the Quran's order where the reciter and the listener bow down. The tradition has treated it that way from the earliest period. The surah opened with a refusal to bow. It ends by prompting the very act it began by describing being withheld. And it does so at the moment the chapter closes.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The surah's structure completes itself in a single sentence. It opened with a command to bow that was refused out of self-importance. It then spent two hundred ayat on communities who refused messengers for the same reason. It ends by describing beings who are not too great for service, and who bow. Nothing is argued in the last ayah. The chapter simply supplies the alternative. It leaves the reader in a position to take it.

crossReferences.why: The refusal this closing ayah answers, at the opening of the same surah, in the same vocabulary.
Describes those with Him as not too proud for His service, glorifying night and day without flagging.
Says all in the heavens and earth bow, and that they fear their Lord above them and do as commanded.

studies.applyIt: Read the surah's first few ayat and this last one together, in one sitting. It takes four minutes. The chapter is built as an arc between a refusal and a bowing, and reading only the ends of it is the quickest way to feel what the two hundred ayat in between are actually for.
studies.explainEasier: The last verse of this chapter talks about those who are with God. They are never too proud to serve him. They praise him, and they bow down to him.
